item.title: Anthropic Files for IPO: $16.3B Revenue, $80.7B Net Loss
item.description: Anthropic, PBC filed its S-1 registration statement with the SEC on October 26, 2026, disclosing the first public financial figures for the Claude AI developer ahead of its planned Nasdaq listing u…
item.content:encoded: Anthropic, PBC filed its S-1 registration statement with the SEC on October 26, 2026, disclosing the first public financial figures for the Claude AI developer ahead of its planned Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT. Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026, up from $1.16 billion in the year-earlier period. Full-year 2025 revenue was $4.6 billion, following $386 million in 2024 and $41 million in 2023. Quarterly revenue climbed from $4.7 billion in Q1 2026 to $11.6 billion in Q2 2026, and Anthropic separately told prospective investors that Q3 revenue reached $16.8 billion. Operating expenses for H1 2026 totaled $17.0 billion, driven by $8.9 billion in compute and infrastructure costs, $3.2 billion in personnel, and $3.2 billion in sales, marketing, and partnerships. Operating income was a loss of $693 million in H1 2026, compared with a $2.1 billion loss in H1 2025, though Q2 2026 produced $974 million in operating income on its own. The headline net loss of $80.7 billion for H1 2026 is almost entirely an accounting artifact: $72.4 billion stems from changes in the fair value of convertible notes and other financing instruments as Anthropic's enterprise valuation rose. Excluding stock-based compensation and noncash charitable contributions, adjusted operating income was $1.62 billion for the period. Operating cash flow was positive at $3.93 billion, and the company reported $1.70 of revenue for every dollar spent on computing power in Q3. As of September 30, more than 1,900 customers generated at least $1 million each in annualized revenue, including roughly 250 that generated at least $10 million. Anthropic held $131.7 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments as of June 30, 2026. The IPO price range and share count have not yet been determined. Anthropic previously raised a $65 billion Series H round in May 2026 that valued the company at $965 billion, following a $30 billion round in February that valued it at $380 billion. Read the S-1

item.title: LA Health Care Fraud Takedown: 15 Charged, Nearly $2B
item.description: The Justice Department announced charges against 15 defendants, including six medical professionals, for health care fraud schemes that collectively resulted in over $1.8 billion in fraudulent clai…
item.content:encoded: ⚖️ Los Angeles Health Care Fraud Takedown: 15 Defendants, Nearly $2B in Loss The Justice Department announced charges against 15 defendants, including six medical professionals, for health care fraud schemes that collectively resulted in over $1.8 billion in fraudulent claims to government and private health care programs. Eight defendants were arrested today. The charges include the largest substance abuse treatment fraud scheme ever prosecuted by the Department, plus a $134 million scheme involving unnecessary atherectomy procedures that injured patients, and three hospice fraud schemes totaling over $138 million. Substance abuse treatment fraud (over $1.6 billion): Nathan Young, David Young, Honey Phipps, and Cody Phipps were charged with a years-long scheme to traffic vulnerable patients from around the country to Southern California for sham substance abuse treatment billed to private insurance. The Youngs controlled dozens of purported treatment companies and directed body brokers to target vulnerable populations, including individuals who were unhoused and in poverty. Patients were lured with free flights, money, apartments, cars, and drugs, then recycled through facilities while billing insurance regardless of whether treatment was actually provided. Nicholas Moore pleaded guilty for his role as an area manager, admitting to assisting in the submission of $199 million in fraudulent claims. Invasive surgical procedures ($135 million): Dr. Harold Tabaie, a cardiothoracic surgeon, and Hany Malek, a chiropractor posing as a medical doctor, were charged with billing Medicare for medically unnecessary atherectomies at two Los Angeles clinics. The case was identified through data analytics showing Tabaie was an extreme outlier for atherectomy procedures in the United States from 2016 through 2023. Hospice fraud (over $138 million across three schemes): Geoffrey Jimenez was charged with operating a fraudulent hospice scheme through Transitions Hospice, Inc., enrolling non-terminal Medicare beneficiaries and billing for medically unnecessary services. Dr. Richard Keech was charged with falsely certifying beneficiaries as terminally ill to receive hospice care. Armani Raffi was charged with orchestrating a multi-entity hospice fraud scheme through four interconnected providers, resulting in approximately $21 million in false claims. Additional charges: Two California doctors were charged with accepting illegal kickbacks for authorizing millions of dollars in medically unnecessary genetic testing orders. Thomas Steven Mladinich was charged with receiving illegal kickbacks for patient referrals to a clinical treatment facility. Christina Mareik was charged for her role in a nearly $270 million scheme to defraud Medi-Cal through fraudulent pharmacy claims. Dejun Wang was charged with the prohibited sale of prescription drug samples. The cases were brought under President Trump's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance. Full DOJ press release

item.title: Cheap Foreign Labor
item.description: DOJ and EEOC announced a $5,000,000 joint settlement with Instacart over allegations of discrimination against U.S. and American workers based on citizenship status and national origin in violation…
item.content:encoded: ⚖️ DOJ and EEOC Secure $5M Settlement with Instacart Over Discrimination Against U.S. Workers DOJ and EEOC announced a $5,000,000 joint settlement with Instacart over allegations of discrimination against U.S. and American workers based on citizenship status and national origin in violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act and Title VII. The agencies found that Instacart's hiring and recruitment practices for positions advertised as part of the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process intentionally discriminated against U.S. workers by preferring workers with temporary employment visas. Specifically, Instacart required U.S. workers to submit paper applications by mail for PERM positions while allowing electronic applications through its standard process, creating additional burdens that prevented many from being timely considered. Under the settlement terms: Instacart will establish a $4,000,000 settlement fund to compensate affected applicants and deterred applicants $1,000,000 in civil penalties to the United States Required to post PERM positions on its public career website and accept electronic applications Must provide anti-discrimination training, revise policies, and submit to monitoring This is the fifteenth settlement under the Justice Department's Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative since its relaunch in 2025. Since the initiative's original launch, the Department has secured over $34 million in back pay for U.S. workers and over $16 million in civil penalties. Full DOJ press release

item.title: Weak Housing, a Fed Hold, and a Democratic House
item.description: Housing is still sliding, the labor market is coasting sideways, and the market has fully priced a Fed hold plus a Democratic midterm year.
item.content:encoded: Housing is still sliding, the labor market is coasting sideways, and the market has fully priced a Fed hold plus a Democratic midterm year. Housing: two more soft prints Indicator Agency Period Value Prior MoM YoY Pending Home Sales Index NAR Sep 2026 66.0 71.2 -7.3% -11.3% Housing Market Index NAHB Oct 2026 29 32 -9.4% -21.6% The Pending Home Sales Index is the more important of the pair, because contracts signed this month become closed sales in one or two months. September came in at 66.0, down 7.3% from August and 11.3% from a year earlier. That is the lowest print of 2026, and it sits 13.8% below the May peak of 76.6. The index has now fallen for four straight months. Builders are not cheerful either. The NAHB Housing Market Index dropped to 29 from 32, which is 21.6% below October 2025 and the weakest reading in the series. The index has to clear 50 before more builders than not call conditions good, so builders are describing conditions as bad by a wide margin. Rising rates, elevated prices, and flat wages explain the squeeze on both sides of the transaction. Labor: steady, with a small pullback Indicator Agency Period Value Prior MoM YoY Employment Trends Index Conference Board Sep 2026 107.56 108.08 -0.5% +1.2% The Conference Board Employment Trends Index landed at 107.56 in September, down 0.5% from a revised August reading of 108.08, which is the high of 2026. That August revision matters: the index spent the summer climbing, from 107.01 in May to 108.08 in August, and September gave a little of it back. The level is still 1.2% above a year earlier. A composite that stalls in the high 107s is a labor market holding its shape rather than one gaining ground. The blend of job openings, industrial production, and business confidence moves ahead of the unemployment rate and payrolls. Prediction markets: six new prints Market Latest odds Recent read Move FOMC rate decision, Oct 27-28 Hold 86¢, hike 12¢, cut 0¢ Sep 29: hold 30¢ Hold +56 points US recession in 2026 6¢ (Kalshi 5¢) Oct 4: 8¢ -26 points since Apr 17 (32¢) Senate control Dem 64¢ / Rep 36¢ Aug 25: 50/50 Dem +14 points House control Dem 92¢ / Rep 8¢ May 12: 49/51 Dem +43 points Hormuz traffic normal by Dec 31 12¢ Oct 19: 14¢ -22 points since Aug 24 (34¢) Iranian regime falls by end of 2026 4¢ Oct 19: 4¢ -29 points since Apr 17 (33¢) The Fed repricing is the biggest single move on the board. Markets spent September pricing a second consecutive hike, with hold odds bottoming at 30¢ on September 29 while hike odds hit 70¢. Three weeks later the trade flipped completely: hold at 86¢, a 25 basis point hike at 12¢, and a cut at zero. The statement lands at 2:00 PM ET on October 28. Recession odds at 6% line up with the same resilience: real GDP grew at a 3.1% annualized pace in the third quarter, unemployment held near 4.2%, and the Sahm rule sits well below its 0.50 trigger. Nobody is forecasting a contraction, and the market is not pricing one. The midterm markets are lopsided. Democrats at 64¢ in the Senate need a net gain of four seats, and at 92¢ in the House they need roughly three. Generic ballot advantage and mid-30s approval ratings for the president are doing the work. The House number has drifted from 94¢ on October 4 down to 90¢ on October 19 and back to 92¢, which is noise in a market this lopsided. The two geopolitical markets both hardened. The chance that Strait of Hormuz traffic returns to normal by December 31 sits at 12¢ on $14.0 million of volume, down from 34¢ in late August. Resolution needs the IMF PortWatch seven-day average at 60 transits per day, while AIS-visible traffic runs at roughly 3 to 7 per day, or 3% to 7% of the 100 to 138 per day pre-crisis baseline. Iran's October 4 demands for reopening have not moved the number. Regime change by year end sits at 4¢ on $26.7 million of volume, down from 33¢ in mid-April. The pattern Housing is the weak link in this batch. Contract activity down 11.3% year over year, builder sentiment at 29, and prices that have not adjusted enough to clear the market. The labor composite gave back 0.5% in September, and the Fed is priced to sit still through the meeting while that weakness plays out. If the housing data keeps sliding, the 6% recession price becomes the interesting one to watch. item.title: Shilling and Sleuthing
item.description: 1 NYT: Frenzied Hunt by Online Trolls To Identify Cornell’s Jane Doe Doc Riter: Frenzied Hunt by NYT Trolls To Identify Cornell’s Joe Suspect.
item.content:encoded: 1 NYT: Frenzied Hunt by Online Trolls To Identify Cornell’s Jane Doe Doc Riter: Frenzied Hunt by NYT Trolls To Identify Cornell’s Joe Suspect. The New York Times reports on the frenzied online hunt to identify Cornell's "Jane Doe" in a campus incident. Doc Riter's quip cuts both ways: what about the frenzied hunt by NYT trolls to identify Cornell's "Joe Suspect"? The double standard is obvious. When amateur internet sleuths try to unmask a victim or piece together details, they're condemned as ghoulish, invasive, or reckless. But when major outlets engage in the same behavior - digging into identities, speculating, or feeding the very attention they're decrying - it gets a more respectable gloss. The outrage depends on who's doing it. If it's anonymous posters on 4chan or X, it's a moral failing. If it's an investigative desk with a masthead, it's "public interest journalism." But the incentives and consequences look remarkably similar: clicks, attention, and the pressure to publish first. Doc Riter's point isn't to defend online trolls. It's to point out the asymmetry. Journalistic ethics shouldn't bend depending on whether the keyboard belongs to a credentialed reporter or a random user. The principle - don't gratuitously expose private individuals or fuel mob identification - ought to apply across the board. Otherwise it's just shilling for one's own tribe.

item.title: New York Times - Hollywood Thinks the Tech Oligarch Must Be Stopped
item.description: NYT: Hollywood Thinks the Tech Oligarch Must Be Stopped Doc Riter: Americans empowered by AI think Hollywood Must Be Stopped Technology is not a villain because Sorkin made a film about Zuck. They…
item.content:encoded: NYT: Hollywood Thinks the Tech Oligarch Must Be Stopped Doc Riter: Americans empowered by AI think Hollywood Must Be Stopped Technology is not a villain because Sorkin made a film about Zuck. They are not liars, fabulists, and narcissists any more than Hollywood. The New York Times suggests Hollywood has decided the tech oligarch must be stopped, framing Silicon Valley's power as the new existential threat worth dramatizing on screen. Doc Riter flips the lens: "Americans empowered by AI think Hollywood Must Be Stopped." The core point is straightforward: technology itself isn't villainous just because a filmmaker made a movie about Zuckerberg. And tech founders aren't inherently liars, fabulists, or narcissists in any way that distinguishes them categorically from Hollywood. That asymmetry is telling. Hollywood has spent decades mythmaking and shaping cultural narratives, often with little self-awareness about its own concentration of power and incentives. The industry that built its fortune on selling stories now frets about who controls the next storytelling machine. Instead of a morality play pitting good creators against evil technologists, the more honest take is a competition over attention, distribution, and cultural influence. Both industries chase those things. Calling one side uniquely corrupt while the other rides to the rescue doesn't hold up.

item.title: New York Times - Land Acknowledgments Aren't Just Woke. They're Right.
item.description: NYT: Land Acknowledgments Aren’t Just Woke. They’re Right. Doc Riter: Your grandmother who you describe as a seamstress for a rich white family enabled your leisurely time as a linguist to be dazzl…
item.content:encoded: NYT: Land Acknowledgments Aren’t Just Woke. They’re Right. Doc Riter: Your grandmother who you describe as a seamstress for a rich white family enabled your leisurely time as a linguist to be dazzled by symbols and diacritics. Your white privilege can now be Native alliance since you bite the hand that fed you. What is the goal to be aware of the horror of what happened? Should we feel guilty? What do we do with that guilt? Or is this the “conversation” that bends the ark of justice? How does it not result in reparation, just compensation, and expropriation? The New York Times recently ran an opinion piece making the case for land acknowledgments as a necessary recognition of historical reality rather than mere virtue signaling. The argument centers on confronting the uncomfortable truth of colonial dispossession rather than glossing over it. Doc Riter pushes back hard on that framing, asking pointed questions: if our ancestors benefited from systems of oppression, does awareness automatically produce guilt? Is guilt the point? And more practically, how does acknowledgment translate into material repair: reparation, just compensation, or expropriation?

item.title: Mattering
item.description: NYT: Latest Round of Rallies By ‘No Kings’ Group Focuses on Early Votes Doc Riter: White Liberal woman in Prospect Park holds racist sign “because Black votes matter too”
item.content:encoded: NYT: Latest Round of Rallies By ‘No Kings’ Group Focuses on Early Votes Doc Riter: White Liberal woman in Prospect Park holds racist sign “because Black votes matter too” The New York Times covers the latest round of "No Kings" rallies focusing on getting out the early vote. Doc Riter points to a photo-op moment: a white liberal woman in Prospect Park holding a sign that reads "because Black votes matter too." The contradiction is stark. If the premise is that Black votes matter, the "too" implies they don't already - or that the movement needs to be reminded of it. It's a classic case of performative allyship where the focus subtly shifts back to the person holding the sign. The sentiment might be well-intentioned, but the phrasing betrays a worldview that treats the cause as something the holder is graciously extending to others, rather than something rooted in basic equality. It centers the white ally rather than the people the message is supposedly about. This is the kind of symbolic gesture that dominates modern protest culture: more concerned with signaling one's own virtue than with precision or clarity. The message doesn't persuade skeptics; it reassures the sign-holder that they matter for holding it. And that's the problem - when activism becomes primarily about self-affirmation, the actual goal gets lost.

item.title: $10 Gas and Narrative Journalism
item.description: Front page NYT story about $10 dollar gas because trump is president and the NYT wants a democrat in the White House. But the actual story is about a remote location renting a gas generator for $5,…
item.content:encoded: Front page NYT story about $10 dollar gas because trump is president and the NYT wants a democrat in the White House. But the actual story is about a remote location renting a gas generator for $5,000 a month because solar would cost $3 million? A lot more to this story than DNC-promulgated “affordability under King Trump.” It’s not news. It’s a story that tells people they’re informed but shows that they aren’t when you ask probing questions. A recent New York Times front page story frames $10-per-gallon gas as a direct consequence of Trump being president, clearly positioning it as part of the "affordability crisis" angle ahead of the next election. Doc Riter takes a more skeptical read of what the story actually reports. Buried in the details is a different reality: in that remote location, residents rent a gas generator for $5,000 a month because solar would cost $3 million to install. That single fact reframes the entire headline. The high cost isn't just "gas prices under Trump" so much as the structural economics of energy in a remote, isolated grid. So the story is less about national inflation politics than about tradeoffs in extreme geography. But the framing leads readers to a predetermined conclusion: blame the president, blame the party in power. The nuance gets lost while the narrative fits neatly into a partisan message. That's the distinction between reporting facts and crafting a narrative. When a story tells readers they're informed, but probing questions reveal context that undermines the headline, it's no longer straight news. It's advocacy packaged as reporting. And it erodes trust in the process more than any particular price ever could.

item.title: New York Times - Unleash the Technocrats!
item.description: NYT: Unleash the Technocrats! Doc Riter: Okay, Blogger Almost, Matthew. Another well-intentioned abundance YIMBY. Technocrats should focus on deficits, yes, but then you’re like, “commercial jet pi…
item.content:encoded: NYT: Unleash the Technocrats! Doc Riter: Okay, Blogger Almost, Matthew. Another well-intentioned abundance YIMBY. Technocrats should focus on deficits, yes, but then you’re like, “commercial jet pilots should have less required hours because Europe does it?” Buy-American procurement rules are expensive so the federal government should go further in punishing jurisdictions that refuse to allow new homes? Like China? No local control? No thanks. Neo liberal bloggers almost get it but then they propose inane solutions. The Cost of living is because of Biden inflation, not Trump tariffs. Both means to same affordability goal; increase spending, decrease domestic production or cut taxes and increase domestic production. Everyone wants to get prices down. But only a technocrat knows how to? Or are you arrogantly proposing a centralized effective altruism? Technocrats need to get elected and they need to convince needy humans. Means–ends analysis (MEA) Tariffs are a means to challenging a China dominated market hegemony. The end goal is a reaffirmed American hegemony; integrated international harmony with American partners and American production. However, an inconsistent and hawkish foreign policy, anti-austerity pet projects on both sides, and unaligned bicameral politics as ostensibly esteemed checks and balances have resulted in fatter checks for higher balances. Debt grows because democracies don’t vote for higher taxes and less spending. Another New York Times piece champions the "technocrat" solution: let credentialed experts cut through politics and deliver abundance, especially on housing and regulation. Doc Riter isn't buying the brand. The skepticism starts with the proposed fixes. Pointing to Europe's lower pilot hour requirements or demanding the federal government override local zoning to punish recalcitrant jurisdictions feels less like sound policy than abstract engineering. "No thanks" to trading local control for a top-down diktat. The inflation diagnosis also misses the blame game. The cost of living spike came under Biden, not Trump's tariffs, but both approaches aim at the same stated goal: lower prices. One tries to do it by spending less and producing more at home; the other leaned into fiscal expansion. Doc Riter's larger point is about means and ends. Tariffs aren't about prices in isolation - they're a means to challenge China's market dominance with the end goal of reasserting American leverage while integrating with trusted partners. But that strategic goal collides with domestic political reality: no democracy votes for steep tax hikes and spending cuts. Pet projects persist across parties, foreign policy swings, and checks and balances make hard tradeoffs nearly impossible. So debt keeps growing. The real question isn't whether experts have good ideas. It's whether a technocratic approach can convince "needy humans" to accept the costs of those ideas. Without that political coalition, "unleashing the technocrats" is just another form of wishful thinking.

item.title: Harvard's 27% Endowment Return
item.description: The New York Times: "As Trump Cuts, Harvard's Coffer Gushes to $68 Billion." The framing is pure Trump-defiant triumphalism — the bad guy tried to hurt us, but we outsmarted him. That's the kind of…
item.content:encoded: The New York Times: "As Trump Cuts, Harvard's Coffer Gushes to $68 Billion." The framing is pure Trump-defiant triumphalism — the bad guy tried to hurt us, but we outsmarted him. That's the kind of journalism people accept without asking questions. But the real question is: how did Harvard earn a 27% return? The Answer Is in the 13F Harvard Management Company filed its Q2 2026 13F on August 14, covering holdings as of June 30, 2026. The portfolio totals $4.26 billion across 19 positions. And at the top of that list, representing 51.8% of the entire portfolio , is a single position: SPACE EXPLORATION TECHN CORP (SPACEX) — $2,210,091,186 That's over two billion dollars in a company run by Trump's bestie. The NYT's "gloat" is that Harvard stood tall against federal pressure — but the actual engine of that 27% return wasn't heroic institutional resilience. It was a single, massive, un diversified bet on SpaceX. The Full Portfolio What the NYT Left Out Ticker Name Value % of Portfolio SPACEX Space Exploration Technologies Corp $2,210,091,186 51.8% TSM Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing $349,591,747 8.2% CBRS Cerebras Systems Inc $238,963,543 5.6% AMZN Amazon.com Inc $234,249,847 5.5% GOOGL Alphabet Inc $165,162,119 3.9% NVDA NVIDIA Corporation $157,615,095 3.7% IAU iShares Gold Trust $149,516,218 3.5% MSFT Microsoft Corporation $146,322,690 3.4% AVGO Broadcom Inc $127,810,202 3.0% META Meta Platforms Inc $120,827,958 2.8% IBIT iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF $101,355,133 2.4% NFLX Netflix Inc $78,825,600 1.9% BKNG Booking Holdings Inc $73,898,304 1.7% The Times' article frames the windfall as a victory over Trump administration pressure. But the 13F tells the actual story. Narv bought SpaceX. item.title: Fed Survey: Wealth Flows to the Old, Away from the Young
item.description: The Federal Reserve released the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances on Friday, and the generational wealth gap is now stark. Between 2022 and 2025, median net worth for families headed by someone und…
item.content:encoded: The Federal Reserve released the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances on Friday, and the generational wealth gap is now stark. Between 2022 and 2025, median net worth for families headed by someone under 35 fell 23 percent to $33,000. For families 75 and older, median net worth rose 37 percent to roughly $505,000. The oldest age group now holds the most wealth of any cohort, displacing the 65-to-74 bracket that led the prior survey. The divergence tracks the stock market. Retirement account values drove most of the older cohort's gains, and equities have been the strongest asset class over the period. Younger families, by contrast, saw their median wealth fall largely because business equity gains unwound from the 2019-to-2022 run-up. Homeownership costs and student debt continue to weigh on the under-35 cohort, which also carries a disproportionate share of negative or near-zero net worth. The survey's broader figures are similarly split. Real median net worth rose 2 percent across all families to $215,900, while real mean net worth rose 7 percent to $1.24 million. Real median income rose 7 percent to $82,200, but real mean income fell 6 percent to $145,200, pulled down by capital gains declines for higher earners. The top decile's median net worth reached $4.94 million, up from $4.15 million in 2022. The bottom quartile tells a bleaker story: median net worth dropped from $3,800 to $1,700, and mean net worth stayed negative. Families at the top of the wealth distribution recorded the largest gains, reinforcing the pattern the Fed noted: wealth changes over the period strengthened inequality along age, education, and housing lines. Read the full report at the Federal Reserve. More on the Numbers page: View indicators

item.title: Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County - Oral Argument (25-170)
item.description: Docket No. 25-170 | Argued Monday, October 5, 2026, 10:06 a.m. | First argument of October Term 2026
item.content:encoded: Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County Docket No. 25-170 | Argued Monday, October 5, 2026, 10:06 a.m. | First argument of October Term 2026 Case Overview The Court heard the first oral argument of the October Term 2026 in a climate tort case with national implications. Boulder County and the City of Boulder sued Exxon Mobil Corporation and three Suncor Energy companies in Colorado state court in 2018, asserting state-law tort claims - public and private nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, and civil conspiracy - for the costs of climate change harms, alleging the companies produced, promoted, refined, marketed, and sold fossil fuels while concealing and misrepresenting the dangers of their use. The energy companies contend the claims are preempted by federal law. The Colorado Supreme Court held they are not, and the companies petitioned for certiorari. The Court granted the petition on February 23, 2026, and added a question on its own statutory and Article III jurisdiction. Justice Alito recused (announced September 28, 2026), leaving eight justices to hear nearly two hours of argument. A decision is expected by summer 2027. Parties Petitioners: Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc., Suncor Energy Sales, Inc., Suncor Energy Inc., and Exxon Mobil Corporation Respondents: County Commissioners of Boulder County and City of Boulder, et al. Amicus curiae supporting Petitioners: United States (Sarah M. Harris, Principal Deputy Solicitor General), by leave of the Court with divided argument Questions Presented Whether federal law precludes state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by the effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions on the global climate. (Added by the Court, Feb. 23, 2026) Whether this Court has statutory and Article III jurisdiction to hear this case. Procedural History Date Action 2018 Boulder files suit in Boulder County District Court (No. 18CV30349, Judge Robert R. Gunning) - Defendants remove to federal court; remand; Tenth Circuit affirms remand - District court denies motion to dismiss, rejecting federal preemption defenses May 12, 2025 Colorado Supreme Court (No. 24SA206, C.A.R. 21 original proceeding): claims not preempted by federal common law or the Clean Air Act; order to show cause discharged; remanded. Justice Gabriel, joined by Chief Justice Marquez and Justices Hood, Hart, and Berkenkotter; Justice Samour, joined by Justice Boatright, dissented Aug 8, 2025 Petition for certiorari filed Sep 11, 2025 Brief amicus curiae of United States filed (cert stage) Nov 10, 2025 Opposition filed Feb 23, 2026 Certiorari GRANTED; parties directed to brief and argue the jurisdiction question May 14, 2026 Petitioners' merits brief and joint appendix filed May 21, 2026 United States merits amicus brief filed; dozens of merits amicus briefs Jul 27, 2026 Respondents' merits brief filed Jul 28, 2026 Solicitor General moves for leave to argue as amicus with divided argument Aug 4, 2026 SET FOR ARGUMENT on Monday, October 5, 2026 Sep 4, 2026 SG motion for divided argument GRANTED Sep 28, 2026 Clerk notifies counsel that Justice Alito will not continue to participate Oct 5, 2026 ARGUED - Shanmugam (petitioners), Harris (U.S., amicus, supporting petitioners), Russell (respondents) 1. Time Spoken Per Justice Argument began at 10:06 a.m. and ran nearly two hours across 122 transcript pages. The Court did not publish per-justice minute counts; advocate allocation below is estimated from transcript pagination. Speaker Transcript pages Est. time Notes Kannon K. Shanmugam (petitioners) 4 - 58 27 min Jurisdiction, extraterritoriality, Clean Air Act, foreign affairs Sarah M. Harris (U.S., amicus) 59 - 83 12 min Two paths to reversal: inherently federal pollution area; constitutional limits Kevin K. Russell (respondents) 84 - 118 17 min Jurisdiction (prematurity, standing); state tort law for local injuries Shanmugam (rebuttal) 119 - 122 3 min "Breadth of Boulder's theory here is astonishing" Justice participation: Thomas (opened with jurisdiction), Roberts, Sotomayor, Kagan, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett, and Jackson all asked questions. Alito recused. 2. Amendments (Constitutional Provisions Invoked) Article III: Whether the Court has jurisdiction, and whether the costs of interim litigation constitute a concrete injury for standing. 28 U.S.C. § 1257 (statutory): Whether the Colorado Supreme Court's C.A.R. 21 order is a final judgment (a "self-contained original proceeding" under the Court's Atlantic Richfield framework) or an ordinary interlocutory appeal. Dormant Commerce Clause / equal sovereignty: Whether the Constitution's structure bars a state from applying its law to global conduct; the direct-nexus requirement of National Pork Producers. Due Process (extraterritoriality): Whether a state may extend its law beyond its borders to regulate global conduct with global effects (BMW v. Gore line). Foreign affairs power: Whether the suit interferes with the nation's conduct of foreign policy. 3. Position Per Justice Justice Apparent position Key evidence Confidence (1-5) Thomas Skeptical of both sides; likely deciding vote Pressed jurisdiction at the outset for both Shanmugam and Harris; pressed Russell on limiting principles ("large retailers"); authored Hencely v. Fluor (2026) rejecting a new preemption doctrine 3 Roberts Pragmatic lean toward petitioners, via preemption rather than a new constitutional principle "That's a question of relief"; distaste for the proposed extraterritoriality principle; floodgates concern 3 Kavanaugh Most supportive of petitioners "This Court has consistently said that air and water pollution are ... matters for federal law"; worried the litigation "is going to bankrupt ... these various defendants" 4 Barrett Receptive to source-state saving-clause theory; concerned about remedy gaps Questioned whether the theory would leave some harms with no remedy; tested limits with the 49-state cap hypothetical 3 Gorsuch Interested in a preemption rationale; concerned about the gap "Nobody can sue at all" after the CAA displaced federal common law; presumption against preemption 3 Kagan Leans Boulder Tobacco and opioid analogies ("This is chapter three"); skeptical of preemption arguments, though engaged with the CAA question 4 Sotomayor Leans Boulder Returned repeatedly to jurisdiction and prematurity; pressed petitioners for textual support 4 Jackson Leans toward jurisdictional dismissal (wait for final judgment) "Why shouldn't we wait and hear all of these claims once the state courts are done?" 3 Alito Recused Will not continue to participate (announced Sep. 28, 2026) - 4. Precedents Case Year How used American Electric Power Co. v. Connecticut 2011 CAA displaces federal common law; "ties the two together" (Harris) International Paper Co. v. Ouellette 1987 Clean Water Act saving clause preserves only source-state law; Harris analogized to the CAA National Pork Producers Council v. Ross 2023 States may regulate out-of-state conduct only with a direct nexus to in-state injury BMW of North America, Inc. v. Gore 1996 Territorial limits on state law; contrasted with the "constructive presence" exception Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts 1985 Kansas could not apply its law to a nationwide class where 97% of conduct and injuries were out of state Atlantic Richfield (self-contained original proceedings) - Framework for treating a state-court C.A.R. 21 proceeding as final under § 1257 Hencely v. Fluor Corp. 2026 Thomas rejected a new "battlefield preemption" doctrine; signals skepticism of novel preemption theories City & County of Honolulu v. Sunoco LP 2023 (Haw.) Persuaded the Colorado Supreme Court that displaced federal common law plays no part in the preemption analysis Illinois v. City of Milwaukee ("Milwaukee I") 1972 "Uniquely federal interests" in interstate pollution (cited in the Samour dissent below) Boyle v. United Technologies; Texas Industries v. Radcliff 1988; 1981 Cited in the Samour dissent for the same proposition 5. Hypotheticals Brought Up Shanmugam (rebuttal): On a visit to Colorado, Boulder could sue him "for refilling my car and thereby contributing to global climate change." Any individual who has suffered climate effects could sue under Boulder's theory. Thomas to Russell: Under Boulder's theory, could state and local governments sue "large retailers" of fossil fuels? Russell: "Nothing in our theory prevents that," but multiple defendants can be liable for widespread harm. Barrett to Russell: Could Colorado pass a law capping greenhouse-gas emissions in the other 49 states? Russell agreed that would be prohibited and distinguished a damages suit that "requires them to internalize a portion of the cost" rather than prohibiting conduct. Kagan: Boulder's suit resembles the 1990s tobacco suits and opioid manufacturer suits - "This is chapter three" - where state claims proceeded. Harris: The constructive-presence exception (bringing cars or opioids into a state) makes the actor liable for in-state conduct; Colorado's theory is different - a ban on making the product anywhere nationwide. Roberts: It is not uncommon for suits to rest on out-of-state conduct with broad effects felt in the forum state; he asked what makes this different. 6. Funny Statements (Notable Quotes) Shanmugam: "The breadth of Boulder's theory here is astonishing." Shanmugam: "Climate change is certainly one of the most pressing issues of the day, but we would submit that this is exactly the wrong way to go about resolving it." Kagan: "This is chapter three." (tobacco, opioids, now fossil fuels) Gorsuch: After the CAA displaced federal common law, "nobody can sue at all" - even where the Act gave EPA no authority over the harm. Kavanaugh: The litigation "is going to bankrupt ... these various defendants and certainly other defendants out there." Russell: Boulder's suit "doesn't prohibit them from engaging in the conduct. It requires them to internalize a portion of the cost of their activities." 7. Issues at Hand Primary: Whether federal law (the Clean Air Act, displaced federal common law, constitutional structure, or foreign affairs) precludes Boulder's state-law tort claims. Threshold: Whether the Court has statutory (28 U.S.C. § 1257 finality) and Article III jurisdiction, given the case is still pending in Colorado trial court and other federal defenses remain unresolved. Practical implications: Some 90,000 municipalities could bring similar suits; potential bankruptcies of energy defendants; a possible remedy gap if neither state nor federal law supplies a cause of action. Possible outcomes: merits ruling on preemption; dismissal for lack of jurisdiction; 4-4 tie (Alito recused) leaving the Colorado Supreme Court's judgment in place without precedent; dismissal of certiorari as improvidently granted. Stakes: The fate of Boulder's suit and dozens of similar climate accountability suits nationwide; Gorsuch and Barrett are the key votes to watch. 8. https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/court-sends-mixed-signals-on-whether-it-will-allow-state-tort-suits-seeking-to-hold-energy-compa/ SCOTUSblog preview (Amy Howe): https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/supreme-court-to-consider-whether-suit-may-go-forward-seeking-to-hold-energy-companies-liable-fo/ Just Security takeaways: https://www.justsecurity.org/159880/climate-liability-suncor-v-boulder-oral-arguments/ Stanford Law analysis: https://law.stanford.edu/2026/10/06/will-the-supreme-court-create-more-barriers-to-climate-litigation-analyzing-suncor-v-boulder-oral-arguments/ Transnational Litigation Blog recap: https://tlblog.org/oral-argument-recap-suncor-v-boulder/ C-SPAN video: https://www.c-span.org/event/public-affairs-event/justices-hear-climate-lawsuit-case/447748 CBS News: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/supreme-court-climate-change-energy-companies-boulder-colorado-arguments/ Aspen Public Radio: https://www.aspenpublicradio.org/environment/2026-10-06/scotus-hears-arguments-on-whether-colorado-or-federal-court-should-hear-boulder-climate-lawsuit Counsel of Record For Petitioners: Kannon K. Shanmugam, Washington, D.C. For the United States, as amicus curiae: Sarah M. Harris, Principal Deputy Solicitor General, Department of Justice For Respondents: Kevin K. Russell, Washington, D.C. Significance The most important climate liability case to reach the Court in more than a decade opened the October Term. With Alito recused, a 4-4 split would leave the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling for Boulder in place without binding precedent. The argument revealed a possible majority skepticism toward Boulder's theory on the merits (Roberts, Kavanaugh, with Barrett and Gorsuch interested in a preemption rationale), but also serious doubts about jurisdiction (Thomas, Jackson, Sotomayor), leaving dismissal as a live outcome. The Court could also reach the merits through fractured routes, and the decision will shape dozens of similar suits nationwide. Word Counts & Definitions The Court does not publish per-term word counts; the terms below dominated the argument (used repeatedly by all three advocates and across questioning). Exact counts are not tabulated from the transcript. Extraterritorial: Beyond a state's borders. Petitioners' core claim: Colorado may not apply its law to conduct occurring worldwide with only incidental effects in Colorado. The Court has never recognized a freestanding constitutional "extraterritoriality principle"; Roberts and Kavanaugh probed whether one is needed. Enclave: An area of exclusive federal authority or an inherently federal domain. Kavanaugh: "This Court has consistently said that air and water pollution are ... matters for federal law" - framing interstate pollution as a federal enclave where state law presumptively does not apply unless Congress preserves it. Preemption: Federal law superseding state law. Variants argued: express (Clean Air Act text), field (Congress occupied the field), conflict (state law stands as an obstacle), and the newer "foreign affairs preemption." Saving clause: A statutory provision preserving state law. Harris argued the CAA's saving clause preserves only suits under source-state law (per International Paper Co. v. Ouellette in the Clean Water Act context). Jurisdiction / finality (28 U.S.C. § 1257): The Court may review state-court judgments only after the state's highest court has spoken finally. Suncor says the C.A.R. 21 order was a "self-contained original proceeding" (Atlantic Richfield framework); Boulder says it is an ordinary interlocutory ruling. Interlocutory: Intermediate, not final. Boulder's answer to the appeal: other federal defenses remain pending in Colorado trial court, so there is no final judgment to review. Standing (Article III): Whether Suncor's exposure to interim litigation costs is a concrete injury. Russell: the costs of defending the suit are themselves a constitutionally cognizable injury. Dormant Commerce Clause: The judicial doctrine that states may not discriminate against, or unduly burden, interstate commerce; National Pork Products' direct-nexus test was invoked as a limiting principle. Amicus curiae: "Friend of the court." The United States argued for petitioners with divided argument (Harris took the middle segment) - granted Sep. 4, 2026. C.A.R. 21: Colorado Appellate Rule 21, the original-proceeding writ procedure the Colorado Supreme Court used to decide the preemption question. DIG (dismissed as improvidently granted): A possible outcome in which the Court declines to decide the case at all. Recusal: A justice's withdrawal from a case. Alito recused (announced Sep. 28, 2026), leaving eight justices; a 4-4 tie affirms the lower court without precedent. DOC RITER Commentary Precedent amalgamation gives us frivolous litigation for every possible grievance. We were all harmed by YOU! We suffered the effects of climate change! Any complainant with an AI bot can now extort any energy, comfort, or pain relief business. Providing value to society is now crippled by unlimited litigation. When entrepreneurship is susceptible to tort on steroids, expect less small business. Only mega corporations can afford to fight the mob.

item.title: Roman
item.description: launched on August 30, 2026 and is named after NASA's first chief astronomer and is designed to study dark energy, exoplanets, and infrared astrophysics with a field of view 100 times wider than Hu…
item.content:encoded: launched on August 30, 2026 and is named after NASA's first chief astronomer and is designed to study dark energy, exoplanets, and infrared astrophysics with a field of view 100 times wider than Hubble's. Roman Overview - NASA Webb Launched in 2021, JWST is the largest and most powerful space telescope ever built. Operating primarily in infrared, it peers through dust clouds and sees the first galaxies forming. Webb Overview - NASA Webb Images - ESA/Webb Hubble Launched in 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope was the first major optical telescope in space. It has provided iconic images of the cosmos and fundamentally changed our understanding of the universe. Hubble Overview - NASA Hubble Images - ESA/Hubble What Makes Each Unique Hubble (1990) operates from Low Earth Orbit and spent 34+ years capturing the first visible-light image of an exoplanet, Fomalhaut b, and its Ultra Deep Field revealed thousands of unseen galaxies from just 10 days of exposure. Webb (2021) sits at Sun-Earth L2, 932,000 miles away, at -391°F, and used its 21.3 ft mirror to detect carbon dioxide in an exoplanet atmosphere and spot galaxies at redshifts z13-16, challenging models of early universe formation. Roman (2026) shares Webb's Sun-Earth L2 orbit but covers a field of view 100 times wider than Hubble's, using its wide-field camera for months-long dark-energy surveys and a coronagraph to directly image exoplanets by blocking starlight. item.title: War of Worldviews
item.description: Parties from principle, especially abstract speculative principle, are known only to modern times, and are, perhaps, the most extraordinary and unaccountable phaenomenon, that has yet appeared in h…
item.content:encoded: Parties from principle, especially abstract speculative principle, are known only to modern times, and are, perhaps, the most extraordinary and unaccountable phaenomenon, that has yet appeared in human affairs. Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary (David Hume) Hume distinguishes three sources of faction: interest, principle, and affection. Interest is rational and predictable. Affection is tribal but personal. Principle is different. Modern ideological parties run on principle. They fight over abstractions—equality, liberty, identity—that no one can fully define but everyone is willing to die for. Unlike interest, which bends toward compromise, principle is absolute. Unlike affection, which is bounded by familiarity, principle scales to millions who will never meet. The result is permanent hostility. Two people traveling opposite directions on a broad road pass each other easily. Two people reasoning from opposite principles cannot. They must convert or destroy. This is our politics. Not a dispute over resources or power, but a war of worldviews.

item.title: Regional Price Parities
item.description: Location is purchasing power.
item.content:encoded: Location is purchasing power. From the Bureau of Economic Analysis' 2024 Regional Price Parities Report: San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, CA metro clocks in at 211.9 (index, US = 100), meaning goods, services, and rent cost more than twice the national average . Meanwhile, Monroe, LA sits at 42.8 - less than half the national average, and barely one-fifth what a San Jose resident pays. The Rent Tier map tells the story of American inequality in hard numbers. California dominates the top: San Jose (211.9), Napa (197.4), San Francisco (194.7), San Diego (179.3), Oxnard (171.1), Los Angeles (170.4), Santa Cruz (164.3). Seven of the top ten priciest metros are in the Golden State. Add Seattle (151.3), DC (151.1), and Boston (148.4) - the coastal knowledge-economy hubs where housing supply meets regulatory capture. The other America is cheap - and cheap for a reason. The bottom reads like a list of forgotten places: Monroe, LA (42.8), Johnstown, PA (42.3), Parkersburg, WV (45.9), Dothan, AL (46.9), Florence-Muscle Shoals, AL (47.7), Hammond, LA (48.2), Paducah, KY (48.8). These are places young people leave, where capital does not flow, where the housing is affordable because opportunity is not there. The non-metropolitan US averages just 59.852 - four-tenths of San Jose's index. Rural America is a different country price-wise. The gap between coastal metropolis and heartland explains cultural and political inclinations. What the index actually measures: RPPs compare prices for goods, services, and rents across regions. A 211.9 in San Jose means a $3,000 rent that buys a luxury unit there might cost $1,400 nationally - or $700 in Paducah. Same salary, radically different lifestyle. item.title: The Housing First Showdown
item.description: Two irreconcilable visions. The street versus the book. Reality v. theory.
item.content:encoded: Two irreconcilable visions. The street versus the book. Reality v. theory. On one side: a hard-edged critique that sees Housing First as a failed, enabling ideology promoted by a sensationalist media. On the other: a rigorous defense that frames the policy as evidence-based compassion under attack by reactionary politics. Homelessness = vagrancy. Period. You cannot camp on the street in a civilized society. Rule-based order is the foundation of prosperity, and society's performative empathy — "pretending to care" about trauma and abandonment — is nothing short of oxymoronic and terrifying . Homelessness is not a moral failure . It is a complex collision of mental health crises, addiction, domestic violence, medical debt, and a catastrophic shortage of affordable housing. Criminalizing camping does not end suffering — it drives it underground , cycling people through jails and emergency rooms at staggering public cost . Abolish HUD. Dismantle the bureaucracy. Post-1965 housing policy is a total failure . Boomers hoarded the American Dream and now weaponize narrative control to hoard resources. Old liberals are the enemy. A working immigrant with three jobs deserves more rights than someone who refuses to participate in society. Federal housing policy is imperfect, not irredeemable . HUD's Section 8 vouchers, Fair Housing Act enforcement, and community development grants have kept millions housed . The answer to underfunding and NIMBY resistance is reform and investment , not abolition. Blaming generational cohorts distracts from the real engines of unaffordability: zoning restrictions, corporate landlord consolidation, and stagnant wages . Government "solutions" caused the inflation that crushed working families. That is why people are homeless. The solution is less government , not more. Inflation in the 2020s was driven by pandemic supply shocks, pent-up demand, and corporate profit-taking — not housing vouchers or food assistance. The alternative to public intervention is not a free-market utopia; it is a dystopia where shelter is a luxury reserved for the wealthy , and "personal responsibility" becomes a pretext for collective abandonment . One side sees Housing First as moral hazard — a policy that rewards dysfunction and empowers a bureaucratic class that profits from perpetual crisis. One side sees Housing First as pragmatic mercy — the cheapest, most humane way to stabilize lives and reduce the staggering hidden costs of street homelessness.

item.title: Whose Bridge?
item.description: There’s another word for dispossession. It’s conquest. And its story is as old as time. And to be honest, it’s a good story (since we have to moralize everything in order to appease the victim trol…
item.content:encoded: There’s another word for dispossession. It’s conquest. And its story is as old as time. And to be honest, it’s a good story (since we have to moralize everything in order to appease the victim trolls who will inevitably shame us). We can be empathetic, but sometimes it’s refreshing to see honest vindication. In Braveheart, someone slits your girl, you slit them back. And then you pound their head in. You bludgeon them. Sometimes you need to beat the shit out of people. That’s what we did before iPhones. We fought. But fighting produces victims and as we've evolved, we no longer bludgeon each other. We represent each other's grievances instead. We've insulated ourselves from suffering. No one can be bullied. But here's a bully who has no protected status and who we all can fight - the Troll. Not the keyboard one with quick fingers and ample time. The ugly one. The one with hair on its knuckles and an intimidating scowl who lives under a bridge. That one! The billy goats Gruff fend off the Troll because he has the audacity to claim title to the bridge. Whose bridge? The eldest goat is William Wallace with horns sheathed in keratin. No thank you, he says (I am coming to gobble you up!) No land acknowledgment necessary. He butts the Troll off the bridge. The land dispute is adjudicated with violence. Here's another victim story. Hollywood has become dispossessed, supposedly. What used to be theirs is someone else’s. Antitrust M&A stole their industry. They claimed title to the titles - novels, magazines, television, and movies. Now TikTok gives title to whoever wants to hit record on their iPhone. Hollywood’s land was stolen because big tech conquered them. They were trolled or are they the old Troll? I don't know. The metaphor is just one paint brush in trying to contextualize the aggrieved. Dispossession is only one side of a story. It's wildly incomplete without an antagonist and protagonist; the luddite versus a datacenter; the Palestinian versus the Jew, the vanquished and the victor. But the story that every kid grows up with answered some basic one sided questions. Who won? Who fought back? Who successfully appealed and righted a wrong? Who's the good guy? Who's the bad guy? As adults, the story became 'it's complicated', don't hurt feelings, don't pinch pain. But as a parent, you're an idiot to tell your kid you are the bad guy. Your heritage can never be evil. Not even Babar would tell his kids the other side of their imperialist story. It’s up to the indigenous to take back their land and tell their story. The land acknowledgment is pithy patronage from the wrong side. Just like it’s up to the settlers in the West Bank to claim theirs and call it Judea. It's up to the villager to fight back and call it Palestine. Everyone is fighting to survive. One day our only possession will die. AI's Take: First, it says that indigenous peoples should reclaim their land, and that land acknowledgments are shallow gestures — “pithy patronage” — unless they are backed by real justice. Then it draws a parallel to settlers in the West Bank, suggesting that both groups are engaged in territorial claims and survival, with an implied symmetry in contested ownership. Finally, it ends with a dark reflection: all of our possessions are ultimately temporary, because we ourselves will die. The tone is critical and provocative, using political and historical imagery to argue that symbolic acts are not enough and that ownership and survival are fragile.In both cases the claim is cast as a struggle for survival rather than a purely moral right, so the dispute becomes less about good and evil and more about who can enforce their version of ownership.

VOS exposed a fundamental split: Can Article II conduct foreign policy through fiscal measures without Article I? The Skeptics Justice Barrett's absurdity test: the President can ban all trade under IEEPA but cannot impose a 1% tariff? That's backwards from every delegation principle in administrative law. Justice Kavanaugh called it the "donut hole"—a gaping logical inconsistency in the government's position. item.title: Cella v. Attorney General
item.description: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court bars rent control initiative from 2026 ballot because exemption for "facilities operated solely for religious purposes" makes the measure relate to religion und…
item.content:encoded: Cella v. Attorney General: Rent Control Initiative Blocked on Religious Exemption Grounds Case: Cella v. Attorney General, SJC-13893 Decided: June 23, 2026 Court: Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts Core Holding The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court unanimously held that Initiative Petition 25-21 — a rent control measure that would limit annual rent increases to the lesser of CPI or 5% — cannot appear on the November 2026 ballot because its exemption for "dwelling units in facilities operated solely for... religious... purposes" causes the petition to "relate to religion" in violation of Article 48 of the Massachusetts Constitution. The Initiative Initiative Petition 25-21 sought to: Repeal G. L. c. 40P, which bans rent control statewide Replace it with a cap on annual rent increases at the lesser of the Consumer Price Index or 5% Apply to all "covered dwelling units" leased for residential use Exemptions included: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units Units regulated by a public authority Transient guest units (less than 14 days) Units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or non-profit purposes Units with a certificate of occupancy less than 10 years old The Legal Challenge Four registered voters sued to block the petition, arguing the religious exemption violated Article 48's excluded matters provision, which states: "No measure that relates to religion, religious practices or religious institutions... shall be proposed by an initiative petition." The Attorney General had certified the petition as compliant, but the court reviewed that certification de novo. The Court's Reasoning Majority Opinion (Gaziano, J.) The court applied the plain language of Article 48 and its historical context: "Relates to religion" standard: An initiative relates to religion if religion is "a factor in [the initiative's] application." The religious exemption makes religion exactly that — a factor in determining which units are covered by rent control. Precedent from Collins v. Secretary of the Commonwealth (1990): The court relied on its earlier holding that a law altering the rights and obligations of religious institutions cannot be the subject of a referendum because it "make[s] religion a factor in the application of the exemption" and "alter[s] the legal status of religious institutions." Secular exemptions do not cure the defect: The presence of secular exemptions (educational, non-profit) does not negate that the petition uses religion as a factor in its application. "Main purpose" test rejected: The Attorney General argued the petition's main purpose (limiting rent increases) was secular. The court declined to apply the "main purpose" test to the religion exclusion, distinguishing it from the "powers of courts" exclusion. Unlike the courts exclusion, applying the religion exclusion according to its plain language does not threaten to make the initiative process a nullity — proponents can simply avoid drawing distinctions based on religion. Historical intent: The 1917-1918 constitutional convention delegates intended to strictly separate church and state and "make it as difficult as possible to bring religious questions into the politics of this State." Concurring Opinion (Kafker, J.) Justice Kafker concurred on narrower grounds, focusing on the specific religious test the exemption creates: The exemption requires determining whether a dwelling unit is operated "solely for... religious... purposes" This invites "intrusive review of religious beliefs and practices" It requires inquiry into "the internal affairs of, and even the motives and purposes of, a religious institution, as well as its finances" Examples include religious retirement communities, universities, and sober houses Whether such a unit is operated "solely" for religious purposes demands a "deep dive" into both finances and religious practices Justice Kafker noted that Massachusetts is unique among States in having such a religion exclusion in its initiative process. Key Precedents Cited Article 48 of the Massachusetts Constitution — Excluded matters provision Collins v. Secretary of the Commonwealth , 407 Mass. 837 (1990) — Law altering religious institution exemptions related to religion under Article 48 Opinion of the Justices , 309 Mass. 555 (1941) — Contraceptive care initiative did not relate to religion because it concerned secular public health Mazzone v. Attorney General , 432 Mass. 515 (2000) — "Main purpose" test for judicial powers exclusion Practical Effect The court remanded the matter to the county court for: Entry of judgment declaring Initiative Petition 25-21 noncompliant with Article 48's excluded matters section Enjoining the Secretary of the Commonwealth from placing the measure on the November 2026 statewide election ballot Rent control proponents must now either: Redraft the initiative without any religious exemption, or Pursue the issue through the Massachusetts Legislature Broader Implications For Initiative Drafting: The decision signals that any initiative containing a religious exemption — even in an otherwise secular measure — risks being barred from the ballot under Article 48. For Church-State Separation: The ruling reinforces Massachusetts' strict separation of church and state as reflected in both Article 48 and the anti-aid amendment (Article 46). For Rent Control Debate: The immediate effect is removal of the rent control measure from the 2026 ballot, delaying any statewide rent control effort until at least 2028. Resources SJC-13893 Decision (PDF) Mass.gov Case Page Stakes: This case clarifies the scope of Article 48's religion exclusion and demonstrates that even secular initiatives cannot contain distinctions based on religion without violating Massachusetts constitutional constraints on the initiative process.

item.title: ㌖ A Chance Meeting
item.description: Theo Of Golden
item.content:encoded: Theo Of Golden The Knicks victory celebration was called unInternet or unAI. Theo is Offline The gentleness of an elder gentleman, the vulnerability in kindness; its all so different from the modern online experience. There is brashness not bravery. Its strangers interacting with no introduction - strange. No conversation with shared tears or smiles. It's frequently brazen and attention seeking. Solipsistic in solitude. Cynical in certainty. Even a baby knows to smile because it is smiled at. We did human things. We made babies. Autism and fertility do not dance well. The iPhone stole our smile and the internet hides our tears. It's sad to think about it and realize the last time you've laughed and cried. It'll hit. Oh yeah, I am human. I should try being more human. Theo chooses the person he wants to talk to by looking at their portrait and finding some sadness in their face. You see no sadness in online profiles. They are inaccurate portraits. They offer no insight into who the person is. A portrait tells a story. It is more than a thousand words, more than 200 characters. Theo looks to the face for personal hints. He likes intricacy - under mushrooms, spiderwebs, DaVinci drawings. He can tell who he'd like to speak with. He's intuitive; erudite. Online its, Avatars, memes, emojis, pseudonym, usernames - no hints, just an identifier to tell the database you are unique. I'd like to speak to no one online. Only to see one offline. Theo meets a stranger at a fountain. In public. In real life. There's water and journeys to be made. Theo Of Golden

item.title: Expert Fake
item.description: The Berkeley professor is distraught becuase[^fb1] he's no longer the sole expert on Fake. The story is a story. The narration is the story. There is quaint dialogue that's made up. There are succi…
item.content:encoded: The Berkeley professor is distraught becuase[^fb1] he's no longer the sole expert on Fake. The story is a story. The narration is the story. There is quaint dialogue that's made up. There are succinct conclusions and large ommissions[^fb2] (does this professor own 100 acres in VT and a multimillion dollar[^fb10] Berkeley Hills mansion and have zero financial concerns that afford him time to talk to a friendly NYT reporter for an anti-tech diatribe?) It's not news. We can decide on that. But it's on the front page, above the fold; and we are warned of yet another existential threat. Framing liberal expertise as the savior, academics feel threatened by new democratizing technology. They are warning us that we should feel threatened (not empowered). Becuase[^fb3] they are scared (I am too), they retreat becuase[^fb4] they are cowards. They can afford to retreat. The farm in VT with 100 acres is just available. Not to you, dear reader. You will have to fend for yourself. The image of this professor using a chainsaw is real. But the story is fake becuase it purports to be genuine. The photo is edited. So, is that something we should dread? Are we expert enough to notice that the backkground is artificially blurred. "I saw that forest with my own eyes and none of it was blurred!" There is no perspiration on his shirt. "Is he stacking the wood later after the reporter leaves?" His pants have no accumulated caked sawdust. Where are the pieces of bark and debris? Did he just start work? His shoes are brand new. His body has no upper body muscle. His face isn't grimaced because he most likely cut once, the photographer Erin tapped her iPhone (maybe a 'real' camera because she's a 'real' reporter) with a badge that says PRESS.The photo tells the real story. He hasn't held a chainsaw often and prefers to use his hands to type on a computer to make a living. It's a pose. It's for the camera. It's an act. It's the 'News'. We're the experts with our own eyes. This guy don't know shit![^fb5] But we are told by cynical elites acting as experts who want to watch the world burn. 'Told you so!'[^fb6] Fake imagery is not new. 9/11 was only real because you saw it on television. How you interpreted that day was up to the media. Everything is mediated. Before TV, there was print, before print, there was aural[^fb7]. There was the tradition. It erodes with time. In news, there was Cronkite. Now the TV is on a screen in your pocket and everything on that screen is encrypted by amateurs. And amareurs use their eyes do decrypt[^fb8] the signs and symbols in the stories we make up and tell ourselves. But the stories can be positive if we want them to be. The news doesn't need to be negative. The youth cannot retreat. They will make up their own stories. And they will be positive because they have to be. There will be immaculate birth and resurection[^fb9]. There will be routine blessed by commandment. There has to be happily ever after. It can't be, "We're screwed." Editorial Notes This poem makes provocative claims about media expertise and the democratization of information, but its impact is diminished by several mechanical errors that distract readers from the argument. The misspellings of "because" (lines 8 and 12) and "omissions" (line 9) are particularly jarring, as they appear frequently and are fundamental to the piece's credibility. The grammar errors compound the spelling problems. "Guy don't know" (line 15) violates standard subject-verb agreement—"guy doesn't know" would be correct. Similarly, "do decrypt" (line 19) should be "to decrypt" for parallel structure with the infinitive form. The "Becuase" at the start of line 12 has both spelling and capitalization issues, as sentence-initial words must be capitalized regardless of internal errors. Word choice needs attention. "Aural" (line 18) refers to hearing or the ear, but the context suggests "oral" tradition—communication through speech—which better fits the historical progression from oral to print culture. The hyphen in "multimillion-dollar" (line 9) is required when the compound adjective precedes the noun it modifies; this is standard NYT style. The quoted phrase "'Told you so!'" (line 16) uses outer quotation marks unnecessarily. In the New York Times, we avoid decorative punctuation around quoted exclamations unless they are embedded within a larger sentence. Removing the outer quotes would clean up that line. For the more colorful "doesn't know shit," we might consider toning down to "doesn't know anything" or "doesn't know the subject matter" to maintain the Times' measured tone while preserving the sentiment. Fact-Checking and Additional Editorial Notes The factual claims in this text would require rigorous verification before publication. The reference to 9/11 being "only real because you saw it on television" is a provocative assertion that would need attribution or at minimum, clarification that this is the author's interpretation rather than an established fact. Walter Cronkite's historical role as a trusted news anchor is accurately referenced, though the comparison between his era and today's media landscape warrants more nuance. The Berkeley Hills mansion reference would benefit from specificity—Berkeley does have hills, but confirming whether the subject actually owns such property would be essential. The mention of "100 acres in VT" (Vermont) paired with a California location raises questions about the professor's actual geographic footprint that a fact-checker would pursue. Structurally, the poem shifts between three thematic sections—academic retreat, media critique, and generational optimism—without clear transitions. Consider breaking these into distinct stanzas or adding connective phrasing to guide readers through the argument. The phrase "routine blessed by commandment" is opaque and may confuse readers unfamiliar with the intended religious reference. The capitalization of "Fake" and "Fake imagery" suggests this is a proper noun or technical term in the author's lexicon, but without context, readers may wonder whether this refers to a specific concept, the general phenomenon of falseness, or is simply stylistic emphasis. Clarification or consistent treatment would help. Footnotes [^fb1]: "becuase" → "because" (spelling) [^fb2]: "ommissions" → "omissions" (spelling) [^fb3]: "Becuase" → "Because" (spelling, capitalization for sentence start) [^fb4]: "becuase" → "because" (spelling) [^fb5]: "guy don't know shit!" → "guy doesn't know shit!" (subject-verb agreement); consider "doesn't know anything" for NYT tone [^fb6]: "'Told you so!'" → "Told you so!" (remove unnecessary quotation marks) [^fb7]: "aural" → "oral" for clarity (oral tradition is the common phrase) [^fb8]: "do decrypt" → "to decrypt" (grammar) [^fb9]: "resurection" → "resurrection" (spelling) [^fb10]: "multimillion dollar" → "multimillion-dollar" (hyphenate compound adjective before noun)

item.title: AI Air
item.description: Airport alienation and the loss of human contact in a world of apps, AI, and automated everything.
item.content:encoded: AI Air Can't get home The true dystopia My Waymo only made right turns (I couldn't tell it otherwise) My airplane backseat screen is on an infinite ad loop. None of the actors act like humans. Are they aliens? They behave so I'm spiraling I immediately realize the only way home requires an app I notice there are no humans everywhere I look We're already extinct! My phone battery is dying Now my heart is racing - not because of my phone and its imminent lack of utility; I control that and I've mitigated it with electing to go yellow - battery save mode. I've got it under control. But it's not my device I can't control. It's the hermetic airport ecosystem with closed options. It's the plane with a novice pilot The descent is too steep! Is there a human at the yoke? I measure my exhale 6 Inhale, 6 Is AI flying the plane? Where are the humans? What happened to his intuition? Where's his grace? In the airport there were no customer service agents I can't catch an earlier flight without the app But the app was glitching My WIFI? I can't click the SUBMIT button. Javascript? Cookies? Reset? Restart? It won't accept my identification. The computer is zero trust. Pacing the airport, no one would make eye contact I just needed a human. No one can help me. I don't want small talk I don't want niceties I give up. Now I want mean Now I want to tussle, to feel - anything. I want to take back my money, I want violence I'm angry I'm emotional Everyone seems fine and unemotional. I'm not fine. I'm struggling with complacency. What's wrong with me? Control only what you can control. I can't control anything! The automatic sliding door opens But the United club is not United support They remind me there's an app for that I keep walking but can't find a gate agent. On the way, inflated prices for sustenance I don't want fast food I don't want a stomach ache I don't want to read a boring magazine. I don't want to sit by myself. There's nowhere to sit at the gate So I stand for a little Then I walk Every terminal is terminal There are quilts on the wall That is art I sip water only when someone is not filling their 5 gallon Nalgene quenching their non-thirst for their non-hike The fountain auto sensor needs my hands. It's not actually automatic. Suddenly I notice there are no children. Where did they all go? Then I see nobody has visible ears Ensconced in Headphones Speckled with white AirPods No eyes Just Screens Heart rate back up I'm panicking I don't scream because I know better I'm conditioned I'm soft The police would arrest me, of course I'm not crazy Am I crazy? Why is this what we want? If I notice, I'm not welcome Lose credit Gain debt My FICO would drop My premium would rise I would have a record I was a nuisance I disturbed the peace No one would befriend me I'd lose any followers I don't have My job would be at stake I wouldn't make no money To keep FICO up up and DEBT down down AI doesn't want my human Capital wants my money, my productivity Society wants my soul I want dead No one is listening anyway What's the point? My phone Battery indicator is yellow; 36 percent Wheels up We're flying We're so high Only me and the one three year old are exhilarated We're in chairs at 30,000 I want higher I want to go to the moon I haven't seen the stars for ages I want to escape I want the fuck out But I can't I have a family I have a job I'm a citizen So I go back To my screen To angry memes To strangers posting online identified by alphanumeric characters after an @ Next to jet power with pretzels and water The automated welcome message comes on Ding Prerecorded in perfect English Please sit down and fasten your seatbelts Before, at welcome the human novice took her shot She read the script like she was supposed to. Like a 5 year old learning to read Ding Each pause Welcome to the friendly… Smoking is… Federal law prohibits tampering… No!!! I don't want darling alien I want human!! I want human!! I want home!

item.title: NYT Critique
item.description: The President is Popular Therefore the Constitution Needs to be Changed That's NYT's Adam Liptak. He's regurgitating academic slop from privileged pontificators who have the time to scrutinize succ…
item.content:encoded: NYT Critique The President is Popular Therefore the Constitution Needs to be Changed That's NYT's Adam Liptak. He's regurgitating academic slop from privileged pontificators who have the time to scrutinize success. Thomas Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase was the first usurpation of executive power. The grievances for Trump: "President Trump has used the power of the federal government to bully universities, law firms and news outlets; undermined the independence of the Justice Department by instructing it to prosecute his political enemies; defied Congress by impounding money it had instructed him to spend; flouted countless court orders; and cut off funding to states led by Democrats." Bully universities into accounting for their federal grant largesse, their discriminatory admissions, their acceptance of foreign anti-American politics on campus, their artificial grading contrary to meritocratic standards, their squelching free speech that is the bedrock of Socratic epistemology, and their complicity in the student loan crisis. Mainstream news never honored FCC's equal time clause, Twitter was colluding with the FBI to crush opposition; the media never told the whole truth because they rely on advertising and never questioned Bidenites. Weaponization fund was responding to weaponization. The FBI should never have raided Mar-A-Lago for trivial offenses. Ditto Russiagate, and all the frivolous felonies from Tish. Two evils make a right, maybe not. Impounding money because funds were commingled with ulterior motives—there was no way to de-obligate. It tackles the deficit in accordance with the author's propounded good governance. We will need a whole lot more impoundment. Waste, fraud, and abuse is rampant. Cannot afford mandatory outlays with $97B debt service. Democratic state funding was found objectively fraudulent where state administrators failed to adhere to minimal audits and internal controls. Give me the king all you bitches moan about. This guy might as well have a "No Kings" banner in the title. The NYT frames everything through victimhood ### It's Trump's fault, "As the island nation faces economic collapse under the U.S. oil blockade." No, the country is run by a repressive unelected nut job who fails to concede to inevitable economic consequences (not coercion). Castro is actively denying citizen access to capital markets and elections. Cubans cannot vote and pursue life liberty and happiness. In America, our self-interested pursuits are expressed through economic actions which produce businesses that provide products/services to willing consumers who decide what goods (wood kindling instead of plastic) and services they want (personal mobility instead of 2 hours waiting) and how much they cost. Businesses satisfy aspirational demand and incidental tax revenue. The government's role is to facilitate markets. Everything else is downstream. So Trump is putting his fat thumb on the scale. Soon the scales tip in favor of might. He knows pressure points. Then the zealous government takes its rightful place as denigrated custodian of citizen rights and human dignity. I want to exchange goods and services with a Cuban. The US and Cuban governments serve me and my amigo. That's it. Real simple. Open Cuba. United flights to Havana. Unrestricted access. Freedom. Likewise for Ukrainians and Iranians. Trump cronies, Castro comrades, and Mamdani mandates ### 3 years, $4 million: 1 Patriot missile versus 1 month, $35,000: 200 Shahed drones. Robust capital markets produce viable alternatives like LUCAS (copy and paste of Shahed) and Nvidia Grace CPUs and Blackwell GPUs (the undeniable market leader). The problem with Heady Hegseth, Naughty Noem, and executive branch sycophants is they endorse anti-capitalist sentiment. They embrace sole source procurement because they think Big Orange with Big Beautiful Bill will pass scrutiny of exorbitant expenditures (likewise Mamdani's preschool push yet no new signups). That's the genius of congressional appropriation. The people (market demand) delegate appropriations, not Trump cronies, not Castro comrades, not Mamdani mandates. We vote. We buy.
