item.content:encoded: SpaceX IPO: $18.7B Revenue, $28.5T TAM, Dual-Class Control Executive Summary Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) filed its preliminary Form S-1 registration statement on May 20, 2026, revealing $18.7B in FY 2025 revenue and a $28.5 trillion total addressable market spanning space, connectivity, and AI. The company plans a dual-listing on Nasdaq Stock Market and Nasdaq Texas under ticker SPCX , with lead underwriters Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, BofA Securities, Citigroup, and J.P. Morgan. Despite filing with impressive scale metrics—9,600 satellites, 650 launches, 10.3M Starlink subscribers—the prospectus leaves key terms blank: offering size, price range, and valuation remain placeholders, suggesting the company is timing the market amid ongoing macro uncertainty. item.title: The Baumol Effect: Why Services Get Expensive
item.description: Baumol and Bowen, 1960s: wages in low-productivity sectors (healthcare, education) rise because they compete with high-productivity sectors (tech, manufacturing). Costs climb cumulatively, no produ…
item.content:encoded: The Baumol Effect A string quartet playing Beethoven in 2026 needs the same four musicians for the same thirty minutes as in 1966. Output is flat. But those musicians aren't earning 1966 wages. Wages rise everywhere. Even in jobs where output per hour has not changed. Manufacturing / tech: A worker with robots builds more cars than five assembly-line workers in 1970. Productivity rises, wages rise, prices fall. Healthcare, education, law, arts: A nurse changes a bandage, a professor grades an essay — same time in 2026 as 1966. Productivity doesn't budge. But wages still rise — because if a nurse can make more at Amazon, she leaves. Costs climb — without a productivity gain to justify it. 80% probability of more 2026 tech layoffs than 2025 ( More tech layoffs in 2026 than in 2025? ) → displaced workers enter low-productivity channels where output-per-hour gains do not compress costs; wage competition goes up, Baumol effect accelerates Job cuts Q1 2026: 217K ( Job Cuts Report ) → modeled peak at 275K in some months; actualized Q1 lighter than projected peak, still meaningfully elevated on a baseline basis 10-yr Treasury at 4.47% ( 10-yr Treasury Yield ) → hospitals and universities run 25-year bond programs at this floor; a 1% upward move on a $2T healthcare and education corporate/government municipal bond stack = roughly +$20B/year in additional debt-service cost April interest on debt: $97B ( Interest on Debt ) → one month of interest costs at a 4.47% marginal borrowing rate; compounding against expanding debt levels each rate cycle adds the equivalent of one full service-sector salary band annually Monthly deficit: April +$215B ( Monthly Budget Deficit ) → seasonal tax receipts create a one-month buffer; structurally the deficit runs deeper on mandatory programs that do not compress with productivity WTI at $91.06, Brent at $103.40 ( Oil (WTI) , Oil (Brent) ) → tight crude elevates logistics and mobility costs for labor-intensive delivery; a hospital, school, or day-care cannot substitute labor the way a factory can Consumer sentiment at 49.8 ( Consumer Sentiment ) → households Below 50 on UMich survey where 100 = 1966 baseline; perceived purchasing power erosion is a Baumol feel rather than a headline figure — services are being consumed at prices that only relatively higher earners can sustain U.S. petroleum exports at 12,881K bbl/day ( U.S. Petroleum Exports ) → energy output is elevated domestically; however the service sector — hospitals, schools, assisted living — absorbs cost through labor, with no productivity lever to respond

item.title: Berkshire Hathaway's Q1 2026 13F Filing
item.description: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway filed its Q1 2026 13F on Friday, revealing a $263B portfolio with 90 positions.
item.content:encoded: Berkshire Hathaway's Q1 2026 13F Filing Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway filed its Q1 2026 13F on Friday, revealing a $263B portfolio with 90 positions. Top holdings: Occidental Petroleum ($17.2B) Chubb ($11.2B) Kraft Heinz ($7.3B) Delta Air Lines ($2.6B) DaVita ($2.3B) The filing shows continued focus on energy and insurance, with OXY and Chevron making up nearly 7% of the portfolio combined. Notably, Berkshire reduced its position in Apple by 15% during the quarter, reflecting Buffett's ongoing caution about tech valuations. The conglomerate also initiated a new position in HP Inc., signaling interest in the personal computing sector. In other moves, Berkshire exited its stake in Wells Fargo completely, ending a long-held investment that dates back to the 1980s. The sale aligns with Buffett's recent comments about the challenges facing traditional banks in a low-interest-rate environment. Overall, the 13F filing underscores Berkshire's shift toward tangible assets and cash-generative businesses, while maintaining a substantial cash reserve of $189B for future opportunities.

item.title: Diaper Grift
item.description: California's $12.5M free diaper program reveals the inefficiency of state-administered charity - costing $0.50 per diaper through nonprofit middlemen when private markets deliver at $0.43 with bett…
item.content:encoded: Diaper Grift The press release tells you the feel-good story. Free diapers for needy families! The numbers tell the feel-bad reality. Only 'participating' hospitals. Only Baby2Baby diapers. Only one route for taxpayer dollars to flow: from the state budget, to a nonprofit's overhead, to a single vendor's warehouse, to a limited set of families. The budget tells you everything. The Unit Economics Line Item FY25-26 FY26-27 Diaper manufacturing cost $3.8M $7.6M Warehouse & logistics $0.8M $1.6M Direct program costs $1.6M $2.2M RFI exploration (Phase 2 commercial distribution) $0.5M — State operations $0.7M $1.1M Total $7.4M $12.5M 80 million diapers ÷ $12.5 million = $0.156 per diaper in direct acquisition. But the program doesn't stop at acquisition. It layers warehousing, state administration, and "direct program costs" that absorb another $5.3 million over two years. The effective cost per delivered diaper, when you include bureaucracy, is $0.50 — higher than Amazon's retail price for a comparable product. The Private Alternative Amazon sells Pampers Swaddlers 108-count for $45.99 delivered. That's $0.426 per diaper with: Choice of brand and size Home delivery No eligibility verification No nonprofit overhead No state employee salaries No feasibility studies for phase two A restricted-use voucher or direct cash transfer would cost less per family helped, empower parents to choose the diaper that fits their child, and eliminate layers of middlemen. But that would allocate resources through individual preference rather than bureaucratic contract. Baby2Baby's Balance Sheet Form 990 filings show the organization's financial structure: COO compensation: $239,742 Net revenue from gala: $2.4 million Net assets: $70.4 million In-kind donations: 614 The group's board and "angels" consists of LA philanthropists and entertainment executives. The annual gala generates millions in revenue that sustains the organization's operations and salaries. When taxpayer money enters this model, it flows through a well-funded nonprofit apparatus that excels at fundraising but not at minimizing overhead. Why This Pattern Persists Outsourcing to a nonprofit solves the political problem of "handing out cash" while creating an administrative ecosystem that requires: Contract management Reporting requirements Monitoring and compliance Brand stewardship Each layer adds cost. The result: $0.50 per diaper when the market delivers the same product at $0.43 with choice and convenience built in. The Real Allocator Private capital allocation means price discovery, competition, and innovation driving down costs while expanding choice. State-administered charity means appropriation, bureaucracy, and contracting driving up costs while narrowing options. California could simply give families a restricted-use benefit card loaded with the equivalent budget. Parents buy diapers where they shop, choose brands that work, and avoid the warehousing, nonprofit salaries, and state operations that consume 40% of the budget. Instead, the state chose a model that benefits: The nonprofit's fundraising narrative The vendor's negotiated contract The board's social capital The bureaucracy's budget justification Every stakeholder except the one who actually needs the diaper. Bottom Line Total program cost: $0.50+ per diaper Private market cost: $0.43 per diaper Administrative overhead: 40% of budget Choice: Zero — families receive what Baby2Baby provides Transparency: Budget documents obscure real unit costs The state could have achieved better outcomes by putting that money back in YOUR pocket. It chose ITS pocket instead. It's a grift. The families getting the diapers are the last ones to benefit from the money spent in THEIR name. item.title: Chatrie v. United States
item.description: Supreme Court to hear oral argument on Fourth Amendment geofence searches - whether warrantless location data collection violates constitutional privacy rights
item.content:encoded: Chatrie v. United States: Geofence Searches and the Fourth Amendment Case: Chatrie v. United States Docket: 25-112 Argued: 2026 Decision Expected: June/July 2026 Core Legal Question Whether the warrantless use of a geofence search — where law enforcement obtains location data from Google for all devices within a defined geographic area during a specific time window — violates the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures . What Is a Geofence Search? A geofence search allows law enforcement to: Define a geographic area (the "geofence") Specify a time window Obtain location data from Google for all devices that were within that area during that time Identify potential suspects without a warrant or individualized suspicion This technique has become increasingly common in criminal investigations, particularly for crimes like burglary, robbery, and vandalism where physical proximity to the crime scene is relevant. Constitutional Issue The Fourth Amendment requires that searches be reasonable. Traditionally, a search required: A warrant supported by probable cause, OR A recognized exception to the warrant requirement The government argues geofence searches fall under the third-party doctrine — that individuals have no reasonable expectation of privacy in information voluntarily shared with third parties (like Google, which collects location data for its services). Petitioner's argument: Modern location tracking reveals intimate details of life, and the third-party doctrine should not apply to the comprehensive, continuous surveillance that geofence searches enable. Precedents Likely to Shape the Decision Carpenter v. United States (2018) Held that cell-site location information (CSLI) requires a warrant. Established that historical location data is protected by the Fourth Amendment. Riley v. California (2014) Required a warrant to search a cell phone during an arrest. Recognized that modern digital devices contain vast personal information. Katz v. United States (1967) Established the "reasonable expectation of privacy" test. Information voluntarily shared with third parties may lose Fourth Amendment protection. United States v. Jones (2012) GPS tracking of a vehicle constitutes a search under the Fourth Amendment. Arguments Structure Petitioner (Chatrie) Position Geofence searches are unconstitutional because: They constitute general rummaging through private digital history No individualized suspicion for hundreds/thousands of devices swept Chilling effect on movement and association Google acts as unwilling government informant with massive data trove Third-party doctrine doesn't apply to comprehensive, warrantless surveillance Respondent (United States) Position Geofence searches are permissible because: Location data is voluntarily shared with third parties (third-party doctrine) The search is limited in time and space — not a general warrant Investigative technique less invasive than physical search Good faith reliance on existing legal authority Necessary for modern law enforcement in the digital age Key Themes to Watch During Oral Argument 1. Digital Privacy Expectations How does the Court frame privacy expectations in location data? Does geofence data reveal "intimate details" of life? Distinction between voluntary sharing and pervasive surveillance 2. Scope and Scale How many devices can be searched without a warrant? What limits should exist on geographic and temporal scope? Can the government conduct multiple overlapping geofence searches? 3. Technological Understanding Will justices grasp geofencing mechanics? Expect multiple "what if" hypotheticals testing boundaries: - Smaller vs. larger geographic areas - Longer vs. shorter time windows - Different data providers (Google vs. others) 4. Practical Implications Effect on criminal investigations and digital evidence collection Role of private sector (Google's data retention policies) Implications for other digital surveillance techniques Potential Outcomes Ruling for Chatrie (Petitioner Wins) Geofence searches require a warrant Strong Fourth Amendment protection for location data Law enforcement must use traditional methods (witnesses, cameras, other evidence) May require legislative solution for regulated geofence access Ruling for United States (Government Wins) Geofence searches permissible without warrant under third-party doctrine Broad latitude for digital investigation techniques Enhanced law enforcement tools but reduced privacy protections Possible call for legislative regulation instead Narrow Ruling Court crafts case-specific test May uphold some geofence uses while limiting others Leaves broader questions for future cases Justice Questioning Patterns to Watch Conservative bloc: May defer to law enforcement but emphasize property/trespass principles. Liberal bloc: May expand privacy rights beyond Carpenter, concerned about government surveillance. Swing justices: Likely to probe practical effects, notice-and-consent frameworks, and whether alternative methods exist. Broader Implications This case will determine: Digital privacy scope in the age of continuous location tracking Third-party doctrine viability as technology evolves Law enforcement capabilities for investigating crimes in digital environments Balance between security and liberty in the 21st century The ruling will affect not just geofence searches but also other emerging surveillance techniques that rely on data collected by private companies. Amendments Referenced Fourth Amendment: Protection against unreasonable searches and seizures What's at Stake If the Court rules for Chatrie: Law enforcement will need warrants for geofence searches Location data receives heightened Fourth Amendment protection Similar digital surveillance techniques may be restricted If the Court rules for the United States: Warrantless geofence searches become a standard investigative tool Broad expansion of government access to digital data without judicial oversight Potential for widespread use across thousands of investigations annually Stakes: This case will shape the future of digital privacy and define the limits of government surveillance in an era where our movements are constantly tracked by private companies. Resources Supreme Court Docket 25-112 Complete case docket with all filings, briefs, and procedural history Oral Argument Transcript (PDF) Complete word-for-word transcript of oral arguments Oral Argument Audio (MP3) Full audio recording from the Supreme Court Oral Argument Podcast Apple Podcasts feed of Supreme Court oral arguments SCOTUSblog Case Coverage Expert legal analysis, justice voting patterns, and predicted outcomes Key Precedents Carpenter v. United States (2018) Cell-site location information requires a warrant under the Fourth Amendment Riley v. California (2014) Search of cell phone during arrest requires a warrant Katz v. United States (1967) Established the reasonable expectation of privacy test United States v. Jones (2012) GPS tracking of a vehicle constitutes a Fourth Amendment search Timeline Cert. Granted: Early 2025 Oral Argument: 2026 Decision Expected: Late June / Early July 2026 Related Cases: Carpenter v. United States (2018), Riley v. California (2014), Katz v. United States (1967)

item.title: 1996: The Last Time Bipartisanship Worked on Immigration
item.description: In 1996, Congress passed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act with a 97-3 Senate vote. President Bill Clinton signed it into law.
item.content:encoded: 1996 to 2026: Only citizens are eligible to vote In 1996, Congress passed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act with a 97-3 Senate vote. President Bill Clinton signed it into law. The bill strengthened border enforcement, mandated employer verification, and explicitly prohibited non-citizens from voting in federal elections. Current House joint resolution seeks to reaffirm this same principle.

item.title: The Shrinking Middle Class Myth
item.description: A new AEI report challenges the populist narrative that America's middle class is hollowing out. Using an absolute definition (constant purchasing power thresholds) rather than Pew's relative appro…
item.content:encoded: The Shrinking Middle Class Myth A new AEI report challenges the populist narrative that America's middle class is hollowing out. Using an absolute definition (constant purchasing power thresholds) rather than Pew's relative approach, the data tells a different story. The "core" middle class did shrink slightly: from 36% of families in 1979 to 31% in 2024. But here's what the doom-sayers miss: the upper-middle class tripled from 10% to 31%. Meanwhile, those below the middle class fell from 54% to 35%. In 2024, for the first time in US history, more families were above the core middle class (35%) than below it (34%). Combined, the lower-, core, and upper-middle classes now represent 78% of families, up from 70% in 1979. The upper-middle class now receives half of all family income. The authors argue that declining middle-class shares reflect people moving up , not down. The pie grew, and everyone got a bigger slice. Download PDF The lesson: be skeptical of any claim that everyone's getting poorer while the rich get richer. Both can be true. But if the poor are getting richer too, that's not a crisis.

item.content:encoded: NYC's Preliminary Racial Equity Plan New York City has released its Preliminary Racial Equity Plan, charting community equity priorities and outcome indicators across multiple city agencies. While the stated goal is addressing historical inequities in areas like education, housing, and criminal justice, the extensive bureaucratic apparatus required to monitor and enforce these outcomes feels inherently inefficient. The city's persistent focus on categorizing residents and prioritizing specific demographic groups raises questions about the long-term economic and social implications for a metropolis that fundamentally requires meritocratic engines of growth. item.title: FY 2027 Budget Request
item.description: The White House released its Fiscal Year 2027 budget request today, a "skinny budget" that signals a massive shift in federal priorities. The proposal calls for a staggering $1.5 trillion in total…
item.content:encoded: FY 2027 Budget: Defense Surges, Everything Else Shrinks The White House released its Fiscal Year 2027 budget request today, a "skinny budget" that signals a massive shift in federal priorities. The proposal calls for a staggering $1.5 trillion in total defense funding, while stripping 10% from non-defense discretionary spending to target what the administration calls "woke and wasteful" programs. The request serves as the opening salvo in the 2027 appropriations cycle, setting the stage for a contentious battle in Congress over the nation's fiscal direction. Key Highlights: Defense Spending: A $1.5 trillion total request, representing a major year-over-year rise. This includes a $251 billion increase in base defense discretionary spending and $350 billion in a new reconciliation bill. Non-Defense Discretionary: A $73 billion (10%) reduction in base spending, targeting programs the administration describes as "weaponized and wasteful." Energy and Environment: Substantial cuts to climate and environmental programs, including $15.2 billion from Department of Energy programs and reductions in EPA environmental justice grants. NASA: A 23% reduction to NASA’s budget (totaling $18.8 billion). The request maintains support for Artemis lunar exploration but calls for terminating over 40 missions and eliminating STEM engagement programs. The proposal reflects a hard-line fiscal conservative approach, prioritizing military strength and border security while aggressively scaling back the administrative state and green energy initiatives. View the full budget (PDF)

item.title: Birthright on the Brink
item.description: The Supreme Court oral arguments in Trump v. Barbara (2026) have resurrected a 19th-century linguistic ghost: the distinction between physical presence and legal "allegiance." Justice Gorsuch, ever…
item.content:encoded: Birthright on the Brink: Domicile and the 19th Century Mind The Supreme Court oral arguments in Trump v. Barbara (2026) have resurrected a 19th-century linguistic ghost: the distinction between physical presence and legal "allegiance." Justice Gorsuch, ever the originalist, pushed counsel on whether the 14th Amendment's "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" clause requires more than just being on U.S. soil. He zeroed in on "domicile"—a concept that, in the 1860s, implied a voluntary submission to the sovereign’s protection in exchange for loyalty. The debate took a sharp turn into the history of American slavery. Critics point out that enslaved people were brought to these shores without consent, yet their children’s citizenship was a cornerstone of the Reconstruction Amendments. Some historical legal theories even argued that slaves remained "allegiant" to their African countries of origin until emancipated—a narrative that complicates the "voluntary" requirement for birthright. The stakes are contemporary. If birthright citizenship hinges on a parent's "allegiance" or "domicile," what happens to the children of modern exploitation? Modern child slaves or victims of trafficking don't choose their domicile. If the law requires a voluntary pact of allegiance, these most vulnerable individuals could be legally erased from the nation they were forced into. Global context suggests the U.S. remains an outlier. According to the Law Library of Congress, the vast majority of countries—particularly in Europe and Asia—do not grant unconditional jus soli (birthright citizenship). As the Court weighs these 19th-century definitions, they aren't just parsing grammar; they are deciding if the American experiment of "all born here" survives the modern era. Read the LoC Report

item.title: Case-Shiller Decline Continues
item.description: The Case-Shiller National Home Price Index dipped to 326.612 in January, down 0.1% from December's 326.969. The index has been drifting lower since peaking at 331.608 last June, shedding roughly 1.…
item.content:encoded: Case-Shiller Decline Continues into 2026 The Case-Shiller National Home Price Index dipped to 326.612 in January, down 0.1% from December's 326.969. The index has been drifting lower since peaking at 331.608 last June, shedding roughly 1.5% over seven months. {{chart:Case-Shiller National Home Price Index}} Home prices are not crashing, but they are no longer rising. Affordability constraints from mortgage rates above 6% have capped buyer demand while inventory has slowly rebuilt. The result is a market where sellers still list high but eventually cut, and buyers pick through stale listings looking for motivated counterparts. Year-over-year, January's reading is down 0.3% from 327.752 last March. The annual gains that characterized the post-pandemic era have flipped negative. Whether this stabilizes or accelerates depends on rates, and rates depend on the Fed, and the Fed is watching the same labor market data everyone else is. View housing indicators

item.title: Job Openings down 358,000
item.description: February job openings dropped to 6.88 million, down 358,000 from January's revised 7.24 million. January was revised up from an initial 7.18 million, making the month-over-month decline look steepe…
item.content:encoded: Job Openings down 358,000 February job openings dropped to 6.88 million, down 358,000 from January's revised 7.24 million. January was revised up from an initial 7.18 million, making the month-over-month decline look steeper than it might have otherwise. Still, the 4.9% monthly drop signals the labor market remains stuck in a tightening-to-loosening transition that started last fall. The nonfarm side tells a similar story. February nonfarm employment came in at 158.466 million, down 92,000 from January's revised 158.558 million. {{chart:Job Openings}} The JOLTS data has been noisy month to month, but the trend is unmistakable. Openings peaked near 7.5 million in 2022 and have stair-stepped lower since. February's print sits near the bottom of the post-pandemic range, well below the 7+ million readings that characterized a tight labor market. What the data does not show is the other side of the equation. Hiring remains tepid, layoffs have not surged, and the quit rate has stayed subdued for over a year. Workers are holding on. Employers are holding off. The result is a labor market that is neither hot nor cold but frozen in place. View employment indicators

item.title: The President is a Steward of the White House
item.description: Judge Richard Leon granted a preliminary injunction today blocking all physical development of the proposed White House ballroom at the former site of the East Wing. The order in National Trust for…
item.content:encoded: Judge Richard Leon granted a preliminary injunction today blocking all physical development of the proposed White House ballroom at the former site of the East Wing. The order in National Trust for Historic Preservation v. National Park Service (D.D.C., 25-4316) bars demolition, site preparation, excavation, foundation work, and any other construction activity unless strictly necessary for safety and security of the White House grounds. Order (PDF) · Memorandum & Opinion (PDF) The 35-page opinion traces White House construction authority back to the Residence Act of 1790 , which authorized commissioners to "provide suitable buildings for the accommodation of ... the President." Judge Leon wrote: "The President of the United States is the steward of the White House for future generations of First Families. He is not, however, the owner!" The court found that 3 U.S.C. § 105(d)(1), which authorizes funds for "care, maintenance, repair, alteration, refurnishing, improvement, air-conditioning, heating, and lighting," covers ordinary upkeep — not wholesale demolition and new construction of a $400 million ballroom funded by private donations routed through a "convoluted funding scheme" resembling a " Rube Goldberg contraption ." In plain terms: the President is the tenant, Congress is the landlord. You can't gut the kitchen and build an addition without asking first. The injunction takes effect 14 days from today. Defendants named in the order include the National Park Service, Department of the Interior under Secretary Douglas Burgum, General Services Administration, the Executive Office of the President, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and the Office of the Executive Residence. The Court further ordered that no such work shall proceed absent express authorization from Congress. Defendants must file a compliance status report within 21 days after the order takes effect.

item.title: One Bad Taste
item.description: OneTaste founder Nicole Daedone was sentenced to nine years in prison and former Head of Sales Rachel Cherwitz to 78 months for forced labor conspiracy (E.D.N.Y., 23-CR-146). Judge Gujarati also im…
item.content:encoded: One Bad Taste OneTaste founder Nicole Daedone was sentenced to nine years in prison and former Head of Sales Rachel Cherwitz to 78 months for forced labor conspiracy (E.D.N.Y., 23-CR-146). Judge Gujarati also imposed a $12 million forfeiture judgment against Daedone and awarded $887,877.64 in restitution to seven victims. Both were convicted by a federal jury in June 2025. DOJ press release · Govt Rule 29 opposition (PDF) The government had filed opposition to the defendants' Rule 29 motion for acquittal, arguing it was procedurally improper and that the First Amendment does not shield criminal conduct carried out in spiritual garb. Nine victim-witnesses testified to patterns of psychological, financial, sexual, and physical coercion spanning 2006 through 2018, including being coerced into becoming sexual "handlers" for OneTaste's initial investor and performing sex acts with prospective clients under threat of termination, demotion, and financial ruin. U.S. Attorney Nocella stated: "Coercion disguised as wellness or empowerment is still exploitation and it is a crime that causes harm to vulnerable victims." FBI ADIC Barnacle added that Daedone and Cherwitz "preyed on vulnerable women, coercing them into a calculated forced labor conspiracy" through "repeated psychological manipulation and sexual abuse."

item.content:encoded: Think-Tank Main Street These are the think-tanks that squander your money in good faith. Benevolent bookworms ingest Main Street. Opportunity Insights is a non-partisan, not-for-profit organization based at Harvard University and directed by Raj Chetty, John Friedman, and Nathaniel Hendren. They conduct scientific research using "big data" on how to improve upward mobility and work collaboratively with local stakeholders to translate these research findings into policy change.

item.title: Calcium Oxide Energy Storage
item.description: Calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts with water in a violently exothermic release — up to 1,155 kJ per kilogram of CaO. The reaction is simple, ancient, and reversible. Heat calcium hydroxide back abov…
item.content:encoded: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + Δ Calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts with water in a violently exothermic release — up to 1,155 kJ per kilogram of CaO. The reaction is simple, ancient, and reversible. Heat calcium hydroxide back above 512°C and you recover the oxide and the water. What you store is not electrons in lithium or pumped uphill in a reservoir. You store energy in a chemical bond that sits at ambient temperature indefinitely, loses nothing to self-discharge, and costs almost nothing per unit of stored heat. The Thermodynamics CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + 65.2 kJ/mol The reverse: Ca(OH)₂ + heat → CaO + H₂O The round-trip efficiency hovers around 70-80% depending on insulation and recovery method. Compare to lithium-ion batteries at 85-95% but with degradation over 10-15 years, or pumped hydro at 70-85% but requiring geography. Calcium hydroxide stores heat at 400-600°C in a powder that sits in a bag on a shelf. No charge cycles. No capacity fade. No fire risk from dendrites. It does not care if you use it tomorrow or in thirty years. Scale Global quicklime production is roughly 350 million tonnes per year. The infrastructure to produce, transport, and handle CaO is mature — it is one of the oldest industrial chemicals on Earth, used in cement, steel, water treatment, and agriculture. The supply chain exists. The material is abundant. Limestone (CaCO₃) is the most common sedimentary rock on the planet. You calcine it at 900°C to get CaO, then you hydrate it to store energy, then you calcine it again to release. The cycle is: Charge : Apply heat (solar thermal, industrial waste heat, nuclear) to Ca(OH)₂ → CaO + H₂O Store : CaO sits inert at ambient temperature for hours, days, months, years Discharge : Add water → Ca(OH)₂ + heat (up to 500°C steam) Cache Energy — This Is Real Cache Energy out of Champaign, Illinois is building this. Solid-state thermochemical storage at 1,000°F, tested down to –40°F charge retention. No combustion. No moving parts in the charger or discharger. Dispatch range from 1 to 1,000 hours. 30+ year design life. Ships in a standard container and sets up in 1-2 days. The lease model is the play: zero upfront capex, performance-guaranteed, no site prep required. "The asset is ours. The output is yours." Heat as a service. You pay for thermal BTUs, not batteries, not infrastructure, not engineering studies. Their product page lists the attributes: simple (no moving parts), stable (ambient temperature storage, non-reactive material), seamless (plugs into existing process), flexible (hourly to annual dispatch), rapid (1-2 day deployment), transportable (charge at point A, discharge at point B). Applications District heating. Store summer solar thermal. Discharge in winter for building heat. No battery, no grid dependency, no seasonal storage penalty. Industrial process heat. Cement, glass, ceramics, and chemical manufacturing need temperatures between 300-900°C. Current solutions burn natural gas. Thermochemical storage provides dispatchable heat from intermittent renewable sources. Grid-scale backup. Not for electricity directly — for heat. 70% of global energy demand is thermal, not electrical. Store the heat chemically, convert to steam turbine power when needed. Spatial and temporal arbitrage. Charge at point A (where energy is cheap or abundant), discharge at point B (where heat is needed). Transport the material, not the energy. The Catch The reaction causes particle attrition — repeated cycling breaks down the granules, reducing reactivity over hundreds of cycles. Researchers mitigate this with structural supports (Al₂O₃, TiO₂ matrices) or by operating with larger particle beds where surface area loss is manageable. The energy density by mass (1 MJ/kg for the reaction itself) is lower than hydrocarbons (45 MJ/kg for natural gas), so you need volume. But you also need nothing else — no pipeline, no combustion chamber, no emissions controls, no carbon tax. Why It Matters The energy transition is mostly an electricity story. But electricity is 20% of global final energy consumption. The other 80% is heat, transport, and industrial processes. Batteries solve the electricity storage problem. Nothing mainstream solves the heat storage problem at scale. Calcium looping does. It is not sexy. It is not a startup pitch. It is limestone and water and thermodynamics that have been understood for two hundred years. The cache is the point. You write energy to a chemical disk. It sits. You read it back when you need it. No self-discharge. No calendar aging. No supply chain dependency on cobalt, lithium, or rare earths. Just calcium, oxygen, and hydrogen — the three most abundant reactive elements on Earth. Cache Energy | Product

item.title: The Religious No Kings
item.description: Was not Religion the first No Kings?
item.content:encoded: The Religious No Kings Was not Religion the first No Kings? Before there were secular republics, before Magna Carta, before the French Revolution guillotined its way through divine right, there was a people who looked at earthly authority and said: No. The God of Abraham did not negotiate with Pharaoh. He sent plagues. The Hebrew Bible's book of Judges frames the demand for a King as apostasy — the people reject God's direct governance and beg for a man in a crown, and God warns them what that crown will cost: their sons, their daughters, their fields, their freedom. Samuel 8:11-18 reads like a libertarian pamphlet. The King will take. The King will take. The King will take. Religion, particularly monotheism, was the original anti-tyrannical project. It posited an authority higher than any man. No emperor, no pharaoh, no Caesar could claim supremacy when God stood above. The early Christians were fed to lions not because they were meek, but because they refused to burn incense to the emperor's genius. They were ungovernable. Their refusal to worship the state was the first civil disobedience, and the state killed them for it. The Protestant Reformation doubled down. Luther at Worms: "Here I stand, I can do no other." The individual conscience against the institutional machine. The printing press was their social media, and the Pope was their overreach. They decentralized spiritual authority just as the Enlightenment would later decentralize political authority. The trajectory is clean: from God above Kings, to reason above God, to the individual above all. What Do Atheists Want? The Freedom From Religion Foundation lists fifty staff and board members. Lawyers, editors, IT directors, a marketing department. They want what every anti-tyrannical movement has wanted: the removal of an illegitimate authority from the machinery of governance. In their case, the illegitimate authority is religious doctrine embedded in state power. Their position is structurally identical to the Reformers. Luther said the Pope has no authority over the civil magistrate. The FFRF says the pastor has no authority over the school board. The mechanism is the same: separation. The target is different. But here is where it gets interesting. If religion was the first No Kings, then atheism is the logical endpoint of that same impulse. You reject earthly Kings in favor of divine authority. Then you reject divine authority in favor of reason. Then what? You are left with the individual, standing alone, accountable to nothing but natural law and the social contract. The arc bends toward autonomy. Every step removes a layer of sovereignty above the self. The Paradox The paradox is that the No Kings movement has itself become a kind of church. The $550 billion, up from $256 billion Walton family funded the No Kings protests. A billionaire funds the anti-authority movement. The funded movement manufactures consent. The consent produces a mandate. The mandate becomes authority. The circle closes. Billionaires donate to foundations which then fund nonprofit organizations and grassroots movements. These groups create the appearance of organic popular support while their funding sources remain obscured. The No Kings protest has a King. His name is the DNC. His cathedral is a non-profit foundation. His tithe is tax-deductible. "To be GOVERNED is to be watched, inspected, spied upon, directed, law-driven, numbered, regulated, enrolled, indoctrinated, preached at, controlled..." The list is exhaustive and exhausting. But notice: preached at . The secular state still preaches. It just calls its sermons policy. The FFRF wants freedom from religion. But freedom from is always freedom toward something else. Remove the cathedral and you get the TED talk. Remove the sermon and you get the policy brief. Remove the priest and you get the professor. The pulpit doesn't disappear; it changes clothes. Boston Common The Real Question The question is not whether atheists are right that religion has no place in governance. They are. The question is whether the project of removing authority ever terminates, or whether it simply replaces one priesthood with another. The Hebrews wanted a King. God gave them Saul. They got what they asked for. Every No Kings movement eventually produces a new King. The French Revolution produced Napoleon. The Russian Revolution produced Stalin . The American Revolution produced a presidency that now spends $1.5 trillion on national defense and $92 billion a month servicing debt. The No Kings protest is produced by the Democrat political machine . They want their King back whoever the nominee may be. The first No Kings was religion. The latest No Kings is funded by billionaires. Between those two facts lies the entire problem of human governance: you cannot remove authority without creating it. For the religious, that something is God. For the Left, it is supposed to be the Constitution, the rule of law, and the electorate . But it only applies with their electorate in charge.

item.title: Cox v. Sony Music Entertainment
item.description: Supreme Court unanimously reverses billion-dollar judgment, holding ISPs cannot be held contributorily liable for customer infringement without proof of inducement or a service tailored to infringe…
item.content:encoded: Cox v. Sony: Can ISPs Be Liable for Customer Copyright Infringement? Case: Cox Communications, Inc. v. Sony Music Entertainment, et al. Case Number: 24-171 Oral Argument Date: December 1, 2025 Decision Date: March 25, 2026 Vote: 9–0, reversed and remanded Opinion Author: Justice Thomas Concurrence: Justice Sotomayor (joined by Justice Jackson) The Question Whether Internet service providers can face copyright liability for providing service to customers they know are infringing, or whether safe harbor protections under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act shield them from suit. The Arguments Cox's Position Cox argues it cannot be held liable for its customers' illegal conduct merely for failing to terminate their service. Counsel E. Joshua Rosenkranz stated: "The Fourth Circuit held that a provider of basic communications infrastructure to millions of homes and businesses can be held liable because it did not kick enough accused infringers off the Internet." Rosenkranz emphasized that neither copyright law nor tort law permits this theory. He cited Twitter v. Taamneh , where the Supreme Court held there is no duty requiring service providers "to terminate customers after discovering that the customers were using the service for illegal ends." The critical point: providing generic internet service is fundamentally passive. Knowledge that some customers infringe does not transform that service into active inducement. Sony's Position Sony argues Cox's conduct crosses from passive to culpable. The company provided ongoing service to "habitual abusers"—customers Cox itself identified as repeat infringers—knowing infringement would continue. Counsel Paul D. Clement stated the distinction plainly: a "one-and-done sale of an item that can be used in a way to infringe but is generally used lawfully" differs fundamentally from providing service "to known infringers with substantial knowledge that what they themselves called habitual abusers would continue to infringe." Clement highlighted admissions in the record that Cox employees disregarded copyright law. He argued Cox's position would render the DMCA "a dead letter" if ISPs could "take tens of thousands of copyright notices and throw them in the trash" with no consequences. Secondary Liability: Judge-Made, Not Statutory The Copyright Act does not expressly create secondary liability. Section 501(a) provides that "[a]nyone who violates any of the exclusive rights of the copyright owner" is an infringer—but it says nothing about holding third parties liable for someone else's infringement. The two recognized categories of secondary copyright liability are entirely judicial creations: Contributory liability: A party that knowingly induces or materially contributes to another's infringement. Developed through decades of lower-court decisions, notably Gershwin Publishing Corp. v. Columbia Artists Management (2d Cir. 1971). Vicarious liability: A party that has the right and ability to supervise infringement and a direct financial interest in it. Rooted in agency and respondeat superior principles. The DMCA's safe harbor provisions in § 512 presuppose that some form of secondary liability exists—otherwise, as Clement argued, there would be nothing to limit. But the statute never codifies the standard. It merely conditions safe harbor protection on compliance with certain requirements (lack of knowledge, repeat infringer policy, response to takedown notices), assuming without stating that non-compliance could expose ISPs to liability. This gap between statutory text and judicial doctrine is where Cox v. Sony lives. The majority narrowed contributory liability to two express tracks—inducement and tailoring—while declining to recognize any broader statutory framework. The concurrence argued this leaves a vacuum where Congress intended ISPs to have incentives to cooperate with copyright holders. Core Legal Tension The Court grappled with a straightforward but elusive question: What separates passive enablement from culpable material contribution? The Inducement Standard Under Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Studios v. Grokster (2005), secondary liability requires that a defendant act with the purpose of fostering infringement. This demands more than knowledge—it requires intent directed at promoting violations. Deputy Solicitor General Malcolm L. Stewart emphasized this during argument: "Both in copyright law and more generally, this form of secondary liability is reserved for persons who act for the purpose of facilitating violations of law. Because Cox simply provided the same generic Internet services to infringers and non-infringers alike, there is no basis for inferring such a purpose here." Knowledge Versus Purpose Justice Elena Kagan pressed Cox on whether corporate conduct matters at all. Rosenkranz conceded: Cox could be "the worst corporate citizen of all time and still it doesn't matter, that there would be no liability." What matters legally is purpose, not degree of responsibility. This raises a paradox Justice Kagan identified: if Cox wins, why would ISPs continue cooperating with copyright holders through notice systems? Clement replied that willful blindness—deliberate refusal to read takedown notices—could itself satisfy the standard for aiding and abetting. The DMCA Safe Harbor Problem The DMCA § 512 provides a limited liability safe harbor for ISPs that meet four conditions: lack knowledge of infringement, lack financial benefit from it, implement a repeat infringer policy, and respond expeditiously to takedown notices. But the statute assumes some relationship between compliance and liability. If there is no liability for habitual infringement, why have safe harbors at all? Clement highlighted the tension: "Why bother with a safe harbor? Why limit liability... if there's no liability to limit?" Critical Hypotheticals Justice Elena Jackson posed the hardest case: a customer directly tells Cox "I am addicted to infringing on the Internet. I've been sued before... and Cox, based on where I live, is my only option." Rosenkranz acknowledged it "pushes the envelope" but held his ground: Cox would bear no liability even in that scenario. Direct infringement suits against the customer remain available. Justice Jackson followed with a common law question: Would ordinary aiding-and-abetting principles suffice? Rosenkranz said no, common law, like copyright, requires "a culpable act." Stakes This case determined whether copyright law treats internet service as a commodity (with passive protection) or as a potential partner in infringement when knowledge and ongoing relationship are present. Cox prevailed. ISPs have broad legal room to provide generic service without policing customer conduct. The ruling significantly narrows secondary copyright liability for providers of general-purpose services. The Decision The Supreme Court unanimously reversed the Fourth Circuit's judgment holding Cox contributorily liable. Justice Thomas, writing for a 7-Justice majority, held that a service provider is contributorily liable for a user's infringement only if it intended that the provided service be used for infringement —and that intent can be shown in only two ways: The Two-Track Framework for Secondary Liability Inducement: The provider actively encouraged infringement through specific acts—marketing the service as a tool for piracy or taking affirmative steps to promote illegal use. This track follows Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Studios v. Grokster (2005). Service Tailored to Infringement: The provider offers a product incapable of "substantial" or "commercially significant" noninfringing uses. This track follows Sony Corp. v. Universal City Studios (1984)—the Betamax case. The majority held that there is no third option . "Knowledge plus material contribution"—or even "knowledge plus inaction"—cannot satisfy the standard. Thomas emphasized: "Under our precedents, a company is not liable as a copyright infringer for merely providing a service to the general public with knowledge that it will be used by some to infringe copyrights." Applied to Cox The Court found neither track satisfied: No inducement: Sony had "no evidence of marketing to promote infringement," and Cox repeatedly discouraged infringement in its terms of service and communications. No tailoring: "Cox simply provided Internet access, which is used for many purposes other than copyright infringement." Generic internet service has abundant commercially significant noninfringing uses. The Court vacated the billion-dollar judgment and remanded for further proceedings. The Sotomayor Concurrence Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Jackson, concurred only in the judgment. She argued the majority "unnecessarily limits secondary liability" and "dismantles the statutory incentive structure that Congress created" through the DMCA. Sotomayor would retain the "knowledge plus material contribution" test and argued that other common-law theories of secondary liability—such as aiding and abetting—remain available. Under her approach, Cox still wins, but only because Sony failed to prove enough affirmative conduct, not because the legal standard forecloses the theory entirely. The DMCA After Cox The majority dismissed Sony's argument that the DMCA's safe harbor provisions presuppose underlying contributory liability. Thomas wrote that Sony "overreads" the statute. The concurrence, however, highlighted the tension: if ISPs face no contributory liability for ignoring repeat infringement, the DMCA's repeat-infringer policy requirements and notice-and-takedown framework lose much of their practical force. As Clement argued at oral argument: "Why bother with a safe harbor? Why limit liability... if there's no liability to limit?" Resources Supreme Court Opinion (March 25, 2026) Supreme Court Docket 24-171 Oral Argument Audio Oral Argument Transcript (December 1, 2025) SCOTUSblog: Court rejects billion-dollar judgment (March 26, 2026) SCOTUSblog Case Page

item.title: Noem v. Al Otro Lado - Oral Argument Analysis
item.description: Analysis of the March 24, 2026 Supreme Court oral argument in Noem v. Al Otro Lado, examining whether asylum seekers stopped at the Mexican border have "arrived in the United States"
item.content:encoded: Noem v. Al Otro Lado Oral Argument Analysis - March 24, 2026 Case Overview Docket: No. 25-5 Argued: March 24, 2026 Issue: Whether an alien who is stopped on the Mexican side of the U.S.-Mexico border has "arrived in the United States" within the meaning of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. §§ 1158(a)(1), 1225(a)(1), 1225(a)(3)) Petitioner: Kristi Noem, Secretary of Homeland Security Respondent: Al Otro Lado, Inc. (immigrant rights organization) Lower Court: Ninth Circuit (ruled for respondents in October 2024) Background The case centers on the "metering" policy employed by U.S. Customs and Border Protection since 2016. Under this policy, officials at U.S.-Mexico border ports of entry turned back noncitizens (including asylum seekers) to wait on the Mexican side before being processed. The policy was discontinued by the Biden administration in 2021, but the Trump administration has indicated it may reinstate it. The Ninth Circuit held that noncitizens who present themselves at a port of entry - even if physically located in Mexico - have "arrived in the United States" under federal immigration law and must be allowed to apply for asylum. Issues at Hand Primary Issue Statutory Interpretation: Does "arrives in the United States" require physical presence within U.S. borders, or does presenting at a port of entry suffice? Constitutional Questions Separation of powers - Executive discretion in border management Treaty obligations under U.N. Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees Practical Implications Whether the government can legally turn away asylum seekers at the border Potential reinstatement of the metering policy Impact on asylum seekers waiting in Mexico Resources Supreme Court Docket Audio (MP3) Transcript PDF Apple Podcasts SCOTUSblog Coverage Oral Argument Summary The argument lasted approximately 80 minutes. Assistant to the Solicitor General Vivek Suri argued for the government, while Kelsi Corkran argued for the respondents. Petitioner's Position (Government) Suri argued that "in ordinary English," a person "arrives in" a place when they are physically there - not standing at the threshold. He invoked the Court's 1993 decision in Sale v. Haitian Centers Council , which held that the extraterritorial application of refugee protections did not apply. Key arguments: "You can't arrive in the United States while you're still standing in Mexico" The policy is a reasonable exercise of executive discretion International treaties apply to actions "within the United States," not outside Respondent's Position (Al Otro Lado) Corkran argued that Congress intended to provide asylum protections to those seeking refuge at our doors, and that presenting at a port of entry constitutes "arriving." Key arguments: The statute uses "arrives in" not "enters" Those waiting in line at a port of entry are at the threshold of the U.S. The government cannot condition access to asylum on illegal border crossing Justice Questions and Positions Chief Justice John Roberts Explored where exactly the line should be drawn Asked whether "how many people are in line" affects the analysis Appeared sympathetic to government's position that physical presence is required Justice Clarence Thomas Asked about international law and its bearing on the dispute Inquired whether U.N. Convention applies extraterritorially Justice Sonia Sotomayor Skeptical of government's interpretation Pressed on whether the policy violates the letter and spirit of refugee protections Noted that the government "lets in workers with permits" and other categories Observed: "They've arrived. They are knocking at the door." Expressed concern about creating a system where only those who cross illegally can access asylum Justice Elena Kagan Identified what she called a "massive superfluity problem" with government's interpretation If "arrives in" means must be in U.S., then "physically present in U.S." becomes redundant Suggested the government reading renders part of the statute meaningless Justice Neil Gorsuch Pressed on line-standing scenarios: "So anybody at the water's edge of the Rio Grande on the Mexican side has arrived?" Explored what it means to be at a port of entry Justice Brett Kavanaugh Noted potential inequity: those who cross illegally get asylum hearings, those who wait legally do not Acknowledged the case presents "a close question" on statutory interpretation Justice Amy Coney Barrett Pressed on what "arrives" means: "How close do you have to be?" Asked about areas without ports of entry Explored the line between "arrives in" vs. "arrives at" Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson Sympathetic to challengers Raised mootness question - since policy is no longer in effect, is there a live controversy? Challenged: "Your suggestion that the United States would say, 'Unless you can figure out a way to illegally cross, we're not going to entertain that claim,' seems very peculiar" Queried how justices have authority to review if case is moot Justice Samuel Alito Asked about "knocking at the door" analogy Questioned whether someone "arrives in" a country by approaching but not entering Key Precedents Cited Sale v. Haitian Centers Council (1993) - Extraterritorial application of refugee protections 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1) - Asylum application eligibility 8 U.S.C. § 1225(a)(1) - Inspection requirements 8 U.S.C. § 1225(a)(3) - Paroled aliens must be inspected Hypotheticals Posed Gorsuch: "Anybody at the water's edge of the Rio Grande on the Mexican side has arrived?" Barrett: "Could you say that someone arrives in the United States if they're at a portion of the border that does not have a port of entry?" Alito: "Does a person 'arrive in' the United States by approaching but not entering?" Kagan: "If we say 'arrives in' means you must be within U.S. territory, what work is 'physically present' doing in the statute?" Notable Statements Sotomayor: "They've arrived. They are knocking at the door." Suri (for government): "You can't arrive in the United States while you're still standing in Mexico. That should be the end of this case." Jackson (to Suri): "Your suggestion that the United States would say, 'Unless you can figure out a way to illegally cross, we're not going to entertain that claim,' seems very peculiar." Analysis and Predictions Based on argument dynamics, the Court appears likely to rule for the government: Conservative majority sympathetic - Roberts, Alito, Thomas, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett all expressed skepticism toward respondents' reading Liberal justices divided - Kagan identified statutory problems with government's position; Sotomayor and Jackson defended challengers Key textual argument - Kagan's "superfluity" point may not have swayed the majority Practical concerns - Court's recent pattern of deferring to executive on immigration matters A decision is expected by late June or early July 2026. Amendments Referenced Fifth Amendment - Due Process (raised in context of procedural rights) U.N. Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees - International treaty obligations Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees - U.S. obligations under international law Analysis compiled from SCOTUSblog, Reuters, and C-SPAN coverage.

item.title: fomc april 2026
item.description: Prediction markets show overwhelming consensus that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady at the upcoming April meeting, with markets pricing in essentially no probability of a rate cut or hike.
item.content:encoded: FOMC April Rate Decision Prediction markets show overwhelming consensus that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady at the upcoming April meeting, with markets pricing in essentially no probability of a rate cut or hike. Meeting Date: April 28-29, 2026 Hold Probability: 95% Cut Probability: 4% Hike Probability: 0% {{chart:FOMC Rate Decision - April 2026}} Market Context: The March FOMC meeting resulted in a hold as expected, with the Fed maintaining its patient stance amid mixed economic signals. Oil prices have surged 41% year-to-date, with WTI crude now above $90/barrel - a development the Fed is closely monitoring for potential inflationary pressure. Recession odds have climbed to 31%, up from 23% at the start of the year. Despite softening labor market indicators, the Fed appears positioned to remain on hold through the April meeting, awaiting more clarity on the inflation trajectory and the impact of energy price increases on consumer spending. The next rate cut is not expected until later in 2026, with prediction markets pricing in a 25 basis point cut by the June or July meeting at roughly 55-60% probability. item.title: Oversight Committee Launches Investigation Into Rampant Taxpayer Fraud in California Hospice Programs
item.description: WASHINGTON — Following alarming reports that California officials failed to properly safeguard federal funds, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman James Comer (R-Ky…
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — Following alarming reports that California officials failed to properly safeguard federal funds, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.) and Oversight Committee Republicans today launched an investigation into rampant taxpayer fraud in California's hospice programs. In a letter to California Governor Gavin Newsom, the lawmakers emphasized that the Newsom administration has been aware of state audit reports of hospice fraud for at least four years but has failed to prevent or detect it and has enabled hospice providers to defraud the American taxpayer and exploit vulnerable patients. "Recent reporting has revealed alarming evidence of fraudulent activity in California's hospice programs, including agencies overbilling Medicare and fraudulently enrolling beneficiaries without their knowledge. In California, your administration's Departments of Public Health, Social Services and Health Care Services all have a role in overseeing federally funded hospice programs. The Committee is concerned your administration does not have sufficient internal controls to prevent and detect fraud and is not conducting proper oversight of these hospice programs." Investigation Background The Committee's investigation into Minnesota's federally funded social service programs exposed widespread failures by state agencies to conduct oversight and prevent fraud, with similar schemes now appearing in California's hospice programs. According to a March 29, 2022, report from the California State Auditor, Los Angeles County has seen a 1,500 percent increase in hospice providers since 2010, with providers overbilling Medicare by at least $105 million in a single year. In addition, a whistleblower reported that California has minimal safeguards to prevent fraudsters from obtaining hospice licenses, including allowing individuals living abroad to secure them, and described schemes in which fraudsters recruit seniors. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services recently estimated that Los Angeles County alone represents $3.5 billion in hospice fraud, and that 18 percent of all hospice billing in the United States comes from this single county. "Last year, California Attorney General Rob Bonta called hospice fraud in California, specifically in Los Angeles County, 'an epidemic.' The March 2022 audit report highlighted several red flags and key warning signs of fraud: many providers are listed at the same address; very low patient counts compared with the rest of the State; patients listed as terminally ill were later discharged alive; excessive billing for services that may not have been provided; and staff were shared across multiple hospice providers." The Committee is requesting documents and communications regarding California's oversight and internal controls to detect and prevent fraud for its federally funded hospice programs. Related: This investigation follows a pattern of federal scrutiny of state social service programs. See previous coverage: "Despite claims, massive SNAP fraud is rare" — an article from The Boston Globe that cited a legal welfare advocate who stated fraud is not "borne out by our experience" while Massachusetts refused to cooperate with federal USDA fraud investigations. item.title: Oversight Committee Launches Investigation Into Rampant Taxpayer Fraud in California Hospice Programs
item.description: WASHINGTON — Following alarming reports that California officials failed to properly safeguard federal funds, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman James Comer (R-Ky…
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — Following alarming reports that California officials failed to properly safeguard federal funds, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.) and Oversight Committee Republicans today launched an investigation into rampant taxpayer fraud in California's hospice programs. In a letter to California Governor Gavin Newsom, the lawmakers emphasized that the Newsom administration has been aware of state audit reports of hospice fraud for at least four years but has failed to prevent or detect it and has enabled hospice providers to defraud the American taxpayer and exploit vulnerable patients. "Recent reporting has revealed alarming evidence of fraudulent activity in California's hospice programs, including agencies overbilling Medicare and fraudulently enrolling beneficiaries without their knowledge. In California, your administration's Departments of Public Health, Social Services and Health Care Services all have a role in overseeing federally funded hospice programs. The Committee is concerned your administration does not have sufficient internal controls to prevent and detect fraud and is not conducting proper oversight of these hospice programs." Investigation Background The Committee's investigation into Minnesota's federally funded social service programs exposed widespread failures by state agencies to conduct oversight and prevent fraud, with similar schemes now appearing in California's hospice programs. According to a March 29, 2022, report from the California State Auditor, Los Angeles County has seen a 1,500 percent increase in hospice providers since 2010, with providers overbilling Medicare by at least $105 million in a single year. In addition, a whistleblower reported that California has minimal safeguards to prevent fraudsters from obtaining hospice licenses, including allowing individuals living abroad to secure them, and described schemes in which fraudsters recruit seniors. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services recently estimated that Los Angeles County alone represents $3.5 billion in hospice fraud, and that 18 percent of all hospice billing in the United States comes from this single county. "Last year, California Attorney General Rob Bonta called hospice fraud in California, specifically in Los Angeles County, 'an epidemic.' The March 2022 audit report highlighted several red flags and key warning signs of fraud: many providers are listed at the same address; very low patient counts compared with the rest of the State; patients listed as terminally ill were later discharged alive; excessive billing for services that may not have been provided; and staff were shared across multiple hospice providers." The Committee is requesting documents and communications regarding California's oversight and internal controls to detect and prevent fraud for its federally funded hospice programs. Related: This investigation follows a pattern of federal scrutiny of state social service programs. See previous coverage: "Despite claims, massive SNAP fraud is rare" — an article from UC Berkeley that cited a legal welfare advocate who stated fraud is not "borne out by our experience" while Massachusetts refused to cooperate with federal USDA fraud investigations. Read the letter to Governor Newsom . View in News

item.title: Military Drones
item.description: Drone warfare is now an industrial and budget problem as cheap one-way systems, loitering munitions, and reusable ISR platforms force militaries to rethink cost, survivability, and air defense econ…
item.content:encoded: Military Drones The key military question is no longer whether drones matter. It is whether a state can produce enough of them, field them fast enough, and force the enemy to spend more on defense than the attacker spends on offense. Cheap one-way attack drones changed the arithmetic. A reusable UAV has to survive. A loitering munition only has to find a target once. That difference matters because modern air defense missiles, radars, and trained crews are expensive, while a mass-produced drone can be attritable by design. Drone Country Type Cost Reach Best Use MQ-9 🇺🇸 🛰️ Reusable $$$ 27h / 1,850 km ISR/Strike TB2 🇹🇷 🛰️ Reusable $$ 27h / 150+ km Strike-Recon Switchblade 600 🇺🇸 💥 Loitering $$ 40m / 40 km Anti-Armor Shahed-136 🇮🇷 / 🇷🇺 🎯 One-way $ 2,000+ km Saturation FLM 136 (LUCAS) 🇺🇸 🎯 One-way $ 1,000+ km Attritable Strike Lancet 🇷🇺 💥 Loitering $/$$ 40-70 km Counter-Fires Orlan-10 🇷🇺 👁️ ISR $ 16h / 120 km Artillery Spotting Legend Cost $ = low $$ = medium $$$ = high $/$$ = low to medium Terms ISR = intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance; SAMs = surface-to-air missile systems Best Use ISR/Strike = persistent surveillance plus precision attack; Strike-Recon = lighter reconnaissance with limited strike capacity; Anti-Armor = attacks on tanks and armored vehicles Best Use Saturation = mass attacks designed to overwhelm defenses; Counter-Fires = hunting artillery and launchers; Artillery Spotting = target detection and correction for indirect fire The useful distinction is not simply drone versus no drone. It is reusable platform , loitering munition , and one-way attack drone . Reusable Platforms Systems like the MQ-9 Reaper and Bayraktar TB2 are valuable because they combine surveillance with strike capacity. They help commanders find targets, verify them, and engage them with relatively low risk to pilots. They are not cheap in absolute terms, but they are cheaper than losing crewed aircraft in many contested environments. Their weakness is survivability against a serious integrated air defense network. A slow UAV with a predictable orbit is useful in permissive or partially contested airspace. It becomes much less comfortable when the enemy has layered radar, electronic warfare, and interceptors. Loitering Munitions The most important conceptual shift is the rise of the loitering munition. A system like Switchblade 600 or Lancet compresses scout and shooter into the same object. A unit does not need to identify a target, send coordinates back, wait for artillery or aircraft, and hope the target stays put. The munition can search, confirm, and strike. That matters most against mobile assets: artillery pieces air-defense launchers logistics vehicles command posts near the line This is one reason drone warfare keeps migrating down the chain of command. Smaller formations can now perform missions that once required more centralized fires. One-Way Attack Drones The Shahed-136 model matters because it makes strategic harassment cheap. It is not exquisite. It does not need to be. If a state can launch large numbers of long-range one-way drones at power infrastructure, depots, ports, or urban targets, the defender faces a painful decision: spend expensive interceptors accept damage disperse and harden everything This philosophy has led to the development of systems like the FLM 136 , or LUCAS , which was reverse-engineered by the U.S. from recovered Shahed platforms. Often described as the "Corolla of drones," the LUCAS is a cheap, mass-produced one-way system that prioritizes volume and cost-imposition over technical elegance. That is the real innovation. It is not elegance. It is cost imposition. An interceptor-heavy defense model is hard to sustain when the attacker can keep sending relatively cheap airframes. Even when most drones are shot down, the attacker may still be winning the economic exchange. The New Competition The military competition around drones now turns on five things: Production volume Component supply chains Software and guidance resilience Electronic warfare resistance Cost exchange against air defense The best drone is not always the most sophisticated one. In many campaigns, the best drone is the one a country can build in quantity, train on quickly, and replace without strategic pain. That is why the glamour of premium systems can mislead. A state may own a handful of excellent UAVs and still lose the drone war if the other side can manufacture thousands of adequate ones. What This Means Military drones are becoming less like boutique aerospace programs and more like munitions plus software. The center of gravity is shifting from prestige platforms to scalable production. The country that masters drone warfare will not just design good aircraft. It will integrate: affordable airframes navigation and targeting software battlefield networking electronic warfare adaptation rapid replenishment The future belongs to the side that can make drones routine rather than exceptional. Notes Public cost figures for military drones are inconsistent across contracts, export packages, and production runs. That is why category-level cost profiles are more useful than pretending every open-source unit price is directly comparable. Sources U.S. Air Force MQ-9 Reaper Fact Sheet AeroVironment Switchblade 600 Baykar Bayraktar TB2 CSIS: The Hunt for Cheap Mass RUSI analysis on drone and air-defense economics

item.title: National Zoning Atlas
item.description: The National Zoning Atlas has digitized zoning codes across 9,200+ jurisdictions covering 185 million people, reading over 1 million pages of zoning regulations to build a searchable, interactive m…
item.content:encoded: National Zoning Atlas The National Zoning Atlas has digitized zoning codes across 9,200+ jurisdictions covering 185 million people, reading over 1 million pages of zoning regulations to build a searchable, interactive map of how American land can be used. The findings are striking. Most residential land in the country is zoned exclusively for single-family homes. Minimum lot sizes, parking requirements, and density restrictions lock out duplexes, triplexes, and small apartment buildings from the vast majority of buildable land. In Connecticut, 76% of single-family land requires minimum lot sizes of 80,000 square feet or more. In New Hampshire, only 5.6% of buildable land has access to both water and sewer services. The atlas is already driving policy. Colorado passed legislation eliminating minimum lot sizes over 2,000 square feet for single-family homes, citing NZA data. Montana used its state atlas to pass bipartisan statewide land use reforms. Salem, Massachusetts eliminated parking requirements for new apartments after reviewing the map. Founded by Sara Bronin, the project won the 30th Heinz Award for the Economy in 2025. Explore the Atlas | About the NZA

item.title: Interleukin-10
item.description: IL-10 is a small protein your immune system produces to calm inflammation. When you get injured, your body floods the area with pro-inflammatory signals to fight infection and start healing. IL-10…
item.content:encoded: Interleukin-10 IL-10 is a small protein your immune system produces to calm inflammation. When you get injured, your body floods the area with pro-inflammatory signals to fight infection and start healing. IL-10 is the off switch. It tells immune cells to stand down once the job is done. A February 2026 study in Science Immunology from Michigan State found that IL-10 is also the reason men resolve pain faster than women. Monocytes (a type of white blood cell) produce IL-10 and signal directly to pain-sensing neurons to shut them off. Male monocytes produce significantly more IL-10 than female monocytes because testosterone drives production. When researchers blocked male sex hormones, the advantage disappeared. The same pattern showed up in human data. Researchers at UNC Chapel Hill tracked patients after car accidents and found men had higher circulating IL-10 levels and resolved pain faster. Women experienced longer-lasting pain, not because of perception or reporting differences, but because their immune systems produced less of the molecule that actively resolves it. "The difference in pain between men and women has a biological basis. It's not in your head, and you're not soft. It's in your immune system." Geoffroy Laumet, MSU. Mice without IL-10 develop lethal gut inflammation under normal conditions. The molecule also enhances B cell function and antibody production. Researchers are now exploring whether treatments can boost IL-10 production to resolve pain faster without opioids. Science Immunology: IL-10 Sex Differences in Pain | MSU Press Release | Wikipedia: Interleukin 10

item.title: Section 8 Meet Amendment 4
item.description: New York just hit a constitutional wall in its voucher enforcement strategy after the Appellate Division held that forcing landlords into Section 8 conflicts with Fourth Amendment protections.
item.content:encoded: Section 8 Meet Amendment 4 New York just hit a constitutional wall in its voucher enforcement strategy after the Appellate Division held that forcing landlords into Section 8 conflicts with Fourth Amendment protections. On March 5, 2026, the Appellate Division, Third Department, in Matter of People of the State of N.Y. v Commons West, LLC affirmed lower court rulings that struck down Executive Law section 296(5)(a)(1) to the extent it makes refusal to rent to Section 8 tenants unlawful. The court reasoned that New York's source of income law effectively compels participation in a federal program that requires property inspections and access to landlord records through the Housing Assistance Payment contract. In the panel's view, that setup creates a constitutional problem because participation is no longer voluntary at the state level. Attorney General Letitia James responded the same day, emphasizing that voucher holders deserve safe and dignified housing and confirming that her office is reviewing the decision. The immediate consequence is legal uncertainty for enforcement against landlords who reject Section 8 vouchers in areas covered by this ruling. The larger consequence is a direct constitutional collision between fair housing goals and search and seizure limits. Resources: Attorney General James statement, March 5, 2026 Matter of People of the State of N.Y. v Commons West, LLC, 2026 NY Slip Op 01253

item.content:encoded: Debt %, CPI, Housing Market, and Wagner Dept Interest The CBO's latest budget outlook projects a $1.9 trillion deficit this year. But interest costs tell the real story. Interest outlays hit $1.0 trillion in 2026 and will double to $2.1 trillion by 2036. For every dollar borrowed, 66 cents services debt. Interest will exceed defense spending every year and triple it by decade's end. This mirrors California and New York City, where long-term structural spending obligations outpaced revenue growth until refinancing became unmanageable. You cannot negotiate with compound mathematics. When deficits drive debt to 120 percent of GDP, interest becomes the fastest-growing budget item, crowding out everything else. California's pension obligations and NYC's 1970s crisis followed the same logic: overspending built on diffuse political accountability becomes an anchor on the budget. Tax increases, service cuts, or defaults are the only paths forward. {{chart:Interest on Debt}} View government spending and revenue indicators Congressional Budget Office: Director's Statement on the Budget and Economic Outlook for 2026 to 2036 Consumer Price Index (CPI) The Consumer Price Index stands at 325.252 in January 2026, up 2.4% year-over-year. Core inflation remains sticky at the 3% range, though headline CPI moderated from the September peak of 3.0%. December posted 2.7% YoY growth, holding steady as the Fed navigates the dual mandate of price stability and full employment. {{chart:CPI}} View all consumer indicators Housing Market Median home prices declined to $396,800 in January 2026, down 2.1% from December's $405,400 and falling from the June peak of $432,700. The decline reflects cooling demand as higher mortgage rates persist—the 30-year fixed rate hovered near 6.2% through the period. Existing home sales fell to 3.91M (seasonally adjusted annual rate) in January, marking an 8.4% decrease from December.
