item.title: Jobs, Small Biz, Optimism, Oil, Scroll
item.description: January saw payroll growth of 130,000 jobs, slightly above the 127,000 added in December. The labor market continues adding jobs at a steady pace despite broader economic uncertainty, driven by str…
item.content:encoded: Jobs, Small Biz, Optimism, Oil, Scroll January saw payroll growth of 130,000 jobs, slightly above the 127,000 added in December. The labor market continues adding jobs at a steady pace despite broader economic uncertainty, driven by strength in leisure and hospitality services. December: 158,497,000 January: 158,627,000 Monthly Change: +130,000 (+0.1% MoM) The consistent monthly additions keep the economy near full employment, though employment growth has slowed from the faster pace seen earlier in 2025. Job cuts announcements remain elevated, suggesting ongoing corporate restructuring even as hiring continues. {{chart:Total Nonfarm Employment}} View all employment indicators Small Business Optimism Slides to 99.3 The NFIB Small Business Optimism Index declined to 99.3 in January from 99.5 in December, signaling cautious business sentiment. Small business owners remain below the 100-point expansion threshold, reflecting concern about economic conditions and policy uncertainty. December: 99.5 January: 99.3 Change: -0.2 points Small businesses account for nearly half of U.S. economic activity and are often the first to react to changing conditions. The slight decline suggests business owners are holding back on capital spending and hiring plans despite steady job creation in the broader economy. {{chart:Small Business Optimism Index}} Read the NFIB report American Optimism Hits Record Low A new Gallup poll reveals that American optimism about future life quality has collapsed to 59.2% in 2025 - the lowest level since measurement began nearly two decades ago. The deterioration has been sharp: optimism declined 9.1 percentage points since 2020, with 3.5 points of that drop occurring between 2024 and 2025 alone. The data breaks down starkly by political affiliation. Democrats plummeted 7.6 points in 2025, while Republicans remained essentially flat. Hispanic adults and those identifying as Democrats showed the greatest year-over-year declines, with Hispanic optimism falling more sharply in the past year than Black adults despite historically lower Black optimism levels. The gap between current life satisfaction and future life expectations reveals deep anxiety: while Americans' views of their present lives haven't recovered to 2020 lows, their expectations for the next five years have deteriorated significantly. At current trends, Gallup estimates roughly 24.5 million fewer people consider themselves optimistic about their future compared to 2020. Read the Gallup analysis Venezuela Oil: Trump Opens Door for Investment The Trump administration issued new general licenses authorizing U.S. oil companies to rehabilitate and repair existing assets in Venezuela, following the capture of Nicolás Maduro in January and a $2 billion oil supply deal . Energy Secretary Chris Wright met with Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez this week as the U.S. pursues a $100 billion reconstruction plan for Venezuela's energy infrastructure. The licenses cover maintenance of oil and gas operations, refurbishment of exploration and production equipment, and shipping logistics. Companies are still awaiting final licenses to actually drill for new crude, but this marks Trump's doctrine of "American energy dominance" reshaping global oil markets - leveraging Venezuelan, Guyana, Saudi Arabian, and UAE production to reduce dependence on Russian oil and reshape geopolitical leverage. Investment thesis: Oilfield service companies like HAL (Halliburton) and SLB (Schlumberger) are positioned to capitalize on rehabilitation contracts. Existing operators like Chevron and Spain's Repsol can optimize existing investments. Venezuela holds the world's largest crude reserves; unlocked production shifts global energy dynamics. Infinite Scroll is Nicotine Companies engineer addictive engagement because profit motive demands engagement. The problem isn't disclaimers - it's that consumers want what is bad for them. We sue tobacco makers but sue for what? The remedy isn't regulation or warnings. Stop buying and they stop selling. Externality mitigation requires personal agency, not litigation. How to advise without being sycophantic? How to engage without addiction? Until those questions shift corporate incentives, expect more addictive design, more lawsuits, and the same cycle repeating. item.content:encoded: Restaurant Performance Index Slides to 99.3 in December The National Restaurant Association's monthly performance gauge fell 0.8% to 99.3 in December, marking the lowest reading since March and signaling softening demand across the restaurant industry. Both current conditions and future outlook weakened, as operators reported the first net decline in same-store sales in nine months. Restaurant Performance Index: 99.3 (-0.8% MoM, contraction territory below 100) Current Situation Index: 98.3 (-1.0% MoM, sixth consecutive month below 100) Same-Store Sales: 98.3 (-2.0% MoM, first net decline since March) Customer Traffic: 96.8 (-1.2% MoM, eleventh consecutive month of declines) Expectations Index: 100.2 (-0.6% MoM, mixed six-month outlook) Sales weakness accelerated dramatically. Only 37% of operators reported rising sales year-over-year, down from 47% in November, while 53% reported declines. Traffic deteriorated further with 60% of operators seeing lower traffic and just 28% reporting gains. Despite the pessimism, capital spending remains elevated - 51% of operators made recent equipment investments and 53% plan spending over the next six months. Operators remain uncertain about the broader economy, with only 25% expecting improvement in the next six months. {{chart:Consumer Sentiment}} View business indicators

item.title: I Need a New Butt!
item.description: Mississippi's Court of Appeals ruled that an elementary school administrator was wrongfully terminated for reading an age-appropriate children's book to second graders, establishing that school dis…
item.content:encoded: I Need a New Butt! Mississippi's Court of Appeals ruled that an elementary school administrator was wrongfully terminated for reading an age-appropriate children's book to second graders, establishing that school districts must prove book content violates professional standards rather than dismissing educators on subjective grounds. The Legal Framework: The case involves competing interests: school district authority over curriculum versus educator free speech and due process rights. The court applied the standard from public employee speech cases, requiring school districts to demonstrate that an educator's conduct actually violated established professional standards or district policy. The district cannot rely on administrative disapproval alone. Mississippi law also protects employees from termination that is "arbitrary and capricious." The Facts: On March 1, 2022, Toby Price, Assistant Principal at Gary Road Elementary School in the Hinds County School District, read "I Need a New Butt!" by Dawn McMillan to a second-grade class during Read Across America Day when the scheduled reader failed to appear. The book, published in 2014, contains humorous references to bodily functions appropriate for its intended audience. District Superintendent Delescia Martin placed Price on administrative leave the same day and terminated his employment two days later, citing unprofessional conduct. Price appealed to the School Board, which upheld the termination. Why It Matters: The ruling reverses a troubling trend in K-12 education where administrators dismiss educators without substantive evidence. The court found the district failed to prove the book was inappropriate and noted that the school library contained many books with similar content that had previously been read to students without incident. The decision protects educators from arbitrary termination based on subjective administrative preferences rather than established standards or policies. It reinforces that fostering a love of reading should not expose teachers to employment termination. Resources: Mississippi Court of Appeals Ruling (Jan. 27, 2026) - Full opinion reversing termination decision "Educator Fired for Reading 'I Need a New Butt!' to Students Must Be Reinstated" - Mississippi Free Press article

item.title: Madison on the Purse: Separation of Powers and Legislative Encroachment
item.description: James Madison observed that an energetic executive confronts a legislature wielding control of the purse—a structural imbalance that threatens the separation of powers. The legislative power to app…
item.content:encoded: Madison on the Purse: Separation of Powers and Legislative Encroachment James Madison observed that an energetic executive confronts a legislature wielding control of the purse—a structural imbalance that threatens the separation of powers. The legislative power to appropriate funds gives Congress a facility for encroachment that no constitutional restriction can fully prevent. The Constitutional Framework The Appropriations Clause (Article I, Section 9) vests the power of the purse exclusively in Congress: "No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law." This grants Congress not merely oversight but direct control over executive operations through funding decisions. Madison recognized this structural reality while drafting the Constitution and later reflected on its implications for constitutional design. The Problem Madison's concern centered on what he called an "inherent strength" in the legislative power—the ability to withhold, condition, or direct spending without explicit constitutional violation. Unlike the executive's veto power, which is direct and visible, or the judicial power, which operates through specific cases, the legislature's control of appropriations operates as a constant structural pressure. An energetic executive may be vigorous in its constitutional powers, but it remains financially dependent on Congressional will. This creates what constitutional scholars identify as an asymmetry in the separation of powers : the executive cannot effectively resist legislative encroachment when Congress threatens funding, yet no mechanism exists to compel Congressional spending. The executive either complies with Congressional directives—even those that may exceed legislative authority—or faces operational collapse. Why It Matters Madison's observation exposes a fundamental tension in constitutional design. The Framers intended three co-equal branches, yet the appropriations power tilts that equilibrium toward the legislature in practice. Modern disputes over impoundment, conditional spending, and legislative riders on appropriations bills all trace to this structural reality. The observation remains relevant for debates over: Presidential enforcement discretion vs. Congressional mandate through appropriations Whether funding conditions can exceed the scope of legislative authority The limits of Congressional power to "defund" executive actions Resources Federalist No. 48 - James Madison discusses separation of powers and the legislative tendency toward encroachment (Yale Law School - Avalon Project) Federalist No. 51 - On the structure of government and internal checks (Yale Law School - Avalon Project) U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 9, Clause 7 - Appropriations Clause (Congress.gov Constitution Annotated) Lincoln v. Vigil, 508 U.S. 182 (1993) - On legislative control of agency discretion through appropriations (Justia Supreme Court Center)

item.title: FOMC Holds as Predicted, Consumer Sentiment Rebounds

item.content:encoded: FOMC Holds as Predicted, Consumer Sentiment Rebounds The Federal Reserve made its January rate decision official this week, holding the federal funds rate steady as expected. Meanwhile, consumer sentiment improved significantly, suggesting households are gaining confidence despite persistent economic uncertainty. The FOMC Decision: As markets predicted, the FOMC voted to keep rates unchanged at the January 27-28 meeting. The 95¢ probability in prediction markets proved accurate - a hold was the overwhelming consensus. The decision reflects confidence that inflation remains manageable and the labor market, while cooling, remains resilient enough to avoid aggressive cutting cycles. {{chart:FOMC Rate Decision - January 2026}} Dollar Weakens in January: The U.S. dollar lost ground in January, with the Dollar Value Index declining to 119.28 from December's 120.57 (-1.1% MoM). The softer dollar reflects softer rate hold expectations and suggests traders are pricing in potential cuts later in 2026, despite this month's hold decision. {{chart:Dollar Value Index}} View trade indicators Consumer Sentiment vs. Confidence - Mixed Signals: Consumer sentiment improved notably in January, rising to 56.4 from December's 52.9 - a 3.5-point gain suggesting better household optimism. However, The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index painted a more pessimistic picture, plummeting to 84.5 from December's 94.2 (-10.3% MoM). The divergence suggests near-term sentiment is brightening while longer-term expectations are souring. {{chart:Consumer Sentiment}} {{chart:Consumer Confidence}} View all consumer indicators

item.title: Congress Completes All 12 FY2026 Appropriations Bills
item.description: By January 30, the Senate passed five of the 12 fiscal year 2026 appropriations bills on a bipartisan 71-29 vote, totaling $1.639 trillion in net base discretionary spending. The package also inclu…
item.content:encoded: FY2026 Appropriations: $1.639T Budget with Major Workforce Cuts By January 30, the Senate passed five of the 12 fiscal year 2026 appropriations bills on a bipartisan 71-29 vote, totaling $1.639 trillion in net base discretionary spending. The package also includes a two-week continuing resolution for the Department of Homeland Security to allow time for further negotiations. That's $38.6 billion more than FY2025, driven partially offset by a 10% federal workforce cut and $11.7 billion clawed back from the IRS. The Numbers at a Glance What Changed from Last Year Department FY2026 (billions) FY2025 (billions) % Change Defense $882.5 $848.2 +4.0% Labor-HHS-Education $298.0 $287.2 +3.8% Transportation-HUD $163.9 $162.0 +1.2% Commerce-Justice-Science $80.3 $78.5 +2.3% Homeland Security ⭐ $71.4 $67.1 +6.4% State Department-Foreign Ops 📉 $58.7 $60.2 -2.5% Energy-Water $61.0 $59.0 +3.4% Interior-Environment $40.8 $41.2 -1.0% Mil Construction-VA $43.2 $42.0 +2.9% Financial Services $28.2 $27.8 +1.4% Agriculture 🌾 $25.9 $24.1 +7.5% Legislative Branch $5.1 $5.0 +2.0% TOTAL $1,598.0 $1,643.0 -2.7% Biggest winners: Defense (military personnel received 3.8% pay raise) Labor-HHS-Education (protections kept most public health intact) Homeland Security (FEMA boost of $4.7 billion) Losers: State Department (2.5% cut in foreign operations and diplomacy) EPA and Interior (modest reductions) Corporation for Public Broadcasting (eliminated entirely) The DOGE Effect The Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency left its mark, though Congress didn't go as far as requested: Reform Impact Federal Workforce 10% reduction (est. $20B+ savings) IRS Funding Additional $11.7B clawed back NIH Cuts Congress rejected 40% cut; agency got $415M increase instead CDC Cuts Congress rejected 50% cut; maintained current funding BARDA Received full $1B despite Trump request for 36% cut Congress also imposed minimum staffing requirements at Social Security, Labor, Education, and HHS to prevent reorganizations without legislative approval. Sources CRS Appropriations Status Table House Committee on Appropriations Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget Analysis

item.content:encoded: Life Expectancy and Factory Activity Up U.S. life expectancy reached 79 years in 2024, the highest ever recorded, driven by the largest decline in drug overdose death rates on record. Overall mortality decreased 4% year-over-year, with overdose deaths falling 26.2% as synthetic opioid deaths dropped 35.6%. Key Figures: Life Expectancy : 79 years (up from 78.4 in 2023) Overall Death Rate : 722.1 per 100,000 (down from 750.5) Drug Overdose Deaths : 79,384 total; rate fell from 31.3 to 23.1 per 100,000 (-26.2%) Synthetic Opioids : Down 35.6% (from 22.2 to 14.3 per 100,000) Cocaine Deaths : Down 26.7% (from 8.6 to 6.3 per 100,000) Methamphetamine Deaths : Down 19.8% (from 10.6 to 8.5 per 100,000) The improvement extends across demographic groups, with the largest gains among younger people and Black non-Hispanic populations. Other significant shifts include COVID-19 dropping out of the top 10 causes of death, while suicide entered as the 10th leading cause. Heart disease, cancer, and unintentional injuries remain the top three causes. item.title: "Equal Time" Rule: An Artifact of the 1934 Communications Act
item.description: The equal time rule requires broadcast stations to offer equal opportunities to legally qualified political candidates. Enacted in 1934 as Section 315 of the Communications Act, this provision beca…
item.content:encoded: "Equal Time" Rule: An Artifact of the 1934 Communications Act The equal time rule requires broadcast stations to offer equal opportunities to legally qualified political candidates. Enacted in 1934 as Section 315 of the Communications Act, this provision became a cornerstone of broadcast regulation that shaped electoral communication for nearly a century. The Framework: The rule mandates that if a broadcast station allows one legally qualified candidate for the same office to use its facilities, it must provide equal opportunities to other candidates. "Equal" refers to time, charges, and conditions of access. The rule applies exclusively to broadcast television and radio, not cable, satellite, or streaming platforms. The Legal Mechanics: Broadcasters cannot censor candidate speech but gain a safe harbor if all candidates receive equal access Stations may charge rates no higher than the lowest commercial rate for similar time "Use" by one candidate triggers obligations for others, even if the first candidate appeared as a guest on a news program Certain news formats (bona fide news interviews, on-the-spot news coverage, debates) carry exemptions Why It Endures Despite Fragmentation: The rule persists as a relic of the scarcity rationale: broadcast spectrum was finite, requiring licensees to serve the public interest. Cable, satellite, and digital platforms shattered that scarcity, yet Section 315 remains unamended. Broadcasters operate under dual regulations - the equal time mandate alongside editorial discretion traditionally afforded newspapers. Contemporary Friction: Election cycles test the rule's boundaries. When a candidate announces candidacy during a news appearance, does that trigger equal time obligations for others? When a sitting president governs on camera, do appearances constitute campaign "uses"? The FCC has issued countless rulings clarifying distinctions between news coverage and campaign activity. Resources: FCC Statutes and Rules on Candidate Appearances & Advertising - Section 315 and implementing regulations FCC Media Bureau Guidance - Current FCC guidance on equal opportunities Congressional Research Service Report - Policy analysis and legal context

item.content:encoded: Pending Home Sales Slide While Consumers Keep Spending Divergent signals from the housing and consumer sectors. December's sharp decline in Pending Home Sales contrasts with November's resilient consumer spending—a timing gap that obscures whether momentum has shifted since the start of the year. Pending Home Sales Index Down December pending home sales dropped to 71.8, a 9.3% decline from November's 79.2. The index remains well below long-term averages, signaling continued weakness in the housing market despite lower mortgage rates. {{chart:Pending Home Sales Index}} The decline underscores softening housing demand as homebuyers navigate affordability constraints and seasonal slowdowns heading into year-end. As a leading indicator, this weakness typically precedes slower existing home sales in the coming weeks. View housing market indicators Consumer Spending Remains Steady Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) rose to $21,409.7B in November, up 0.5% from October's $21,301.0B. While this data trails December's pending home sales report, consumer spending continues to support economic growth despite headwinds in housing and tightening labor markets. {{chart:Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE)}} The modest increase reflects consumers' persistent purchasing, though growth rates remain below pre-pandemic trends. This resilience suggests consumers are still engaging the economy even as housing activity cools, bolstering the case for a soft landing scenario. View consumer indicators

item.description: Home sellers outnumbered buyers by a record margin in December, marking a dramatic shift in market power toward home shoppers. With 631,535 more sellers than buyers, this 47.1% imbalance is the lar…
item.content:encoded: Buyers: 47% More Than Sellers Home sellers outnumbered buyers by a record margin in December, marking a dramatic shift in market power toward home shoppers. With 631,535 more sellers than buyers, this 47.1% imbalance is the largest gap in over a decade - and it's accelerating. Sellers vs. Buyers Gap: 47.1% (+7.1 percentage points MoM, +22.2 points YoY) Homebuyers in Market: 1.34M (-5.9% MoM, lowest since 2013) Sellers in Market: 1.97M (-1.1% MoM) National Home Price Growth: 0.1% YoY (slowest since June 2023) Median Days on Market: 65 days (+9.5% MoM) The buyer retreat accelerated dramatically. While sellers also pulled back, they did so at half the pace of buyers, creating unprecedented imbalance. High home prices, stubbornly elevated mortgage rates (6.19% for 30-year), and economic uncertainty drove many buyers out of the market entirely. Dallas experienced the sharpest price decline - down 7.6% YoY with 86.8% more sellers than buyers. Meanwhile, the Sun Belt dominated buyer's markets, while the entire Northeast and Midwest contained all five seller's markets. {{chart:Number of Days on Market (Median)}} View housing indicators

item.title: Canada Affirms Despair
item.description: A Canadian with mental illness is now claiming discrimination for being denied Medical Aid in Dying (MAID). What was framed as compassionate end-of-life care has become a cultural statement about t…
item.content:encoded: Canada Affirms Despair A Canadian with mental illness is now claiming discrimination for being denied Medical Aid in Dying (MAID). What was framed as compassionate end-of-life care has become a cultural statement about the value of life itself. The Shift from Palliative to Preventive MAID began as a narrow policy for patients with terminal illnesses and unbearable physical suffering. It has steadily expanded to include psychological suffering, and now to those deemed to have "irremediable illnesses and persistent intolerable suffering" - language deliberately vague enough to encompass depression, anxiety, and general despair. Governor Hochul of New York captured the sentiment: "If a suffering New Yorker made the difficult choice to die, who am I to stand in their way?" The question itself reveals a philosophical trap. The Cultural Collapse What this signals is not compassion. It signals the absence of a formidable cultural heritage strong enough to derail nihilism. When a society offers medical assistance in dying to the mentally ill rather than cultural remedies - meaning, purpose, community, laughter - it has lost respect for life itself. This is not about autonomy. This is not about equality. An Alternative Reality Some have lived in abject poverty where "irremediable illnesses and persistent intolerable suffering" was never suggestive of an inalienable right to death. They endured the slings and arrows. They chose laughter and life. They recovered. They persisted. Maybe they thrived. But their whole life, they suffered. And that, ladies and gentlemen, is the meaning of life. To be or not to be. Resources: New York's MAID Law Canada's Expanding MAID Criteria Read the journal entry

item.title: NYC $10.4B Short
item.description: Comptroller Mark Levine projects historic budget gaps following misbudgeting from the Adams administration. This marks the first time since the Great Recession that New York City faces shortfalls o…
item.content:encoded: NYC $10.4B Short Comptroller Mark Levine projects historic budget gaps following misbudgeting from the Adams administration. This marks the first time since the Great Recession that New York City faces shortfalls of this scale this late in the fiscal year. The Numbers: FY2026 Shortfall : $2.2 billion FY2027 Projected Gap : $10.4 billion Underlying cause : Adams administration overspending and chronic underbudgeting of recurring expenses The Problem The shortfalls stem not from economic weakness - tourism, Broadway, commercial leasing, and stock market gains continue to support strong tax revenues. Instead, chronic mismanagement created structural gaps. The city budgeted below actual spending needs on rental assistance, overtime, shelter, public assistance, Department of Education due process cases, and MTA contributions, totaling $3.8 billion in unbudgeted FY2026 expenses alone. Where It's Coming From The comptroller identified systemic underbudgeting across multiple departments: Rental Assistance : $795 million gap in FY2026 alone (projected $2 billion in FY2027) Shelter & Capacity : $630 million (non-asylum seeker) Overtime : $727 million Public Assistance : $641 million MTA Contributions : $392 million DOE Due Process Cases : $558 million This pattern repeated for years - the Adams administration consistently underfunded known, recurring expenses, relying on year-end adjustments and one-time accounting measures to appear balanced. Mayor Mamdani faces the difficult task of crafting a balanced preliminary budget in February. Comptroller Levine pledged to work with the new administration and Albany to close the gaps. Resources: Budget Briefing Presentation - Charts and visualizations (includes budget gap trends, chronic underbudgeting breakdown, and revenue projections) FY 2027 Budget Preview - Full analysis Comptroller's Press Release - Full announcement Press Briefing Video - Comptroller Levine's presentation

item.title: Monday
item.description: by Billy Collins
item.content:encoded: Monday by Billy Collins The birds are in their trees, the toast is in the toaster, and the poets are at their windows. They are at their windows in every section of the tangerine of earth— the Chinese poets looking up at the moon, the American poets gazing out at the pink and blue ribbons of sunrise. The clerks are at their desks, the miners are down in their mines, and the poets are looking out their windows maybe with a cigarette, a cup of tea, and maybe a flannel shirt or bathrobe is involved. The proofreaders are playing the ping-pong game of proofreading, glancing back and forth from page to page, the chefs are dicing celery and potatoes, and the poets are at their windows because it is their job for which they are paid nothing every Friday afternoon. Which window it hardly seems to matter though many have a favorite, for there is always something to see— a bird grasping a thin branch, the headlights of a taxi rounding a corner, those two boys in wool caps angling across the street. The fishermen bob in their boats, the linemen climb their round poles, the barbers wait by their mirrors and chairs, and the poets continue to stare at the cracked birdbath or a limb knocked down by the wind. By now, it should go without saying that what the oven is to the baker and the berry-stained blouse to the dry cleaner, so the window is to the poet. Just think— before the invention of the window, the poets would have had to put on a jacket and a winter hat to go outside or remain indoors with only a wall to stare at. And when I say a wall, I do not mean a wall with striped wallpaper and a sketch of a cow in a frame. I mean a cold wall of fieldstones, the wall of the medieval sonnet, the original woman's heart of stone, the stone caught in the throat of her poet-lover. From The Trouble with Poetry and Other Poems (Random House)

item.title: Warm Collectivism
item.description: PGE's new Base Services Charge decouples utility usage from service, matching energy bills to customer income levels and shifting cost burdens from low-income households. The policy rolls out March…
item.content:encoded: Warm Collectivism PGE's new Base Services Charge decouples utility usage from service, matching energy bills to customer income levels and shifting cost burdens from low-income households. The policy rolls out March 2026. What It Does: Separates fixed service costs from usage-based charges Adjusts billing based on customer income levels Redistributes cost burden away from lower-income customers Why It Matters: This represents a fundamental shift in utility pricing philosophy - from market-based pricing to income-adjusted subsidies. Customers with higher incomes pay proportionally more to offset lower-income customers' bills, socializing energy costs through the utility system. Learn more | View in Journal 41,000 Jobs Added (ADP) December private employment reached 134,588,000, representing continued stability in the private job market as the year closed. December : 134,588,000 (+41,000 MoM) {{chart:Private Employment}} The steady addition reflects ongoing business hiring despite economic uncertainty. Employment gains remain relatively flat month-to-month, suggesting a labor market at equilibrium without significant acceleration or deterioration. View employment indicators Job Openings Decline 4% (JOLTS) Job openings fell to 7,146,000 in November, reflecting a tightening in available positions as employers moderate hiring demands. November : 7,146,000 (-303,000 MoM, -4.1%) {{chart:Job Openings}} The decline suggests employers are becoming more selective in filling positions. Labor market tightness continues to ease, creating a more balanced dynamic between job seekers and available opportunities after years of intense worker shortages. View employment indicators Services PMI Accelerates to 54.4 December Services PMI surged to 54.4, marking the strongest reading since October and signaling robust expansion in the services sector as year-end activity accelerated. December : 54.4 (+1.8 points MoM) {{chart:Services PMI}} The sharp uptick indicates strong business activity, new orders, and employment in services. item.title: Childhood Immunization Schedule Revised
item.description: HHS released a comprehensive reassessment of the U.S. childhood immunization schedule, reducing the core routine vaccines from 17-18 diseases down to 11. The new consensus schedule focuses on vacci…
item.content:encoded: Childhood Immunization Schedule Revised HHS released a comprehensive reassessment of the U.S. childhood immunization schedule, reducing the core routine vaccines from 17-18 diseases down to 11. The new consensus schedule focuses on vaccines where international agreement exists, moving other vaccines to "shared clinical decision-making" status for individual risk assessment. The 72-injection figure for 2024 includes multiple recurring doses: annual influenza vaccines (up to 18 doses from age 6 months to 18 years), COVID-19 boosters, and RSV monoclonal antibodies. The new schedule moves influenza and COVID-19 to shared clinical decision-making, significantly reducing cumulative injection burden over childhood. Injection Reduction Breakdown: Category 2024 Injections 2026 Core Routine Core 11 Vaccines 40 36 Annual Influenza (up to 18 years) 18 0 COVID-19 Boosters 8 0 RSV Monoclonal Antibodies 2 0 Hepatitis A 2 0 Rotavirus 2 0 Meningococcal B/ACWY 1-2 0 Total 72 36 Note: The 2026 total of 36 represents only the core routine vaccines. Non-core vaccines (influenza, COVID-19, etc.) remain available but are no longer routinely recommended, reducing the standard schedule by approximately 50% while maintaining access for individual clinical decisions. Core Vaccine Dose Breakdown (2026 Schedule): The 11 core vaccines require multiple doses over childhood: DTaP (Diphtheria/Tetanus/Pertussis) : 5 doses Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) : 4 doses Pneumococcal : 4 doses Polio (IPV) : 4 doses MMR (Measles/Mumps/Rubella) : 2 doses Varicella (Chickenpox) : 2 doses HPV (Human Papillomavirus) : 1 dose Total: 22 core doses The 36 figure includes slight scheduling variations and potential catch-up doses. Schedule Comparison: # Disease/Vaccine 2024 2026 1 Measles Yes Yes 2 Mumps Yes Yes 3 Rubella Yes Yes 4 Polio Yes Yes 5 Pertussis Yes Yes 6 Tetanus Yes Yes 7 Diphtheria Yes Yes 8 Hib Yes Yes 9 Pneumococcal Yes Yes 10 HPV Yes (2-3 doses) Yes (1 dose) 11 Varicella Yes Yes — Hepatitis A Yes No — Hepatitis B Yes (birth) No — Rotavirus Yes No — Meningococcal B Yes No — Meningococcal ACWY Yes No — Influenza Yes No — COVID-19 Yes No — Dengue Yes No — RSV Monoclonal Antibodies Yes No All vaccines remain covered by insurance without cost sharing. The shift emphasizes informed consent over mandates, aligning the U.S. with peer nations' practices while maintaining vaccine availability for parents who choose them. View HHS Assessment CDC Immunization Schedules HHS Fact Sheet: CDC Childhood Immunization Recommendations CDC Acts on Presidential Memorandum

item.title: ICE's Mobile Facial Recognition
item.description: ICE has deployed a mobile facial recognition app called Mobile Fortify on government-issued phones used by immigration enforcement agents. The app allows agents to perform contactless biometric sca…
item.content:encoded: ICE's Mobile Facial Recognition ICE has deployed a mobile facial recognition app called Mobile Fortify on government-issued phones used by immigration enforcement agents. The app allows agents to perform contactless biometric scans that match individuals against federal databases such as IDENT and the FBI's National Crime Information Center. This enables real-time identification of people during immigration enforcement operations, dramatically accelerating arrest capability. The app's existence was revealed in June 2025 through leaked materials, sparking immediate concerns from lawmakers and civil rights organizations. Resources: Mobile Fortify - Wikipedia - Technical overview of the app, its capabilities, and documented concerns ICE Deploys Mobile Facial Recognition App to Accelerate Arrests - Details on the deployment and implications Markey Letter to ICE on Mobile Facial Recognition - Congressional questions on transparency and accuracy

item.title: Inclusionary Housing
item.description: Columbia St LLC sued Cambridge over a mandate forcing developers to surrender 20% of floor area to permanent affordable housing without payment. The ordinance exemplifies unchecked government land-…
item.content:encoded: Inclusionary Housing Columbia St LLC sued Cambridge over a mandate forcing developers to surrender 20% of floor area to permanent affordable housing without payment. The ordinance exemplifies unchecked government land-use authority - seizing private property for public benefit while exempting everyone else. Fifth Amendment: "nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation." Massachusetts Article X: "no part of the property of any individual can, with justice, be taken from him... he shall receive a reasonable compensation therefor." Cambridge imposed this citywide in 2016 with zero analysis. Columbia alone finances affordable housing policy. The unconstitutional conditions doctrine prevents government from forcing value transfers without showing why. Sheetz v. County of El Dorado (2024) clarified that broad regulatory takings violate this principle just as much as ad hoc exactions. Dolan (1994) and Koontz (2013) established the framework. Cambridge satisfies none of it. Why It Matters This case tests whether cities can extract permanent property transfers through regulation while applying uniform rules rather than individualized findings. If Cambridge wins, municipalities nationwide gain authority to extract substantial private assets from selected developers. If Columbia wins, cities must prove direct nexus and proportionality before imposing affordability mandates. The outcome reshapes land-use authority across the country. Resources Columbia St LLC v. City of Cambridge complaint - Full filing with ordinance text (Exhibit A)

item.title: The Longest Fast: Angus Barbieri's 382-Day Record
item.description: In 1965, a Scottish man named Angus Barbieri checked into a hospital and stopped eating solid food for 382 consecutive days. Starting at 456 pounds, he survived on only vitamins, electrolytes, tea,…
item.content:encoded: The Longest Fast: Angus Barbieri's 382-Day Record In 1965, a Scottish man named Angus Barbieri checked into a hospital and stopped eating solid food for 382 consecutive days. Starting at 456 pounds, he survived on only vitamins, electrolytes, tea, coffee, and sparkling water before breaking his fast on July 11, 1966, with a boiled egg and buttered bread - a moment captured by newspaper photographers waiting to document the event. Barbieri's medical team was astonished. He lost 276 pounds without hospitalization for most of the fast, maintaining his discipline from his home in Tayport while making regular checkups. By the time he broke his fast, his body had adapted so completely that he said food had lost all temptation - a psychological shift doctors found as remarkable as the physical transformation. The Guinness Book of Records officially recognized his achievement in 1971 as the longest recorded fast without solid food. As of 2025, Barbieri still holds this record, though Guinness no longer actively promotes fasting records due to safety concerns. After his fast, he settled in Warwick with his wife Mary and two sons, and a 1973 medical study confirmed he maintained a healthy weight with no lasting ill effects. Read full article on Wikipedia

item.description: Massachusetts recorded 44 fire deaths in 2025, a decline from 50 in 2024. More than 90% of fatalities occurred at home, with seniors aged 65+ accounting for 55% of victims despite representing just…
item.content:encoded: Massachusetts Fire Deaths Drop 12% in 2025 Massachusetts recorded 44 fire deaths in 2025, a decline from 50 in 2024. More than 90% of fatalities occurred at home, with seniors aged 65+ accounting for 55% of victims despite representing just 17% of the population. Key Statistics: 2024 Deaths: 50 fatalities 2025 Deaths: 44 fatalities (12% decline) Children Lost: 1 (down from 3 in 2024) Seniors (65+): 24 deaths (55% of fatalities) The Gabriel House Assisted Living fire in Fall River claimed 10 lives in a single incident - the deadliest Massachusetts fire in decades. Smoking materials remained the leading cause in 21 fire deaths, particularly dangerous when combined with medical oxygen use. Only 16 of 30 residential fires with determinable smoke alarm status had working alarms. Read the full report

item.title: Food Intelligence
item.description: Award-winning health journalist Julia Belluz and nutrition scientist Kevin Hall reveal how your food environment shapes eating behavior more than willpower. The book shows "how diseases like obesit…
item.content:encoded: Food Intelligence Award-winning health journalist Julia Belluz and nutrition scientist Kevin Hall reveal how your food environment shapes eating behavior more than willpower. The book shows "how diseases like obesity and type 2 diabetes are not a result of a failure of will power; they are consequences of food systems working as designed." The book breaks down how protein, fat, carbs, and vitamins actually impact your body and explores metabolism science. Protein differs fundamentally from carbohydrates and fat - it contains nitrogen, a critical element your body uses to build muscle, enzymes, antibodies, and hormones. Metabolism is the biochemical process that converts food into energy and new tissue, determining how your body processes and stores what you eat. View in Media

item.title: 68,000 MA Noncitizen SNAP Participants
item.description: In 2023, 68,000 noncitizens collected SNAP benefits in Massachusetts.
item.content:encoded: 68,000 MA Noncitizen SNAP Participants In 2023, 68,000 noncitizens collected SNAP benefits in Massachusetts. Noncitizen: Individuals residing in the United States who are not natural-born or naturalized citizens. These include lawful permanent residents, refugees, asylees, those granted a stay of deportation, and undocumented individuals. Lawfully present noncitizens are subject to additional nonfinancial eligibility criteria. Undocumented individuals are not eligible to receive SNAP benefits, but may be nonparticipating members of SNAP households. Deemed income: Individual sponsors of certain noncitizens may be subject to sponsor-to-noncitizen deeming, which counts the sponsor's income and resources as part of the noncitizen's income and resources when determining eligibility for SNAP. Massachusetts ranks among the higher states for noncitizen SNAP participation, placing it in the mid-to-upper tier nationally alongside California (352,000), Florida (330,000), and Illinois (63,000). Massachusetts maintains a 14.10 percent payment error rate in SNAP administration - among the worst nationally. Starting in fiscal year 2028, federal penalties will apply to states exceeding a 6% error threshold, potentially costing Massachusetts 10-15 percent of its SNAP benefit costs. item.title: Posts for December 27, 2025
item.description: Mayor Daniel Lurie signed Ordinance No. 258-25 on December 23, 2025, establishing the Reparations Fund. The ordinance had passed the Board of Supervisors on December 16 with unanimous support.
item.content:encoded: Mayor Lurie Approves Reparations Mayor Daniel Lurie signed Ordinance No. 258-25 on December 23, 2025, establishing the Reparations Fund. The ordinance had passed the Board of Supervisors on December 16 with unanimous support. The fund is authorized to receive monies—whether appropriated or donated—to support and implement the recommendations in the San Francisco Reparations Plan 2023 , submitted by the African American Reparations Advisory Committee and prepared by the Human Rights Commission. The ordinance designates the Human Rights Commission as the administrator of the fund, with authority to expend monies solely for purposes of supporting and implementing the Reparations Plan's recommendations. The Reparations Plan outlines methods to provide restitution, compensation, and rehabilitation to individuals who are Black and/or descendants of chattel enslaved persons and who have experienced proven harm in San Francisco, including displacement from urban renewal activities conducted by the former San Francisco Redevelopment Agency between 1954 and 1973. The ordinance becomes effective 30 days after the Mayor's signature, meaning it will take effect around January 22, 2026. See updated Reparations article in News section.

item.title: The Sacred and the Profane
item.description: From: Against the Machine by Paul Kingsnorth
item.content:encoded: The Sacred and the Profane From: Against the Machine by Paul Kingsnorth "The will to power, to wellbeing, to wealth, triumphs over the will to holiness and to genius. ... Spirituality is on the wane, [in] a time of bourgeois ascendancy. The knight and the monk, the philosopher and the poet, have been superseded by a new type the greedy bourgeois conqueror, organizer, and trader ... In the new machine-made industrial-capitalist civilization of Europe and America, the spiritual culture ... based on a sacred symbolism and sacred tradition, is being irrevocably annihilated." - Nikolai Berdyaev , The Bourgeois Mind and Other Essays (The Stanhope Press, 1934) The Annihilation of Tradition The Machine doesn't just displace the sacred with the material. It replaces inquiry with ideology, reporting with advocacy. When UC Berkeley academics defend welfare expansion not through rigorous analysis but through appeals to moral righteousness, when federal fraud investigations are ignored because they contradict a preferred narrative, we're witnessing exactly what Berdyaev diagnosed: the complete annihilation of any tradition that values truth-telling over tribal solidarity. The bourgeois mind, once purely materialist, has been supplanted by the ideological bourgeois—the wealthy donor class and their proxy intellectuals who demand "equitable" systems that benefit the poor while actually creating dependency and control. They've weaponized the language of compassion. Meanwhile, the actual worker—the one pulling three jobs—is erased from the conversation entirely. See related journal entry

item.title: California Faces $2.5 Billion CalFresh Bill
item.description: Federal legislation enacted in July 2025 just handed California a major fiscal problem. Starting in federal fiscal year 2028, states will shoulder part of SNAP benefits costs—determined by their pa…
item.content:encoded: California Faces $2.5 Billion CalFresh Bill Federal legislation enacted in July 2025 just handed California a major fiscal problem. Starting in federal fiscal year 2028, states will shoulder part of SNAP benefits costs—determined by their payment error rate (PER). California's 11 percent error rate means the state will pay 15 percent of its CalFresh costs if it doesn't improve. At current spending levels, that's nearly $1.8 billion annually in new benefit costs, plus another $600 million in administrative expenses. Total estimated impact: $2.5 billion per year. Payment Error Reductions California has struggled to lower its PER since federal fiscal year 2017, hovering around 11 percent—consistently above the 10 percent threshold that triggers the highest cost-sharing tier. According to the state auditor's December 2025 report, the largest source of CalFresh errors stems from inaccurate wage and salary reporting at application and recertification. County workers fail to capture participants' true earned income, or beneficiaries underreport earnings due to limited understanding of rules. The state already submits corrective action plans to federal regulators, but implementation remains slow. Recent state legislation provided funding for PER reduction work, yet Social Services stated it hasn't had time to hire additional staff or finalize specific strategies. A Timing Problem The OBBBA's cost-sharing formula takes effect in less than three years for federal fiscal year 2028, with the state's PER from FFY 2025 or 2026 determining the tier. If California doesn't substantially reduce its error rate in the next 18 months, it will begin writing very large checks. Even if the state lowers its PER to 8–10 percent, it will still owe 10 percent of CalFresh costs—roughly $1.2 billion annually. Against a projected $20 billion operating deficit for state fiscal year 2026–27, these new mandatory costs threaten both the CalFresh program and the state's broader budget balance. item.title: The Monk and the Machine
item.description: Paul Kingsnorth's new book dissects how technology and modern capitalism have reshaped humanity, offering a critique rooted in spiritual and economic analysis. Meanwhile, billionaire Alex Karp, co-…
item.content:encoded: The Monk and the Machine Paul Kingsnorth's new book dissects how technology and modern capitalism have reshaped humanity, offering a critique rooted in spiritual and economic analysis. Meanwhile, billionaire Alex Karp, co-founder and CEO of Denver-based data analytics firm Palantir, purchases the 3,700-acre St. Benedict's Monastery in Old Snowmass, Colorado, for $120 million. The property, built in the 1950s by Trappist monks seeking a life of silence and prayer, will be converted to a private residence. The monastery sits on prime real estate featuring a 24,000-square-foot main building, three creeks, and senior water rights in the Roaring Fork Valley. 'Want is the acid. Capitalism is the battery. Growth is the engine. Greed is the forming energy that moves us to where we are inevitably headed...Modernity is a machine for destroying limits.' View in Media

item.content:encoded: Consumer Confidence Down Consumer confidence fell sharply in December to 89.1, down 3.8 points (-4.1%) from November's 92.9. December : 89.1 (-3.8 points, -4.1% MoM) November : 92.9 3-Month Trend : Declining from 95.5 (October) The Conference Board's survey of 3,000+ households reveals weakening consumer sentiment across expectations and current conditions. This drop underscores consumer anxiety about employment, inflation, and overall economic stability despite recent market strength. Sentiment vs. Confidence While confidence fell, sentiment rose to 52.9 in December (up from 51 in November). The two surveys measure different aspects: UMich focuses on current personal finances and future buying intentions, while Conference Board tracks expectations about employment and general business conditions. The Sentiment uptick likely reflects relief from lower inflation and stable housing markets, while the Confidence decline suggests erosion in job security outlook and economic growth expectations as the year closes. {{chart:Consumer Confidence}} View all consumer indicators

item.title: The Poor Side of Town
item.description: The Poor Side of Town
item.content:encoded: The Poor Side of Town The federal government has failed at urban renewal. Centralized planning with top-down directives has yielded disastrous results. Policies to intervene in low-cost neighborhoods and "reform" them have been ineffective. We now have established municipal funds to pay retroactively for their adverse impacts. Continued misallocation of funds will bankrupt cities and prove that upward mobility is best achieved through organic local development coupled with that big ugly word CAPITAL. It may not be pretty, healthy, safe, and decent at times, but local wealth accumulation and self-determination is superior to social engineering driven by sophisticated academia and aloof bureaucrats. Mr. Husock demonstrates that the true path to opportunity rests in neighborhood self-determination and the individual entrepreneur. Explore in Media

item.content:encoded: War, Reparations, and Dying Build Ships Congress's annual defense authorization includes $30.96 billion ($20.84 billion requested). The DDG–51 destroyer program receives $6.34 billion in hull construction plus $5.40 billion additional for "workforce and shipyard enhancements". Read: S.2296, §4101, FY2026 Defense Authorization Reparations Fund San Francisco formally established a Reparations Fund—turning a political idea into a budget structure with defined legal plumbing. The ordinance creates the fund to receive appropriated or donated dollars, but it does not set a specific appropriation amount. No spending authority follows without a separate vote. Read: San Francisco Administrative Code Amendment MAID in America Euphemism often ends up in public policy. "Medical aid in dying" sanitizes what it's doing and we drift from suicide prevention to assisted suicide where fewer people stand up for our inconvenient life. Read the journal entry

item.title: War Bill
item.description: The Senate authorized $30.96 billion for Navy shipbuilding in FY2026—$10.1 billion more than the Pentagon requested. The increase, concentrated in destroyer production and a new workforce investmen…
item.content:encoded: War Bill The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 is a massive bill - about 3,100 pages long. The Senate took the executive branch's $20.84 billion shipbuilding request and authorized $30.96 billion instead, a $10.1 billion increase to build more destroyers. The increase centers on the DDG–51 guided-missile destroyer program—the Navy's workhorse for force projection—and introduces an explicit new line item: $5.4 billion in "wage and quality of life enhancements" for shipyard workers and industrial base infrastructure. That category did not exist in the executive request. It is a direct congressional statement that the shipbuilding industrial base is underfunded relative to production demand. Item (SEC. 4101) FY2026 Request Senate Authorized Change Notes CVN Refueling Overhauls $1,779,011,000 $1,779,011,000 — Carriers held at requested level DDG 1000 $52,358,000 $52,358,000 — Next-gen destroyer line held steady DDG–51 $10,773,000 $6,335,173,000 +$6,324,400,000 Baseline plus $5.3B in add-ons (see below) Wage & quality of life enhancements — surface shipbuilding, ship repair, public/private yards n/a $5,400,000,000 +$5,400,000,000 New line item under DDG–51 Wage & quality of life enhancements (additional) n/a $924,400,000 +$924,400,000 Bracketed add-on under DDG–51 DDG–51 (zero-request line item) — $1,350,000,000 +$1,350,000,000 Separate DDG–51 authorized line DDG–51 Advance Procurement n/a $900,000,000 +$900,000,000 Bracketed add-on Large Surface Combatant Shipyard Infrastructure & Industrial Base n/a $450,000,000 +$450,000,000 Bracketed add-on TAGOS SURTASS Ships $612,205,000 $612,205,000 — Surveillance ships held steady Outfitting $863,846,000 $886,846,000 +$23,000,000 Minor increase Service Craft $34,602,000 $174,602,000 +$140,000,000 YRBM procurement boost Total Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy $20,840,224,000 $30,957,624,000 +$10,117,400,000 48.5% increase The Senate increased the destroyer account from $10.8 million (request) to $6.34 billion (authorized)—a 58-fold expansion. Congress created two new, labeled line items totaling $6.3 billion that did not exist in the Pentagon request: $5.4 billion for "Wage and quality of life enhancements for conventional surface shipbuilding, private ship repair, and public shipyards" $924.4 million for additional wage and quality of life enhancements $450 million for "Large Surface Combatant Shipyard Infrastructure and Industrial Base" This is money to keep shipyard workers employed, competitive, and to upgrade the infrastructure that builds the ships. Congress is betting that the binding constraint on naval force expansion is not design or political will, but human and industrial capacity. Carrier refueling overhauls, the next-generation DDG 1000, and surveillance ships all held at the Pentagon's request level. Congress prioritized destroyer capacity expansion and industrial base resilience, not fleet diversity. The Pentagon is underfunded for the naval industrial commitments Congress believes are necessary. A 48.5% increase in total authorization signals no mere adjustment—it is a fundamental disagreement about resource allocation. The creation of explicit workforce investment line items, rather than burying those costs in ship prices, indicates congressional intention to treat shipyard employment and facility upgrade as strategic assets that transcend individual platforms. Beyond shipbuilding, the 3,100-page bill includes some specific technology requirements: Artificial Intelligence oversight : Creates an "Artificial General Intelligence Steering Committee" and requires "Artificial intelligence model assessment and oversight." (S. 2296, Sec. 1623, p. 23) Quantum readiness : Requires the Department of Defense to develop a "Strategy on quantum readiness." (S. 2296, Sec. 6611, p. 31) AI in anti-money laundering : Requires a "Report on implementation of artificial intelligence into certain anti-money laundering investigations." (S. 2296, Sec. 6032, p. 29) Sources S. 2296 (119th Congress) — BILLS-119s2296es.pdf (SEC. 4101, p. 1784) HII to Build Small Surface Combatants for U.S. Navy

item.description: SF Ordinance No. 258-25 (File 240701) creates a Reparations Fund as a category-four fund to receive appropriated or donated dollars; it establishes the budget mechanism, but the ordinance text does…
item.content:encoded: Updated: December 27, 2025 San Francisco establishes a Reparations Fund Ordinance No. 258-25 (File 240701) establishes the Reparations Fund as a “category four fund” (as defined in Administrative Code § 10.100-1 ) to receive money appropriated or donated “to support and implement” the recommendations in the San Francisco Reparations Plan 2023 , which was submitted by the African American Reparations Advisory Committee (created by Ordinance No. 259-20 ) and prepared by the Human Rights Commission . The Reparations Plan is described as outlining methods to provide “ restitution, compensation, and rehabilitation ” to individuals who are Black and/or descendants of a chattel enslaved person and who have experienced a proven harm in San Francisco, including (as an example) displacement tied to the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency’s urban renewal activities (1954–1973) . San Francisco Reparations Plan The Reparations Plan was published on July 7, 2023 and is the final report and recommendations aimed at addressing harms to eligible individuals in San Francisco through measures described in the ordinance text as “restitution, compensation, and rehabilitation.” Sources: SF.gov report page: African American Reparations Advisory Committee Final Report (July 7, 2023) PDF: African American Reparations Advisory Committee Final Report - July 7, 2023 Legislative Action Sponsors Shamann Walton Chyanne Chen Rafael Mandelman Connie Chan Jackie Fielder Bilal Mahmood Ayes (11) Connie Chan Chyanne Chen Matt Dorsey Jackie Fielder Bilal Mahmood Rafael Mandelman Myrna Melgar Danny Sauter Stephen Sherrill Shamann Walton Alan Wong Ordinance Text SF Legistar: File 240701, Ordinance No. 258-25 (Full Text) Sources SF Legistar: File 240701 (Legislation Detail)

item.title: 69 Is Retarded
item.description: Hamm v. Smith examines whether courts must consider adaptive functioning and cognitive evidence alongside IQ scores when determining if a death row inmate qualifies for Eighth Amendment protection…
item.content:encoded: 69 Is Retarded Hamm v. Smith examines whether courts must consider adaptive functioning and cognitive evidence alongside IQ scores when determining if a death row inmate qualifies for Eighth Amendment protection from execution. The case hinges on whether states can apply rigid numerical thresholds or must weigh comprehensive evidence of intellectual disability. The Question: Joseph Clifton Smith scored 72-78 on five IQ tests over four decades, clustering near Alabama's 70 threshold. While only one score fell below 70, school records show he functioned years behind grade level and was diagnosed with mental retardation in seventh grade. Lower courts found him intellectually disabled; Alabama argues his IQ is simply too high. The Divide: Justices Sotomayor, Barrett, and Kagan pressed Alabama on why adaptive functioning evidence matters so little when all indicia point toward intellectual disability. Justice Gorsuch sought middle ground—states need "leeway" but can't ignore disability claims outright. Justice Kavanaugh signaled openness to lower court discretion. The Stakes: The ruling will clarify how Atkins v. Virginia (2002) and Hall v. Florida (2014) apply nationally, determining whether quantitative metrics (IQ tests) or holistic evidence (adaptive functioning, developmental history) controls in capital cases. Read the full analysis

item.title: Hamm v. Smith
item.description: Supreme Court oral argument examining the application of IQ test scores and adaptive functioning evidence in determining whether a death row inmate is intellectually disabled under the Eighth Amend…
item.content:encoded: IQ Scores and the Death Penalty Case: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department of Corrections v. Joseph Clifton Smith Case Number: 24-872 Oral Argument Date: December 10, 2025 Duration: Approximately 2 hours The Question Whether and how courts may consider the cumulative effect of multiple IQ scores—along with evidence of adaptive functioning and other cognitive impairments—in assessing whether a death row inmate qualifies for protection under the Eighth Amendment's ban on executing individuals with intellectual disabilities. Background Joseph Clifton Smith was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in Alabama in 1997 for a killing committed during a robbery. At the time of his conviction, testing determined that Smith "performed math at the level of a kindergarten-aged child, spelled at a third-grade level, and read at a fourth-grade level." Throughout his childhood and early education, Smith struggled significantly, receiving scores of 74 and 75 on initial IQ tests, eventually placed in special education, and dropped out after failing seventh and eighth grade. In the decades following his sentencing, the Supreme Court issued two foundational rulings: Atkins v. Virginia (2002): Held that the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment bars execution of individuals with intellectual disabilities. The Court left it to states to define intellectual disability. Hall v. Florida (2014): Ruled that states cannot rely on a rigid IQ cutoff (Florida's rule of 70 or below) as dispositive. "Intellectual disability is a condition, not a number." States must consider evidence holistically, including adaptive functioning. The Complication: Over nearly 40 years, Smith underwent five separate IQ tests, scoring 72, 74, 74, 75, and 78. While only one score (72) falls below Alabama's operative threshold of 70 (when accounting for the standard margin of error of +/- 5 points), all scores cluster near the border. Smith's trial court found him competent to stand trial. Federal courts, however, have since considered evidence of his lifelong cognitive and adaptive deficits—school performance two to four years below grade level, diagnosis of mental retardation (at that time) in seventh grade, functional reading and math at elementary levels, and multiple arrests and incarcerations reflecting poor social judgment. Lower Court Rulings: Both the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama and the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals determined that Smith qualifies as intellectually disabled under Atkins , based on a "holistic approach" that considered his multiple IQ scores, adaptive functioning deficits, and developmental history—not simply his lowest score. Alabama sought Supreme Court review. The Arguments Alabama (Solicitor General Robert Overing): Overing argued that Smith has not "come close to proving an IQ of 70 or below." (Tr. p. 8) The lower courts have "changed the rules" and "expanded Atkins " by elevating non-IQ evidence above the critical threshold. Alabama law requires that IQ be the primary measure of intellectual disability; other evidence may supplement but cannot override IQ results. Overing urged the Court to reverse this "expansion" and clarify that states may require a more rigorous showing of low IQ. United States (Assistant to the Solicitor General Harry Graver): Graver contended that Atkins "outsourced the definition of intellectual ability to the states," giving them "significant discretion." (Tr. p. 15) He argued that Alabama's approach—requiring that Smith's "true IQ is likely 70 or below based on all relevant evidence, including his multiple IQ scores all above 70"—represents a reasonable exercise of that discretion. The lower courts impermissibly weighed adaptive functioning evidence to override the preponderance of IQ testing, in the government's view. Joseph Clifton Smith (Seth Waxman, Counsel): Waxman argued that Alabama law, like that of nearly all other states, requires courts to evaluate all probative evidence of intellectual functioning. (Tr. p. 22) When multiple IQ scores cluster near the threshold and expert testimony establishes that those scores alone don't decide the issue, courts must consider comprehensive evidence—including neuropsychological tests, grade school records showing years of below-average performance, and functional deficits. Waxman maintained that the lower courts properly applied established law in finding Smith intellectually disabled. Justice Positions Skeptical of Smith's Claim: Justice Neil Gorsuch: Proposed a test under which states need "a little leeway" to determine whether a defendant has "substantial subaverage intellectual function" as long as they don't treat a single low-70s score as "decisive" and don't "use facts extraneous to IQ scores to outweigh a low score." (Tr. pp. 32-34) His framing appeared to privilege IQ evidence and skepticism toward adaptive functioning as a decisive factor. Sympathetic to Smith's Holistic Approach: Justice Sonia Sotomayor: Questioned whether Alabama's position was tenable, noting that Alabama's "own expert said he had valid scores between 72 and 78 and he relied on all of the other indicia to determine that he believed this person wasn't intellectually disabled"—while Smith's experts "concluded differently, and the district court credited" their conclusions. (Tr. pp. 27-28) Her questions suggested that the state's own testimony supported a holistic inquiry. Justice Amy Coney Barrett: Pressed Alabama on whether it truly ignores adaptive functioning evidence. "It seems to me that Justice Sotomayor is right that there are some Alabama cases that do move on" to consider adaptive functioning. (Tr. p. 38) Her questions suggested openness to lower courts considering adaptive functioning evidence alongside IQ scores. Justice Elena Kagan: Proposed a potential test: "if you have one score that brings you into the 70 minus range, that's enough so that you have to … open the door to a person's evidence" regarding adaptive functioning. (Tr. p. 41) Her approach would appear to prevent states from simply dismissing non-IQ evidence when any score falls near the threshold. Potentially Pivotal: Justice Brett Kavanaugh: Expressed skepticism of Alabama's rigid position, asking "[W]hat's the logic or the rationale behind not having a district court or a trial court or a state court [to] have the ability … to go on and look at more?" (Tr. p. 45) His questions suggested openness to lower courts considering broader evidence, though his ultimate voting position remained uncertain. Critical Hypotheticals and Tensions The Multiple Scores Problem: If a defendant has four IQ scores of 90 and one score of 71, should courts be required to look at adaptive functioning? Waxman agreed "100 percent" that they would not necessarily have to do so, suggesting that courts could hear expert testimony concluding the defendant's IQ is sufficiently high that no further inquiry is needed. This suggests potential common ground on extreme cases but leaves unclear the treatment of Smith's scores (all within a narrow band near 70). Dicta vs. Holding: Alabama argued that post- Hall confusion arose from dicta (non-central language) in Supreme Court opinions, asserting that "there is not a case in which that other evidence has ever trumped IQ in Alabama." Waxman countered that Alabama law and nearly all state law require evaluation of "all probative evidence," implying that IQ alone cannot be conclusive when expert testimony suggests scores don't decide the issue. The Role of Modern Medical Standards: Justice Gorsuch referenced the Court's decision in Moore v. Texas , which held that states should rely on modern medical standards (which emphasize adaptive functioning and contextual evidence) rather than outdated ones. Yet Alabama's current approach arguably de-emphasizes modern psychological understanding that intellectual disability is multifactorial. Likely Outcome The court appeared divided. A potential narrow holding might allow states modest discretion in setting thresholds while requiring that, when IQ scores cluster near a defined cutoff (particularly 70 or just above), courts must consider credible evidence of adaptive functioning and developmental history. Justice Kavanaugh's openness to lower court discretion and Justice Sotomayor's emphasis on the state's own expert conceding a holistic inquiry suggested possible middle ground. Most likely scenario: The Court will not simply defer to Alabama's rule requiring IQ scores below 70 absent extraordinary circumstances. Instead, it may clarify that Hall v. Florida and modern diagnostic standards (which emphasize adaptive functioning) remain binding and that lower courts have discretion to find intellectual disability based on comprehensive evidence when scores cluster near the threshold—but that states retain authority to set reasonable evidentiary standards for what constitutes sufficient proof. Stakes: The outcome affects capital cases nationwide and the underlying question of how courts balance quantitative metrics (IQ tests) against qualitative, multi-factor evidence of cognitive and adaptive impairment in determining fundamental constitutional protections. Florida (2014) Prohibits rigid IQ cutoffs; requires holistic assessment of intellectual disability including adaptive functioning

item.title: Conclusive and Preclusive
item.description: Solicitor General Sauer argued that the President possesses exclusive constitutional authority over executive officials and cannot be constrained by Congress through removal restrictions. Counsel A…
item.content:encoded: Conclusive and Preclusive Solicitor General Sauer argued that the President possesses exclusive constitutional authority over executive officials and cannot be constrained by Congress through removal restrictions. Counsel Amit Agarwal countered that only powers that are truly conclusive and preclusive—such as control over criminal investigations per Trump v. United States —warrant removal authority. Most independent agencies exercise mixed powers (investigative, adjudicatory, rulemaking) that are not exclusively presidential, he argued, and thus removal protections remain constitutional. Justices pressed both sides on where to draw lines: Does criminal investigative authority alone trigger presidential control? If agencies control vast regulatory domains, does independent status survive? Here are the independent agencies identified by The Seila Law (2020) decision: Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Federal Reserve (Fed) Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) Postal Service Board of Governors (USPS) Social Security Administration (SSA) Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) Commission on Civil Rights (CCR) Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission (OSHRC) U.S. Sentencing Commission (USSC) Office of Special Counsel (OSC) Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) Read the full analysis

Supreme Court oral arguments revealed a likely majority ready to expand presidential authority to remove FTC commissioners without cause, potentially reshaping oversight of independent agencies nationwide. The Case: Trump challenges statutory removal restrictions preventing the President from firing FTC Commissioner Jatinder Slaughter except for "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office." Likely Outcome: A narrow ruling favoring Trump, though the Court appears divided on whether to formally overturn Humphrey's Executor (90-year-old precedent) or craft narrow carve-outs for agencies like the Federal Reserve. item.title: Slaughter v. Trump
item.description: Supreme Court oral argument examining constitutional limits on presidential power and statutory interpretation in landmark case with implications for executive authority
item.content:encoded: Trump v. Slaughter: Presidential Power Over Independent Agencies Case: Trump, President of the United States v. Slaughter Case Number: 25-332 Oral Argument Date: December 8, 2025 Duration: 2 hours, 30 minutes, 30 seconds The Question Whether the President has the power to remove Federal Trade Commission (FTC) commissioners protected by a "for cause" removal statute limiting removal to "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office." Background Trump nominated Jatinder Slaughter to the FTC during his first term; Biden renominated her in 2023 for a second seven-year term (expiring 2029). In March 2025, Trump fired her via email, citing only that her continued service would be "inconsistent with [the] Administration's priorities." A federal judge ordered her reinstatement; the D.C. Circuit declined to stay that order. Stakes: The ruling will determine whether the President can control independent agencies. The Seila Law (2020) decision identified approximately two dozen multimember independent agencies with similar removal protections, potentially exposing the following to constitutional challenge: Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Federal Reserve (Fed) Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) Postal Service Board of Governors (USPS) Social Security Administration (SSA) Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) Commission on Civil Rights (CCR) Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission (OSHRC) U.S. Sentencing Commission (USSC) Office of Special Counsel (OSC) Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) The Arguments Trump Administration (Solicitor General D. John Sauer): The "for cause" restriction violates Article II executive power. The President must have unfettered removal authority over executive officials. Humphrey's Executor has been "eroded" and should be reconsidered. (Tr. p. 48, ll. 5-8) Slaughter (Counsel Amit Agarwal): Congress has constitutional authority to structure independent agencies with removal protections. The President's duty to execute the law does not permit violation of it "with impunity." Overruling Humphrey's Executor would destabilize "dozens of institutions...that embody a distillation of human wisdom and experience." (Tr. p. 116, ll. 8-15) Justice Positions Likely for Trump: Chief Justice Roberts: Called Humphrey's Executor a "dried husk" (Tr. p. 141, l. 15) Justice Gorsuch: Deemed it "poorly reasoned"; suggested reinvigorating the non-delegation doctrine, asking "Is the water warm, General?" (Tr. p. 45, ll. 7-8) Justice Kavanaugh: Proposed a narrow holding affecting the FTC but preserving Federal Reserve protections (Tr. p. 23, ll. 1-15) Justice Barrett: Questioned whether independent agencies became "something that Congress didn't intend" Likely for Slaughter: Justice Kagan: Resisted carve-outs, arguing constitutional logic "drives you there" regardless of footnotes (Tr. p. 27, ll. 14-24) Justice Sotomayor: Pressed Sauer to name other 90-year-old precedents overruled while "fundamentally alter[ing] the structure of government" Justice Jackson: Proposed letting Congress decide the issue, questioning the government's democratic accountability argument. "I'm trying to understand why you think that Congress is somehow less democratically accountable for the way in which it constructs these agencies and determines the term of office of the officers" (Tr. p. 29, ll. 7-11) Assessment: A clear majority appeared ready to rule Trump has removal power. Less certain: whether the Court would formally overrule Humphrey's Executor or craft a narrow holding. Critical Hypotheticals Multi-Member Structure (Justice Alito): Would structural protections matter if terms were short and no partisan balance requirement existed? Agarwal responded that single-headed agencies with removal restrictions pose greater threats to individual liberty. Carve-Outs (Justice Kavanaugh/Kagan): Kavanaugh proposed excluding Federal Reserve governors as "unique" and "distinct." Kagan countered that footnotes carving exceptions "doesn't do much good if the entire logic of the opinion drives you" there. (Tr. p. 23, ll. 14-15; p. 27, ll. 20-24) Cascade Effect (Justice Jackson): Jackson noted the administration could challenge removal provisions at the NLRB, NRC, Commission on Civil Rights, Sentencing Commission, OSHA Review Commission, and Consumer Product Safety Commission. (Tr. p. 71, ll. 9-24) Central Tensions Article II vs. Article I Authority: Trump administration: Article II vests unfettered removal power in the President. Slaughter: Article I gives Congress authority to structure agencies, including removal protections. Which branch is more "democratically accountable" for agency design? Institutional Stability vs. Constitutional Principle: Agarwal warned that a Trump victory would destabilize "dozens of institutions" built over 90 years. Yet allowing potentially unconstitutional restrictions to stand contradicts bedrock principles. Narrow Holding Viability: Can the Court restrict its holding to the FTC while preserving Federal Reserve protections? Kagan suggested constitutional logic doesn't work by footnote. Likely Outcome A majority appears ready to rule the President has power to remove FTC commissioners without cause. Most likely: a narrow holding distinguishing the FTC from other agencies (particularly the Fed), though Kagan's warnings about constitutional logic may make such distinctions fragile. Formal overruling of Humphrey's Executor : less certain. Immediate effect: Slaughter's reinstatement would likely be vacated. Resources Supreme Court Docket 25-332 Oral Argument Transcript (PDF) Oral Argument Audio (Apple Podcasts) Audio from Court (MP3) SCOTUS Blog Analysis
