item.title: RoboTaxis
item.description: City council members across US cities oppose autonomous robotaxis over job displacement and safety concerns
item.content:encoded: No Drivah As autonomous robotaxi companies push into new markets, city council members are blocking expansion through delay tactics and regulatory scrutiny. The core dispute: job displacement for rideshare drivers versus safety claims. Washington, D.C. Council Member Charles Allen initially championed autonomous vehicles but grew frustrated by delays. A bill to legalize driverless driving stalled in committee, waiting for an overdue safety report that DDOT promised in fall 2025 but pushed to "early 2026." Allen's public frustration: "So odd that the Washington Post Editorial Board goes after me to pass a bill allowing autonomous vehicles to enter DC's market." Mayor Muriel Bowser hasn't issued permits for next-phase testing. Maryland Governor Wes Moore is more supportive. Boston Boston's City Council hearing (July 2025) revealed deep skepticism (because we all know Boston drivahs never cut cornahs). Councilors Henry Santana and Erin Murphy introduced an ordinance creating an advisory council and requiring a full public study before any deployment—explicitly to protect jobs from "robotaxi takeover." Chief of Streets Jascha Franklin-Hodge quipped: "If every robotaxi drives like a confused out-of-state tourist, we will very quickly find them unwelcome on the streets of Boston." His concern: only 40% of robotaxi miles in San Francisco are "productive" (rest are empty repositioning), companies won't share internal data, and Boston's narrow streets and winter weather present unproven challenges. Minneapolis Council Member Jamal Osman : "It will put thousands of people out of work." He emphasized the impact on immigrants and communities of color dependent on ride-sharing income. Council Vice President Aisha Chughtai supports an outright ban: "I want to see the strongest possible regulation of this." Council Member Robin Wonsley recalled the Uber/Lyft entry a decade ago as cautionary: "I have no intention of repeating those mistakes." The Labor Push Autumn Weintraub (App Drivers Union): "Drivers are people. ... They could lose their jobs to an empty seat." Jack Kenslea (UFCW Local 1445): "What that really means is that the money is taken out of the pockets of the hardworking drivers... and putting it into the pockets of Google and robotaxi executives who are just going to laugh all the way to the bank." Industry reps argue new job types will offset losses. This claim hasn't swayed council members. Regulatory Delay Rather than outright bans, cities are using: Mandatory advisory councils and studies Delays in permitting and safety approvals State-level legislative uncertainty If this holds, robotaxi companies will face 12-24 month delays per market. Opposition Summary Minneapolis: Jamal Osman, Aisha Chughtai, Robin Wonsley Boston: Henry Santana, Erin Murphy, Jascha Franklin-Hodge D.C.: Charles Allen Sources Boston.com (July 25, 2025) Minnesota Star Tribune (Dec 4, 2025) Axios (Dec 4, 2025)

item.content:encoded: One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This Omar El Akkad's 2025 National Book Award winner examines Western complicity in global atrocities and the moral fracture experienced by those who believed in liberal ideals. This powerful nonfiction memoir challenges the convenient fictions that allow empires to avoid accountability, tracing how entire populations become invisible to systems built to exploit them. Rules, conventions, morals, reality itself: all exist so long as their existence is convenient to the preservation of power. Otherwise, they, like all else, are expendable." View in Media

item.content:encoded: The historic Kennedy family compound in Hyannis, Massachusetts is on the market for $21.5M. View data Pipe Bomber Identified On January 5, 2021, pipe bombs were placed at the RNC and DNC headquarters in Washington, D.C. The FBI identified Brian J. Cole, Jr. , a 30-year-old bail bondsman's office worker from Woodbridge, Virginia, through surveillance footage, financial records, and cell phone data. Evidence: Video shows the perpetrator placing the DNC bomb at 7:54 p.m. and RNC bomb at 8:16 p.m., wearing dark clothing, gloves, and Nike Speed Turf shoes. Between 2019-2020, Cole purchased pipes, end caps, 9V battery connectors, kitchen timers, electrical wire, and steel wool—all components matching the devices. Notably, he continued purchasing identical parts after January 5 . Cell phone records pinged towers near South Capitol Street, D Street Southeast, and directly adjacent to the RNC—timeline and location matching the suspect's route. Cole's physical profile (5'6", corrective eyeglasses) matched the bomber's description from video surveillance. item.content:encoded: Jobless Claims Initial jobless claims (seasonally adjusted, monthly average) fell to 217,600 in November, down from 226,750 in October, marking a meaningful improvement in labor market health. The decline suggests employers remain cautious with layoffs despite economic headwinds. Claims below 300,000 typically indicate a resilient job market. The recent decline reinforces signals that employers are holding onto workers even as consumer sentiment remains fragile, keeping the labor market as one of the economy's strongest anchors. {{chart:Jobless Claims}} View all employment indicators Conformity Bias Nature retracted a flawed climate study (Kotz et al.) that had been widely used in global financial regulation and policy, including by the Federal Reserve's stress tests. The retraction highlights the importance of rigorous methodology in informing major policy decisions affecting economic growth and interest rates. A single country's erroneous data—Uzbekistan—inflated the study's projections: when removed, global GDP damage estimates fell from 62% to 23% by 2100. Without climate skeptics scrutinizing research, studies like this would proceed unchecked, compromising the integrity of science itself. Read the analysis No Fraud 🙉🙈🙊 The Trump administration is withholding federal SNAP administrative funding from Democratic-led states that refuse to submit recipient data (immigration status, SSN, etc.) requested under executive order. Supporters argue the data strengthens fraud detection; opponents cite privacy violations. A federal judge has blocked the USDA from denying funds based on non-compliance, but the administration intends to proceed. item.title: SF MAHA
item.description: The San Francisco City Attorney filed a sweeping lawsuit against Kraft Heinz, Mondelez, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola, General Mills, Nestlé, ConAgra, Mars, Post Holdings, Kellanov, and WK Kellogg Co.
item.content:encoded: How can we drive more ounces into more bodies more often? The San Francisco City Attorney filed a sweeping lawsuit against Kraft Heinz, Mondelez, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola, General Mills, Nestlé, ConAgra, Mars, Post Holdings, Kellanov, and WK Kellogg Co. The complaint alleges that these companies deliberately designed ultra-processed foods (UPF) to be addictive, targeted children with marketing, and concealed health consequences. Philip Morris entered the food industry with explicit addiction science expertise. Its Director of Applied Research distilled the company's philosophy: "control all of the pleasure drugs that are not regulated." (San Francisco City Attorney Complaint, ¶ 112, p. 25) The Addiction Science The complaint marshals evidence across three criteria the U.S. Surgeon General used to classify tobacco as addictive: 1. Compulsive use despite harm. Patients with diet-related diseases consume UPF despite needing dietary restriction. Rats exposed to industrially-produced sweets show greater resistance to electric shock than when accessing methamphetamine. 2. Psychoactive effects. When UPF was surgically inserted into patients' guts, dopamine levels increased 150-200%—independent of taste, smell, or touch. FDA Commissioner Robert Califf testified that medications for opioid and heroin addiction (naltrexone, pexacerfont) effectively reduce cravings for UPF. 3. Reinforcement. Adults and children consume UPF when satiated. Daily consumers develop increased willingness to work for UPF over time, a pattern absent with non-UPF foods. Health Crisis in Children Type 2 Diabetes : Virtually non-existent in children before 1985; rates skyrocketed from 2001–2017. Projections estimate sevenfold increase by 2060. Pediatric fatty liver disease : Only a handful of cases before 2000; nearly tripled by 2017–2021. Childhood obesity : Rates tripled since the 1970s. Marketing to Children & Artificial Dyes Defendants spent $1.6+ billion annually on advertising to children (by 2006), with $870 million directed at children under 12. Philip Morris's CFO declared in 1987: "We've decided to focus our marketing on kids, where we know our strength is greatest." (San Francisco City Attorney Complaint, ¶ 167, p. 36; citing Hans Storr, Remarks to First Boston Beverage Tobacco Conference, April 1, 1987) Coca-Cola set out to drive individual consumption higher than milk and water. Todd Putman, Coca-Cola's former head of U.S. Marketing, articulated the goal: "How can we drive more ounces into more bodies more often?" (San Francisco City Attorney Complaint, ¶ 170, p. 37; citing Michael Moss, Salt Sugar Fat , 2013, p. 110) Children were a major target. According to Putman, "when they would turn twelve, we'd suddenly attack them like a bunch of wolves" with marketing campaigns. (¶ 170, p. 37; citing Moss, p. 111) Coca-Cola internally acknowledged the predatory logic. A 2005 internal report on targeting children stated: "Teens are at a crucial stage on the learning curve of 'how to be me.'" (¶ 171, p. 37; citing Clinkin Research, Convenience Teens Building Loyalty with the Next Generation , Coca Cola Leadership Council, 2005) The company's rationale was to create lifelong consumers. When Jeffrey Dunn, Coca-Cola President and COO of North and South America, suggested the company stop marketing in public schools, he was called "an embarrassment to the company" and fired shortly thereafter. (¶ 172, p. 37) The industry used petroleum-derived artificial dyes (Red 40, Yellow 6) to appeal to children. Defendants resisted removal despite evidence of behavioral harm. Kellogg pledged removal by 2018 but broke the promise; Mars committed to removing titanium dioxide by 2021, then reversed course. Formulation for Addiction The purpose was explicit: "to understand how to exploit the physiological structures of the human brain, to override the body's natural mechanisms for resisting its addictive qualities, and to evade the body's ability to control intake." (San Francisco City Attorney Complaint, ¶ 120, p. 26) Defendants employed sensory psychologists, fMRI brain imaging, and roboticized taste buds to optimize products. PepsiCo uses robots fitted with human taste buds hardwired into computers to simulate neurochemical responses. Nestlé employs sensory psychologists studying "taste development, perception and food preference in young children." Philip Morris and Kraft conducted joint research into "drivers of acceptance, mood or satiety/drinkability" that "are usually not consciously perceived … but are perceived at the receptor level (ex. Pheromones)." (¶ 122, p. 26) Kool-Aid's marketing loyalty program, the "Wacky Warehouse," was described by Philip Morris's beverage division director as "our version of the Marlboro Country Store." (¶ 185, p. 39) A Philip Morris analysis called it "the most effective kid's marketing vehicle known." (¶ 185, p. 39) Legal Theory The complaint asserts two causes of action: (1) violation of California's Unfair Competition Law, and (2) public nuisance. Plaintiff seeks declaratory relief, injunctive relief, statutory civil penalties, and abatement relief. Products Named in Complaint Kraft Heinz Lunchables, Bagel Bites, Classico, Cool Whip, Country Time, Crystal Light, Jet-Puffed, Miracle Whip, Shake 'N Bake, Stove Top, Sure-Jell, Smart Ones, Boca Burger, Cheez Whiz, A.1. Mondelez Nabisco, Oreo, Ritz, Triscuit, Wheat Thins, Chips Ahoy!, Honey Maid, Cadbury, Sour Patch Kids, Tang, Toblerone, Belvita, Cote d'Or, Swedish Fish, Cheese Nips, Lorna Doone, Fig Newtons, Nilla Wafers, Nutter Butter, Teddy Grahams Post Holdings Alpen, Chips Ahoy, Coco Wheats, Golden Crisp, Honey Bunches of Oats, Honeycomb, Honey Maid, Honey Ohs, Oreo O's, Pebbles, Puffins, Raisin Bran, Waffle Crisp Coca-Cola Coca-Cola, Diet Coke, Coke Zero, Sprite, Fanta, Fresca, Barq's, Minute Maid, FuzeTea, Peace Tea, Powerade, Schweppes, Vitamin Water, Body Armor, Mr. Pibb, Nestea, Tab PepsiCo Pepsi, Mountain Dew, 7UP, Sierra Mist, Starry, Mug, Tropicana, Starbucks Bottled, Gatorade, Propel, Crush, Dr. Pepper, Schweppes, Brisk, Lipton, HiLo, Looza, Maui Style, Cheetos, Chesters, Doritos, Fritos, Lays, Ruffles, Munchies, Munchos, PopCorners, Tostitos, Funyuns, Sabra, Cracker Jack, Rold Gold, SunChips, Cap'n Crunch, Rice-A-Roni, Pasta Roni, Near East, Sobe, Sabritas, Sabritones, Sanitas, Rockstar Energy Drink, Red Rock Deli, Off the Beaten Path, NatuChips, Grandma's, Health Warrior, Quaker General Mills Annie's, Autumn's Gold, Betty Crocker, Bisquick, Boo Berry, Bugles, Cheerios, Chex, Chex Mix, Cinnamon Toast Crunch, Cocoa Puffs, Cookie Crisp, Count Chocula, Dunkaroos, FrankenBerry, Gardetto's, Golden Grahams, Kix, Lucky Charms, Monster Cereals, Nature Valley, Old El Paso, Pillsbury, Progresso, Raisin Nut Bran, Reese's Puffs, Total, Totino's/Jeno's, Trix, Wanchai Ferry, Yoki, Yoplait Nestlé Stouffer's, DiGiorno, Lean Cuisine, Hot Pockets, Tombstone, Jack's Pizza, Sweet Earth, CPK, Nesquik, Ovaltine, Toll House, Abuelita, Sweet Leaf Tea, Dreyer's/Edy's, Drumstick, Kit Kats Kellogg's (Kellanov & WK Kellogg Co.) item.title: More Ounces into More Bodies More Often
item.description: San Francisco's landmark lawsuit against major food manufacturers exposes the deliberate design of ultra-processed foods to be addictive, particularly targeting children.
item.content:encoded: More Ounces into More Bodies More Often San Francisco's landmark lawsuit against major food manufacturers exposes the deliberate design of ultra-processed foods to be addictive, particularly targeting children. The San Francisco City Attorney filed a sweeping lawsuit against eleven major food manufacturers—Kraft Heinz, Mondelez, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola, General Mills, Nestlé, ConAgra, Mars, Post Holdings, Kellanov, and WK Kellogg Co.—alleging systematic exploitation of addiction science and predatory marketing to children. Key allegations: Addiction by Design: Companies deliberately engineered products to be physiologically addictive using sensory psychologists, fMRI imaging, and roboticized taste buds. Philip Morris's explicit strategy: "control all of the pleasure drugs that are not regulated." Targeted Marketing: Over $1.6 billion annually spent on advertising to children, with specific tactics once Todd Putman (Coca-Cola's former U.S. Marketing head) described as "attack[ing] them like a bunch of wolves" when kids turned twelve. Health Crisis: Type 2 diabetes virtually nonexistent in children pre-1985; pediatric fatty liver disease tripled by 2017-2021; childhood obesity rates tripled since the 1970s. Scientific Evidence: The complaint mirrors the Surgeon General's tobacco addiction framework—demonstrating compulsive use despite harm, psychoactive effects (150-200% dopamine increase), and reinforcement patterns. item.title: The Kids Know
item.description: A News Literacy Project study finds most teenagers harbor significant distrust in journalism and lack understanding of how reporting works. The findings underscores what researchers describe as "ov…
item.content:encoded: The Kids Know A News Literacy Project study finds most teenagers harbor significant distrust in journalism and lack understanding of how reporting works. The findings underscores what researchers describe as "overwhelming cynicism" among a generation growing up with skepticism toward the press. The report drew coverage from major outlets including Neiman Lab, Columbia Journalism Review, Education Week, and CNN's Reliable Sources. When asked to think of one thing they think journalists are doing well, roughly 1 in 3 teens (37%) offer negative feedback, saying things such as lying and deceiving (81 responses) or that journalists don’t do anything well (66 responses). Key Findings: 75% of teens distrust journalism 60% believe news is biased 50% think news is fake 40% think news is unreliable 30% think news is not important Read the full study

item.title: Rent Control
item.description: New York's affordable housing stock faces a cascade of financial defaults unless the city acts on policy reforms. Over 50% of affordable buildings have expenses exceeding rental income, jeopardizin…
item.content:encoded: Rent Control New York's affordable housing stock faces a cascade of financial defaults unless the city acts on policy reforms. Over 50% of affordable buildings have expenses exceeding rental income, jeopardizing both tenants and the city's bond rating. The Problem: 56% of Low Income Housing Tax Credit projects citywide show negative cash flow 63,700 units (56% of 112,000 reviewed) operate at deficits 16% of rental projects at high risk of default, up from 8% in four years Insurance costs surged 103% over four years; water rates up 21.5% RGB rent increases averaged below 2% annually while expenses grew 4.1%+ What's at Stake: A $1 billion default cascade would crater the Housing Development Corporation's bond rating, raising borrowing costs citywide and halting the mayor's affordable housing plan. Mayor-elect Mamdani's proposed rent freeze will worsen deficits without corresponding revenue reforms. Required Solutions: Revenue increases (regulatory resets for vacant units, expanded rental assistance, housing stability court for nonpayment), debt restructuring ($1B financing program), and expense cuts (insurance captive, water rate relief, J-51 tax abatement reform). Read full policy brief

item.content:encoded: California's Fiscal Cliff California's structural budget deficit has reached an unsustainable inflection point. The state faces an $18 billion gap in 2026-27, but the real problem emerges after: a $35 billion annual structural deficit by 2027-28. Revenue is growing, but it's fully consumed by mandatory spending from Prop 98 (schools/colleges) and Prop 2 (reserves/debt), both of which auto-scale with revenues. Rainy day funds are depleted, debt deferrals exhausted, and one-time measures exhausted. item.title: California's Fiscal Outlook 2025: $18B Problem Ahead
item.description: California faces an $18 billion budget deficit in 2026-27. Revenues up $11B but consumed by mandatory spending. Structural deficits reach $35B annually by 2027-28.
item.content:encoded: California's $18B Budget Deficit The state has $14 billion in reserves and could likely find additional capacity for budgetary borrowing, if needed. That said, at this point, the state has used over $20 billion in borrowing, one‑time and temporary spending solutions are exhausted, and budget reserves are at about half of their peak. As it stands—with larger forecasted deficits and many fewer tools available to address them—California’s budget is undeniably less prepared for downturns. 2026-27 Deficit: $18B 2027-28+ Deficit: $35B/year California's revenue growth is being fully consumed by mandatory spending (Prop 98 schools/colleges and Prop 2 reserves/debt). Why revenues can't fix this: Prop 98 schools/colleges: Auto-scales with revenue increases Prop 2 reserves/debt: Auto-scales with revenue increases Together: Consume $10B of $11B revenue gain Spending growth outpaces revenue: Health/Human Services: +5.9%/year Education: +5.5%/year Natural Resources: +16.8%/year (wildfire/climate) California has already deployed: Rainy day fund drawdowns Debt deferrals One-time revenue measures Spending cuts Structural deficit (2027-28+): $35B/year LAO forecast assumes no recession . If economy weakens: Income tax revenue collapses (stock-dependent) Sales tax stagnates Real deficit could exceed $35B baseline Source: LAO, California's Fiscal Outlook, November 2025

item.title: Why Real Estate Innovators Beat Liberal Think Tanks on Housing
item.description: Real estate entrepreneurs like Realer Estate solve affordability problems through market innovation - while liberal think tanks waste time bribing homeowners and creating new regulations.
item.content:encoded: How Many Brains to Make a Tank Think? Bribing homeowners w/ $1000 for YIMBY? Military style modular? 50-year mortgages? The Center for American Progress thinks you deserve to live where you want. They propose bribery to get it. Build homes or else. If cities don't build enough homes, the government will bribe existing homeowners to build homes, then subsidize rents with the bribery money. Ezra Klein argues that America's housing crisis stems from a shortage of 2-5 million homes, driven by insufficient construction relative to population. Home prices have risen 50% since 2020, and median first-time homebuyers are now 40 years old (vs. 31 in 2014). The core issue: America is building fewer homes per capita than in 1975. Meanwhile, on the demand side, young entrepreneurs at Realer Estate are fascilitating the hunt for cheap units in NYC. Realer Estate demonstrates that sometimes the solutions come from people who are actually trying to survive. They build things out of necessity while the surplus elite just wants to live where they want and complain about it in the New York Times so Democrats can insert more government into the problem. By the time you build 5 million homes, demographics will have changed. Take all the money from think tank solutions and dump it back in people's pockets. Rescind all government-led affordablity initiatives and let innovators innovate. They'll build more housing and think of better solutions. Source: Ezra Klein, "America's Housing Crisis, in One Chart," The New York Times, Nov. 23, 2025

item.content:encoded: Housing Affordability The Housing Affordability Index rebounded to 104.5 in September, marking a notable recovery from August's 100.6, signaling improved purchasing power for median-income families amid moderating mortgage rates and stable home prices. Latest Data: September : 104.5 (+3.9 points MoM) August : 100.6 (-2.6 points MoM) The substantial month-over-month gain reflects a decline in mortgage rates, which dropped below 6.3% in September from elevated levels earlier in the summer. An affordability index above 100 means a family with median income has excess purchasing power to qualify for a mortgage on a median-priced home. This improvement provides a small reprieve to buyers after a period of compressed affordability, though values remain historically elevated compared to pre-pandemic levels when the index regularly exceeded 110. {{chart:Affordability Index}} View housing indicators

item.description: October brought a steep divergence in U.S. fiscal metrics. While interest payments on the national debt spiked dramatically and overall debt continued its sharp climb, federal tax revenue fell sign…
item.content:encoded: $38,360,841,844,745.79 October brought a steep divergence in U.S. fiscal metrics. While interest payments on the national debt spiked dramatically and overall debt continued its sharp climb, federal tax revenue fell significantly short of September's exceptional performance. {{chart:Tax Revenue}} Latest Data (October): Interest on Debt : $91B (+145.9% MoM) Tax Revenue : $404B (-25.7% MoM) Monthly Budget Deficit : -$284.4B Total National Debt : $38.04 Trillion {{chart:Interest on Debt}} Why the Interest Spike? October's interest spike was amplified by a 43-day government shutdown that ran through mid-November, forcing the Treasury to accelerate interest payments (normally due in early November) into October to avoid default. This timing shift inflated October's interest figure and suppressed November's by roughly $20-25B. Adjusting for this anomaly, the underlying interest trend shows debt service costs climbing steadily as Treasury yields remain elevated. The sharp revenue decline is seasonal—September benefited from quarterly estimated tax payments that don't recur monthly. The cumulative result: a widening deficit and accelerating debt growth. Treasury debt increased 0.84% month-over-month, or roughly $320.7B in new borrowing. {{chart:Treasury Debt Level}} View all government indicators

item.title: FOMC Back to Rate Cut After Wavering
item.description: Prediction markets are pricing an 85% chance the Federal Reserve cuts rates by 25 basis points at the December 10 meeting, with just 15% probability of holding steady.
item.content:encoded: FOMC Back to Rate Cut After Wavering Prediction markets are pricing an 85% chance the Federal Reserve cuts rates by 25 basis points at the December 10 meeting, with just 15% probability of holding steady. {{chart:FOMC December Rate Decision (BPS)}} The Whipsaw : Earlier in November, Fed officials signaled caution and markets priced in a pause at 70%+ probability. Traders braced for the Fed to hold and reassess during the shutdown. But weakening consumer sentiment (now at 51, the year's low) and persistent disinflation flipped the script. The 25BP cut zoomed back to 85% as traders recognized the Fed can't afford to stay idle when demand is softening. PPI (Producer Price Index) has stabilized around 149.8, showing persistent disinflation flowing through the supply chain without new price shocks emerging. View prediction market data

While nominal prices remain supported, the trajectory suggests underlying softness in buyer interest as affordability constraints persist. Median Home Price : October $415,200 (+0.7% MoM from $411,700) The increase of $3,500 MoM represents modest appreciation, though the 0.7% pace falls short of long-term trend growth. The pickup suggests some resilience, but buyer traffic likely remains constrained by affordability pressures. item.title: Institutional Scroll
item.description: If social media replaced infinite scroll with a 'load more' button, engagement would plummet. Young people would redirect that 4 hours/day toward developing actual social skills, critical thinking,…
item.content:encoded: If social media replaced infinite scroll with a 'load more' button, engagement would plummet. Young people would redirect that 4 hours/day toward developing actual social skills, critical thinking, and productive skills. But the adults in power lack imagination. They are too busy scrolling, themselves. Evidence of Institutional Failure 9/11 (2001): The 9/11 Commission Report explicitly blamed 'failure of imagination' for the intelligence community's inability to connect dots. The Commission even prescribed the solution (p. 344): "It is therefore crucial to find a way of routinizing, even bureaucratizing, the exercise of imagination." We didn't. Twenty-three years later, the same machinery grinds on—same processes, same failures. The adults are on their phones, scrolling for ideas. War on Drugs (1971-present): Overdose deaths up 6,900% since 1999. US incarceration rate highest per capita globally. $1.5T+ spent on drug enforcement . Affordability Crisis (2024): Real wages flat since 1979. Housing costs up 250% since 2000. Student debt $1.7T. Proposal? Income-based repayment plans. 50-yr mortgages. Lack of imagination. The Governor Brown DIY Principle "Not every human problem deserves a law." If we stop petitioning institutions to solve our problems, then we have to do the work. So instead of a cookie consent law, just DIY. Reduce time on media that preys on your engagement which hogs your imagination. Replace infinite scroll with a 'load more' button. This site implements exactly this principle. Posts load initially. On the page: showLoadMoreButton() creates a button element with onclick handler → loadMorePosts() fetches next 10 posts asynchronously → button updates with remaining count. No infinite scroll. No autoplay. No algorithmic nudge. Users consciously decide each load. Friction introduced by design = agency restored. You're welcome. (For now, at least. Eventually, this site will need to remunerate my time.)

item.title: Supreme Court Oral Arguments Schedule
item.description: Supreme Court oral arguments schedule for November 2025 term with case summaries and podcast links
item.content:encoded: Supreme Court Oral Arguments Schedule Monday, November 10 LANDOR v. LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS (23-1197) Question Presented: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) and the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause protect religious practices and beliefs in institutional settings. Cert. Granted: 2025 Audio: | Supreme Court Docket GEO GROUP INC. v. MENOCAL (24-758) Question Presented: Whether a government contractor's claim of derivative sovereign immunity under the Yearsley doctrine qualifies for immediate appeal under the collateral-order doctrine. Cert. Granted: 6/2/2025 Audio: | Supreme Court Docket Wednesday, November 5 CONEY ISLAND AUTO PARTS v. BURTON (24-808) Question Presented: Well-settled legal principles dictate that a judgment entered in the absence of personal jurisdiction is void. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) authorizes federal courts to vacate a judgment when it is void. A motion seeking vacatur, however, "must be made within a reasonable time." Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(c)(1). Each of the United States Courts of Appeals other than the Sixth Circuit holds that there is effectively no time limit for moving to vacate a judgment, notwithstanding Rule 60(c)(1)'s "reasonable time" requirement, when the judgment is obtained in the absence of personal jurisdiction. The common thinking among these circuits is that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit is the sole outlier. In this case, it held that Rule 60(c)(1) governs the timing of a motion seeking vacatur of a void judgment pursuant to Rule 60(b)(4). Whether Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(c)(1) imposes any time limit to set aside a void default judgment for lack of personal jurisdiction. Cert. Granted: 6/6/2025 Audio: | Supreme Court Docket LEARNING RESOURCES ET AL. v. TRUMP (24-1287 / 25-250) Question Presented: Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), Pub. L. No. 95-223, Tit. II, 91 Stat. 1626, 50 U.S.C. § 1701 et seq., authorizes the President to impose tariffs. Whether IEEPA’s delegation of authority to the President to impose tariffs violates the nondelegation doctrine. Cert. Granted: 9/9/2025 Audio: | Supreme Court Docket Tuesday, November 4 HAIN CELESTIAL GROUP v. PALMQUIST (24-724) Question Presented: Respondents, citizens of Texas, filed this products-liability suit in state court against Petitioners Hain Celestial Group, Inc., then a citizen of Delaware and New York, and Whole Foods, Inc., a citizen of Texas. Hain removed based on diversity jurisdiction, arguing that Whole Foods should be dismissed as fraudulently joined. The district court agreed, dismissing Whole Foods with prejudice. After two additional years of federal-court litigation and a two-week jury trial, the district court granted judgment as a matter of law to Hain. On appeal, without ruling on the merits, the Fifth Circuit held that the district court erred in dismissing Whole Foods, vacated the final judgment, and ordered the matter remanded to state court to start from scratch. Relying on Respondents' post-removal amended complaint, the panel held, in conflict with several other courts of appeals, that the district court lacked jurisdiction to enter judgment as to the completely diverse parties before it. The questions presented are: Whether a district court's final judgment as to completely diverse parties must be vacated when an appellate court later determines that it erred by dismissing a non-diverse party at the time of removal. Whether a plaintiff may defeat diversity jurisdiction after removal by amending the complaint to add factual allegations that state a colorable claim against a nondiverse party when the complaint at the time of removal did not state such a claim Cert. Granted: 4/28/2025 Audio: | Supreme Court Docket HAMM v. SMITH (24-872) Question Presented: Like most States, Alabama requires that offenders prove an IQ of 70 or less to satisfy the intellectual-functioning prong of Atkins v. Virginia . This case was not close: Smith scored 75, 74, 72, 78, and 74 on five full-scale IQ tests. There is no way to conclude from these five numbers that Smith's true IQ is likely to be 70 or below. So the courts below required Smith to prove only that his IQ "could be " 70 and required the State to bring evidence "strong enough" to "foreclose" and "rule out the possibility" of intellectual disability. The first question presented is: Whether, under a proper application of Atkins , a State can require a claimant to prove an IQ of 70 or less by a preponderance of the evidence. Evaluating multiple IQ scores is "complicated," and "this Court has not specified how" to do it. In the State's view, five scores are more accurate than one, and there are ways to account for that fact. The courts below disagree. The district court relied on Smith's 72 ± 3 to find that his IQ "could be" 69. On remand, the Eleventh Circuit's "holistic approach" asked whether Smith had scores of "about" 75 or less. Counting four out of five scores between 72 and 75, the court found "consistent evidence" that Smith "may" qualify as mildly disabled. Thus, the court "followed the law's requirement," in its view, to "move on" to Smith's adaptive deficits. The second question presented is: Whether courts evaluating multiple IQ scores must find that every valid score of "about" 75 or less supports an Atkins claim. The petition for a writ of certiorari is granted limited to the following question: Whether and how courts may consider the cumulative effect of multiple IQ scores in assessing an Atkins claim. Cert. Granted: 6/6/2025 Audio: Coming Soon | Supreme Court Docket Monday, November 3 RICO v. UNITED STATES (24-1056) Question Presented: Whether the fugitive-tolling doctrine applies in the context of supervised release. Cert. Granted: 6/30/2025 Audio: | Supreme Court Docket HENCELY v. FLUOR CORP. (24-924) Question Presented: Former U.S. Army Specialist Winston T. Hencely was critically and permanently injured by a suicide bomber inside Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan. The bomber, Ahmad Nayeb, worked on base for a government contractor. An Army investigation found that the attack's primary contributing factor was the contractor's actions in breach of its Army contract and in violation of the military's instructions to supervise Nayeb. Hencely sued the government contractor for negligence under South Carolina law. He did not sue the military under the Federal Tort Claims Act. Even so, the Fourth Circuit held that Hencely's state claims are preempted by unspoken "federal interests" emanating from an FTCA exception. Invoking Boyle v. United Technologies Corp., 487 U.S. 500 (1988), the court of appeals held that the FTCA's exception immunizing the government for "[a]ny claim arising out of the combatant activities of the military or naval forces ... during time of war," 28 U.S.C. §2680(j), barred Hencely's South Carolina claims against the contractor. The decision below reaffirmed a 3-1-1 split among the Second, Third, Fourth, Ninth and D.C. Circuits over Boyle's reach when contractors defend against state tort claims by invoking §2680(j). Should Boyle be extended to allow federal interests emanating from the FTCA's combatant-activities exception to preempt state tort claims against a government contractor for conduct that breached its contract and violated military orders? Cert. Granted: 6/2/2025 Audio: | Supreme Court Docket

item.title: Duty of Competence
item.description: When using AI, be sure to cite correct case or face disciplinary scrutiny for not meeting legal competence standards.
item.content:encoded: Duty of Competence When using AI, be sure to cite correct case or face disciplinary scrutiny for not meeting legal competence standards. Big Beautiful Costs (BBC) Trump's $1B Lawsuit : The BBC faces a $1 billion defamation suit from Trump over January 6th coverage cited as editorial error of judgment in conveying the key messages of the speech in a condensed format. UK Household Fee : £174.5/year ($229.68 USD). License fee evasion carries fine of £1,000 BBC Annual Revenue : £3.8B ($5.1B USD) God's Authority Kentucky clerk Kim Davis refused to issue same-sex marriage licenses, citing religious objections. She sought immunity; the court denied it. Personal beliefs are irrelevant to official duties. When a public employee's conscience conflicts with statute, the law prevails. Davis was performing a ministerial function—issuing licenses under Kentucky law—with no discretion to inject personal theology. Qualified immunity shields officials conducting clearly established sovereign business. It does not shelter personal objections to lawful duties. Davis had no immunity because: Same-sex marriage rights were clearly established ( Obergefell , 2015) Issuing licenses is ministerial, not discretionary Immunity protects officials from liability for legal judgment calls, not refusal to perform statutory duties SCOTUS Update: Supreme Court Oral Arguments Schedule - Updated LANDOR v. LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS (23-1197) Examines religious protections in institutional settings under RLUIPA and the Free Exercise Clause. Distinguishes between discretionary official acts (where immunity may apply) and ministerial duties bound by clearly established rights (where it does not). GEO GROUP INC. v. MENOCAL (24-758) Tests derivative sovereign immunity under the Yearsley doctrine. Government contractors cannot claim immunity by proxy; conduct must have been specifically authorized and directed by the government. Immunity is narrow. Under ATR, lenders must verify that borrowers have the capacity to repay loans based on documented income and expenses. 50-year mortgages are classified as non-qualified mortgages (Non-QM), exposing lenders to significant litigation risk and regulatory penalties. This legal restriction prevents predatory lending but also limits borrower flexibility in handling affordability crises. item.title: Sauer's Argument: Tariffs as Regulatory Leverage, Not Taxation
item.description: Solicitor General Sauer defended IEEPA tariffs as non-revenue regulatory measures - tools of foreign policy leverage rather than exercises of Congress's taxing power.
item.content:encoded: The $2000 Tariff Rebate Solicitor General Sauer advanced a sharp reframing of what tariffs represent under IEEPA. He argued that when imposed under emergency authority, tariffs are regulatory , not revenue-raising , and therefore fall within the President's delegated powers to "regulate importation." 1. Tariffs as Behavioral Tools Sauer insisted that IEEPA tariffs are most effective precisely when no one pays them . Their purpose is not to collect money, but to change foreign behavior by creating leverage in trade or security negotiations. Sauer: "The goal is deterrence. It's more effective if no one pays. These are bargaining chips, not tax instruments." He cited the administration's record of using tariffs to pressure trading partners into specific policy actions—most notably, to push China to curb the export of fentanyl precursors —as evidence that such measures function as regulatory sanctions , not fiscal exactions. 2. Regulatory vs. Taxing Function The distinction between regulation and taxation lies at the heart of the case. A tax aims to raise revenue for the U.S. Treasury. A regulation , even if monetary, seeks to alter conduct. Sauer drew parallels to Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act and the Algonquin decision (1976) , where the Court upheld monetary import restrictions imposed to "adjust imports" in the national interest. He argued that IEEPA's phrase "regulate importation" is broader still and can naturally encompass economic penalties meant to induce behavioral change abroad. 3. Breadth of Delegation Sauer characterized IEEPA as a broad delegation - an instrument Congress designed to give the President flexibility in emergencies. He emphasized that the Act authorizes the President to: "Investigate, block, prohibit, or otherwise regulate importation." Under that phrasing, Sauer said, the President may impose monetary exactions as part of a larger regulatory program—so long as the objective is to manage national security or foreign policy risks, not to generate revenue. 4. The Article I–Article II Boundary Critics argued that taxation originates in Article I , and therefore tariff authority must be explicitly delegated . Sauer's response reframed the issue: while tariffs look like taxes, their purpose places them in a different constitutional category . "These are not taxes from the people," he said, "but instruments of foreign policy carried out under authority Congress already conferred." In his view: Article I, Section 8 empowers Congress to regulate foreign commerce and delegate portions of that authority. Article II grants the President independent foreign affairs power to implement those regulations. When Congress delegates "regulate importation," it is delegating the foreign commerce function, not the taxing one. Thus, he argued, IEEPA sits within the zone of concurrent Article I and Article II authority , where broader discretion is permissible. 5. The "Regulatory Tariff" Concept Sauer coined the phrase "regulatory tariff" to describe this hybrid mechanism - a monetary measure not designed to raise revenue but to shape international conduct. He analogized it to sanctions, export controls, or asset freezes , which can have fiscal impact but are understood as regulatory. "A successful tariff collects nothing," he said. "Its success is measured in changed behavior, not receipts." This framing recasts the IEEPA tariffs as part of a foreign policy toolkit , akin to sanctions under the Magnitsky Act or embargoes under TWEA, rather than as taxation under the Internal Revenue Code. 6. The Foreign Policy Context Sauer closed by emphasizing executive flexibility in crises . The President, he said, must have room to use economic tools short of war—particularly in a global economy where coercion often takes financial, not military, form. He linked IEEPA tariffs to broader national security goals: Countering China's synthetic opioid trade Responding to economic coercion by rival states Leveraging reciprocity in bilateral trade In this framing, IEEPA tariffs serve as strategic levers , not fiscal policy instruments. 7. The Core Claim Sauer's fundamental point: IEEPA tariffs are regulatory tools of foreign policy. They derive from Congress's delegation to regulate commerce , not its power to tax. Their success is measured by avoidance, not collection. They lie within the President's constitutional sphere of discretion , especially when tied to national security emergencies. Doctrinal Implications Doctrine Sauer's View Tension Nondelegation "Emergencies" = intelligible principle Boundless scope? Major Questions Not triggered; historical precedent Economic scale issue? Article I Tax Tariffs ≠ taxes when regulatory Any exaction = tax? Article II Broad delegation in foreign affairs Executive overreach? Source: U.S. Supreme Court Oral Argument Transcript, 24-1287, Nov. 5, 2025 .

item.title: The $2000 Tariff Rebate
item.description: Solicitor General Sauer's argument carries a paradox at its core: its success is measured not by what it collects, but by what it prevents. Each avoided payment, each concession extracted abroad, i…
item.content:encoded: The $2000 Tariff Rebate Solicitor General Sauer's argument carries a paradox at its core: its success is measured not by what it collects, but by what it prevents. Each avoided payment, each concession extracted abroad, is framed as a regulatory win - proof that pressure works before the tariff ever takes effect. The Theory When foreign competitors believe tariffs could strike at any moment, they move preemptively: Concede faster in trade negotiations Accelerate domestic or allied-country investment Alter export behavior to avoid triggering penalties In Sauer’s formulation, the tariff isn’t the objective—it’s the deterrent. The real gain lies in avoidance : reshored manufacturing, faster settlements, and behavioral change achieved without revenue collection. The Paradox Ahead If tariffs are “regulatory” only when no one pays , how does that logic hold once revenues are collected and rebated —as in the proposed $2,000 household tariff credit ? Turning deterrence into redistribution risks transforming a foreign-policy lever into a domestic tax program , precisely the line Sauer’s argument seeks to avoid. Full analysis in 7 concepts: Tariffs as Behavioral Tools Regulatory vs. Taxing Function Breadth of Delegation The Article I–Article II Boundary The "Regulatory Tariff" Concept The Foreign Policy Context The Core Claim Read Full Analysis

item.title: Update to Tariff SCOTUS Case
item.description: SCOTUS oral arguments reveal deep skepticism. Can the President impose $195 billion in tariffs under a 1977 emergency act? Justice Kavanaugh grapples with the "donut hole" problem - can the Preside…
item.content:encoded: Update to Tariff SCOTUS Case 1. Wartime Power Delegation and Historical Use General Sauer traced the "regulate importation" phrase back to the Trading with the Enemy Act (1917) , arguing it historically covered tariff-like powers used to restrict enemy trade. Justice Jackson noted this wartime context meant controlling or freezing enemy property , not raising revenue - underscoring that IEEPA's origins were defensive, not fiscal. Sauer: wartime presidents imposed export controls (e.g., on cotton) and used tariff-equivalent powers to restrict trade with enemies. Jackson: that was about prohibition , not taxation . 2. Justice Barrett - Revenue Raisers and Exactions Barrett pressed the key distinction: when does an "exaction of money" become a tax rather than a regulatory tool? She invoked Algonquin , noting that the Court allowed monetary exactions to control import quantities, but only in statutes that expressly dealt with tariffs. Barrett: "Algonquin said Congress could use the exaction of money to control quantity... so why isn't that the same here?" Gutman: "Because IEEPA never mentions tariffs - context matters." 3. Justice Kavanaugh - The "Donut Hole" Hypothetical Kavanaugh highlighted the statute's asymmetry: under respondents' reading, the President could ban all trade but not impose a 1% tariff - an absurd result, he said. Gutman replied humorously: "It's not a donut hole; it's a different kind of pastry." Kavanaugh also noted past presidents have used tariffs as foreign policy tools - for example, tariffs against India during the Ukraine-Russia conflict - to illustrate how the power might operate pragmatically. 4. Justice Alito - Revenue as Incidental, Not Intentional Alito explored whether tariffs might be legitimate if their primary goal is behavioral , not fiscal. "If the President's goal is to change foreign conduct, and raising revenue is incidental, is that permissible?" Katyal replied that intent matters: tariffs are still revenue-raising on their face , and Article I requires explicit delegation for any tax measure - even if no funds are ultimately collected. 5. Barrett on Algonquin and the Scope of Monetary Exactions Barrett revisited Algonquin (1976) and the Trade Expansion Act , asking whether "adjust imports" and "regulate importation" could be functionally equivalent. She noted that Congress in 232 statutes used tariff-related terms , while IEEPA did not - making context decisive. Barrett: "It's natural to read 'adjust imports' to include tariffs when the statute deals with tariffs. But unnatural here." 6. Historical Presidential Practices - What "Regulate Importation" Meant Justices discussed past executive uses of "regulate importation" under TWEA and IEEPA: Embargoes (total prohibitions on enemy trade) Quotas (quantitative limits) Licensing regimes (requiring permission to trade) These were all controls on conduct , not fiscal exactions. None involved raising revenue. Gutman: "Embargoes and quotas are fundamentally different from tariffs - they don't raise money." 7. Hypotheticals - Climate Change and Other Emergencies Several Justices raised hypotheticals testing IEEPA's breadth: Could a President declare climate change a national emergency and impose tariffs on carbon-intensive imports? Could "import regulation" extend to consumer goods or services in peacetime emergencies? These questions probed the Major Questions Doctrine , testing whether Congress truly meant to delegate vast economic power implicitly. 8. Verbs vs. Nouns - "License" vs. "Licensing" A textual debate arose over IEEPA's phrasing: the President may act "by means of instructions, licenses, or otherwise ." Barrett noted that "license" is a noun - implying a permission structure , not a revenue instrument. Barrett: "If Congress meant tariffs, it could have said so. Why not 'tariffs, duties, or otherwise'?" Katyal: "Reading 'license' as hiding a trillion-dollar tax power would be extraordinary." 9. Tariffing Allies like Switzerland Katyal criticized the administration's use of IEEPA tariffs against Switzerland , a country with which the U.S. runs a 39% trade surplus , as proof of overreach. "No President has ever had power to tariff allies with surpluses. To say Congress implied that authority in 1977 is implausible." This underscored the Major Questions theme: enormous economic consequences require clear congressional approval. 10. Fiscal Stakes - $90 Billion at Risk According to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget , of the $195 billion in tariffs collected under the IEEPA measures, $90 billion could be refunded or invalidated if the Court strikes down the program. This reinforces the Article I, Section 8 concern: the power to tax and collect revenue originates with Congress, not the Executive. Doctrinal Undercurrents Nondelegation vs. Major Questions: whether implicit emergency powers can justify explicit taxing outcomes. Explicit vs. Implicit Delegation: contrast between tariff-specific statutes (Sections 232, 301, 201) and the broad IEEPA language. Taxation from the People (Article I): the Framers' requirement of bicameralism and presentment for any tax measure. Article II Foreign Affairs: whether deference abroad can justify executive fiscal measures at home. Source: Supreme Court Oral Argument Transcript, 24-1287, Nov. 5, 2025

item.title: SCOTUS Invalidates IEEPA Tariffs 6-3
item.description: Supreme Court held "regulate importation" does not authorize presidential tariffs. Chief Justice Roberts' majority applied major questions doctrine. Refunds likely in billions.
item.content:encoded: SCOTUS Rules Against IEEPA Tariff Authority In a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court invalidated the President's tariff program under IEEPA. The Court held that "regulate importation" cannot support revenue-raising tariffs without explicit congressional authorization, reasserting Congress's exclusive control over taxation under Article I. Chief Justice Roberts wrote for a splintered majority in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (2026). The Holding IEEPA does not authorize tariffs. The President had asserted unlimited tariff authority of any amount, duration, and scope on any product from any country. The Court rejected this reading. Roberts emphasized that Congress always uses explicit language ("duties," "tariffs," "taxes") when delegating tariff authority in Sections 232, 301, and 201 of the Trade Acts. IEEPA's verbs describe embargo-style controls (block, nullify, prohibit), not taxation. Allowing implicit tariff authority would effect an improper "sweeping delegation of Congress's power to set tariff policy." The Fractured Majority Three justices (Sotomayor, Kagan, Jackson) held IEEPA does not authorize tariffs as ordinary statutory interpretation. Three justices (Roberts, Gorsuch, Barrett) applied the major questions doctrine, reasoning that while "regulate importation" could technically support tariffs, Congress must "clearly" delegate such "extraordinary" powers. Both paths reach the same result. The Dissents Justice Kavanaugh (joined by Thomas and Alito) argued ordinary statutory meaning of "regulate importation" includes tariffs, comparable to embargoes and quotas. He flagged the odd distinction: the President could ban all imports but apparently not impose a 1% tariff. Kavanaugh noted other tariff statutes (Section 232, 201, 301) remain available, so the decision may not substantially constrain future tariff authority - just "the wrong statutory box." Refunds and Impact Importers who paid IEEPA tariffs may be entitled to refunds of billions of dollars. The Government conceded the refund process would be "a mess," with complications from cost pass-through to consumers. Related Howdy Stranger Coverage SCOTUS November 2025 Docket Tariffs as Regulatory Leverage Trump v. Vos: Update Trump v. Vos Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump , 607 U.S. (2026). Full text

item.title: Trump's IEEPA Tariff Authority
item.description: Justices question whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act allows presidential tariffs without clear congressional authorization under Article I.
item.content:encoded: Trump's IEEPA Tariff Authority Cases: Learning Resources et al. v. Trump (No. 24-1287) and Trump v. V.O.S. Selections et al. (No. 25-250) Argued: November 5, 2025 At Issue Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 (IEEPA) authorizes the President to impose tariffs based on language allowing him to "regulate importation." The statute—passed to limit emergency economic powers after the abuses of the Trading With the Enemy Act—contains no mention of tariffs, duties, or taxes. The Trump administration argues that persistent bilateral trade deficits and "lack of reciprocity" in trade relationships constitute an "unusual and extraordinary threat" to national security, thereby justifying tariffs under IEEPA. Constitutional Fault Lines The case sits at the intersection of four major constitutional doctrines: 1. Article I - Taxation from the People Tariffs are a form of taxation , and Article I, Section 8 vests the taxing power in Congress . Under the Constitution's structure, taxation requires both Houses and the President to act jointly. The question: can Congress delegate that taxing authority implicitly, or must it do so explicitly? 2. Nondelegation vs. Major Questions Doctrine Nondelegation asks whether Congress supplied an "intelligible principle" when it authorized the President to act. The Major Questions Doctrine asks whether Congress clearly authorized an action of such sweeping economic and political significance. Together, they test whether "regulate importation" can support what would be one of the broadest delegations of taxing power in U.S. history. 3. Explicit (Narrow) vs. Implicit (Broad) Delegation Every recognized tariff statute— Section 232 (national security), Section 301 (unfair trade), Section 201 (safeguards) —uses explicit language ("duties," "tariffs," "taxes") with clear limits and procedures. IEEPA's verbs ("block," "nullify," "prohibit") describe embargo-style controls, not taxation. Reading "regulate importation" to include tariffs transforms a narrow emergency power into an open-ended fiscal tool. 4. Article II - Executive Foreign Policy Authority The government argues for deference in foreign affairs, where the President traditionally acts with greater independence. Respondents counter that foreign affairs deference does not override Article I's textual allocation of taxing power. Even the Solicitor General conceded the President holds no inherent Article II tariff authority in peacetime . Government's Argument Solicitor General Sauer defended the tariffs by invoking historical and textual continuity: "Regulate importation" historically encompassed tariff authority, from Gibbons v. Ogden through the Trading With the Enemy Act (TWEA). President Nixon's 1971 tariffs under TWEA's identical language were upheld in United States v. Yoshida International , and Congress carried that same language forward in IEEPA. The Court's Algonquin decision held "adjust imports" includes monetary exactions; "regulate" is broader still. Tariffs imposed under IEEPA are regulatory , not revenue-raising - they aim to deter foreign conduct, not collect funds. In foreign affairs, major questions and nondelegation concerns carry less force given Article II's inherent powers. Respondents' Argument Neal Katyal and Benjamin Gutman argued for a narrow reading: Congress always uses explicit language when delegating tariff authority - IEEPA's silence is decisive. IEEPA's structure and legislative history confirm it was meant to constrain , not expand , presidential emergency powers. Allowing an implicit delegation would invert Article I's structure - letting a single branch tax citizens without bicameral approval. They cited the Solicitor General's concession that the President has no independent tariff power , making reliance on IEEPA textually and constitutionally unsound. As a matter of statutory design, if "regulate importation" sufficed, the procedural and percentage limits of Sections 232, 301, and 201 would be meaningless. The Bench Reacts Justice Gorsuch described delegation as a "one-way ratchet": Congress can transfer power by simple majority but can reclaim it only with a supermajority override. He pressed the government on the lack of inherent tariff authority. Justice Sotomayor underscored that tariffs are taxes - revenue-generating by definition - and asked why "regulate" should be read as "tax" when Congress never uses the term that way. Justice Kagan observed that every tariff statute in Title 19 has meaningful constraints - IEEPA has none. Justice Kavanaugh flagged a potential "donut hole": the President could ban all trade but not impose a 1% tariff - a distinction that might make little policy sense. Justice Barrett asked whether any other statute uses "regulate importation" to grant tariff authority; the government cited only TWEA and IEEPA. Nixon's 1971 Tariffs Revisited A flashpoint was the Nixon-era precedent: Government View: Nixon's 10% tariffs under TWEA's "regulate importation" were upheld, and Congress effectively ratified that authority when reenacting the language in IEEPA. Respondents: Nixon initially relied on inherent powers, invoking TWEA only later. Yoshida upheld his action narrowly and explicitly tied future tariffs to the 1974 Trade Act (Section 122) with a 15% cap and 150-day limit. When Congress enacted IEEPA in 1977, it was reacting to executive overreach, not endorsing it. Broader Implications Trade Policy: Upholding the government's view would let any President invoke emergency powers to reshape trade relationships unilaterally. Separation of Powers: It would mark one of the most sweeping transfers of taxing authority from Congress to the Executive in U.S. history. Economic Impact: With billions already collected, trillions could hinge on the outcome. Legislative Consequence: Congress's ability to reclaim delegated power would be severely constrained. Context in Broader Trade Law Trade Promotion Authority (TPA) grants the President discretion to reduce tariffs within negotiated agreements but has never been used to increase them. Reading IEEPA to authorize tariff hikes by emergency declaration would invert that structure - transforming a limited foreign policy tool into a perpetual fiscal power. What Comes Next A decision expected by mid-2026 will determine: Whether implicit statutory language can authorize taxation; How nondelegation and major questions doctrines apply in foreign-affairs contexts; The scope of presidential economic emergency powers; and Whether Article I's taxation clause demands explicit delegation. The Court appears divided - torn between flexibility in foreign policy and the constitutional design that keeps the power to tax squarely with Congress. Full transcript: U.S. Supreme Court Oral Argument, 24-1287 .

Selections et al., landmark cases challenging President Trump's tariff impositions. At stake: whether Congress impermissibly delegated taxing authority to the executive branch under Section 232, 301, and 201 of the Trade Expansion Act. Oral hearing transcript now available in: 📰 News October ADP Employment and Treasury Yield Update Private sector employment increased by 42,000 jobs in October 2025 per ADP following a revised loss of 29,000 jobs in September. This marked a rebound from two months of weak hiring, though the gains were modest and not broad-based. The report highlighted strong growth in trade, transportation, and utilities (+47,000), education and health services (+26,000), and financial activities (+11,000), offset by losses in professional business services (-15,000), information (-17,000), and leisure and hospitality (-6,000). {{chart:Private Employment}} The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield average for October was 4.06% representing a 2 basis point decline from September's 4.08%. This move reflected growing market expectations for Federal Reserve rate cuts, with yields pressured lower by dovish FOMC commentary and softening inflation data. The yield curve remained inverted, with the 2-year Treasury at 3.45%, though the spread narrowed slightly amid speculation of monetary policy easing. {{chart:10-yr Treasury Yield}} 📊 Financials FOMC December Decision Prediction markets show decreasing conviction for a 25 basis point Federal Reserve rate cut at the December FOMC meeting, with Kalshi and Polymarket aggregating probabilities at 65% for a quarter-point decrease versus 32% for no change. This shift in sentiment reflects mounting concerns over labor market cooling and below-target inflation readings, though market participants remain divided on the timing and magnitude of further cuts. {{chart:FOMC December Rate Decision (BPS)}} 📊 Financials Soft Determinism In today's journal entry , reflections on technological determinism and free will emerged amid frustrations with AI-driven trading systems that exhibited hyper-aggressive behavior without contextual memory. The entry questioned whether human agency remains irreplaceable in investment decisions, contrasting AI's data-driven approach with Warren Buffett's emphasis on long-term sagaciousness. item.title: Burry's 13F Filing
item.description: Michael Burry's Scion Asset Management Q3 2025 13F filing, filed with the SEC on November 3, 2025, disclosed significant bearish positions in AI-related stocks, including put options on Nvidia (NVD…
item.content:encoded: Burry's 13F Filing Michael Burry's Scion Asset Management Q3 2025 13F filing, filed with the SEC on November 3, 2025, disclosed significant bearish positions in AI-related stocks, including put options on Nvidia (NVDA) valued at $186.58 million and Palantir Technologies (PLTR) at $912.10 million. These positions represent short bets against the companies, with NVDD (Direxion Daily NVDA Bear 1X Shares) also held as a bearish ETF on Nvidia. Burry had previously disclosed Nvidia puts in Q1 2025, noting they might hedge unreportable long positions, but the Q3 filing omitted this disclaimer, indicating a more direct bearish stance. The market reacted sharply: Nvidia shares fell 3.96% to $198.69, while Palantir dropped 7.94% to $190.74 on November 4, 2025, amid concerns over AI valuations. Burry's social media warnings, including posts referencing bubbles and circular AI financing involving Nvidia and OpenAI, amplified the impact. His fund also added call options on Halliburton (HAL) and Pfizer (PFE), and new equity positions in Molina Healthcare (MOH), SLM Corporation (SLM), and ProShares UltraPro QQQ (QLD). Sources: SEC EDGAR (Scion Asset Management 13F, Q3 2025) ; Investing.com ("Michael Burry buys puts on Nvidia, Palantir," November 4, 2025) ; Quiver Quantitative ("Michael Burry's Scion Asset Management Bets Against Nvidia and Palantir," November 3, 2025) .

item.description: Norah O'Donnell interviews President Trump on wars, the economy, the border, and tariffs.
item.content:encoded: 60 Minutes Trump Interview Try being president for a day. Try running for any political office against a contentious and dishonest 4th estate. Try representing ungrateful people. Try waking up every day knowing so many people hate you but haven’t even met you. Then, try answering to Norah O'Donnell: Full CBS Transcript (official) Trump: I solved eight conflicts and saved (how many?) lives. (we had nine wars on our planet. I solved eight of 'em.) Norah: But what about Russia? (Who's tougher to deal with, Vladimir Putin or Xi Jinping?) Trump: I set economic records in nine months with S&P at all-time highs. (By the way, the stock market just hit-- perfect timing for your show, just hit an all-time high.) Norah: But what about people without a 401(k)? (But for people that don't have 401(k)s, who are not invested in the stock market) Trump: I closed the border to protect American workers. (We had an open border. Now we have a border that's, as you know, absolutely shut) Norah: But what about the brutality of ICE raids? (Have some of these raids gone too far?) item.title: Nimble Kei
item.description: Oregon Senate Bill 1213 aims to legalize the registration and on-road use of Kei trucks, making Oregon the 31st state to permit these efficient, affordable utility vehicles. The bipartisan bill add…
item.content:encoded: Nimble Kei Trucks Oregon lawmakers introduced Senate Bill 1213, a bipartisan effort to legalize the on-road use of Kei trucks, positioning the state as the 31st to allow these compact Japanese utility vehicles on public roads. If passed, the bill would provide flexibility for individuals and small businesses seeking cost-effective alternatives to full-size trucks. Popular Kei Truck Models Suzuki Carry - A versatile mini truck known for durability and off-road capability. Daihatsu Hijet - Compact and reliable, often used for urban delivery. Honda Acty - Fuel-efficient with good ground clearance for varied terrains. Subaru Sambar - Features rear-engine design for better traction. Mitsubishi Minicab - Affordable and simple maintenance. Mazda Scrum - Badged version of the Suzuki Carry, popular in imports. What Are Kei Trucks? Kei trucks, also known as Japanese mini trucks, are lightweight utility vehicles originally manufactured in Japan. They feature small dimensions—typically under 10 feet long and 5 feet wide—and engines of 660cc or less, making them fuel-efficient and ideal for navigating rural roads, job sites, and urban areas. These vehicles are widely used in agriculture, construction, fishing, and municipal services across Asia. In the U.S., they're gaining popularity among farmers, hunters, contractors, and small business owners for their affordability (often $4,000–$15,000) and versatility, serving as alternatives to ATVs, UTVs, and larger pickups. Details of Senate Bill 1213 The bill defines Kei trucks based on size, age, and engine capacity, allowing registration for a standard $63 fee. It establishes a maximum fine of $1,000 for unlawful on-road use, bringing Oregon in line with neighboring states like Washington and Idaho, where Kei trucks are already permitted. “Small businesses, farmers, and Oregonians across our state are asking for practical, cost-effective transportation options,” Sen. Broadman stated. “Kei trucks are nimble, fuel-efficient, and ideal for navigating rural roads, job sites, and tight urban corridors.” States That Ban Kei Trucks As of 2025, 9 states ban Kei trucks on public roads due to safety concerns, size regulations, or lack of compliance with federal standards. If SB 1213 passes, Oregon would join the list of allowing states. Below are the banning states and brief reasons: Connecticut : Bans due to safety standards and vehicle size. Georgia : Recently revoked registrations citing safety risks. Iowa : Prohibits import and registration of non-compliant vehicles. Maryland : Bans based on federal safety regulations. Nevada : Restricts due to emissions and safety concerns. New Jersey : Bans for not meeting FMVSS standards. New Mexico : Prohibits on-road use for safety reasons. Oregon : Currently bans; bill aims to legalize. Vermont : Bans citing vehicle safety and environmental issues. Legalization efforts continue in these states to address safety and utility benefits. Key Companies in the U.S. Market Several U.S.-based companies specialize in importing and selling Kei trucks: Car From Japan : Offers a wide selection of used Kei trucks, including models from Suzuki, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Daihatsu. They handle importation, inspection, and delivery, with prices ranging from $500 to $70,000 depending on condition and mileage. Northwest Mini Trucks : Located in Vancouver, WA, they provide new and used Kei trucks, parts, accessories, and customization services. They emphasize off-road capabilities and offer financing options. Boeki USA : A major importer with warehouses on the East (Paterson, NJ) and West coasts (Vancouver, WA). They focus on high-quality, road-legal vehicles, providing state titling and registration services. These companies report strong demand, with Kei trucks purchased primarily by farmers, hunters, and outdoor enthusiasts, though they're also used in campuses, golf courses, and factories. item.title: Sustainable Abundance
item.description: Tesla's new sustainable abundance mission and Amazon's plan to replace 600,000 jobs with robots highlight a deeper question - who benefits from automation when goods get cheaper but opportunity doe…
item.content:encoded: Sustainable Abundance On one side, the political left frames the rise of AI and robotics as a job-destroying threat . On the other, the right, CEOs, and markets hail it as a source of efficiency, wealth, and abundance . But the real question isn't simply how many jobs are lost or gained - it's what happens after automation makes everything cheaper , when most people no longer own the means of production. Who benefits? And what happens when the gains don't trickle down? The Two Narratives Left-wing: "Robots will destroy jobs, hollowing out the middle class, creating unemployment, inequality, and social instability." Right-wing: "Robots and AI drive productivity, lower costs, raise output, create new markets, and uphold free-market growth." Both perspectives miss a deeper point: productivity gains are inevitable - but the distribution of those gains is what's at stake. Tesla's Mission Shift In its Q3 2025 earnings call , Tesla declared a renewed mission of "sustainable abundance." Tesla's ambition now goes beyond electric vehicles and renewable energy. With projects like its humanoid robot Optimus and full self-driving (FSD), Tesla claims it can usher in a world where poverty is eliminated and advanced services become universally affordable . In plain terms: Tesla is betting that automation and AI will not only replace human labor but make goods and services so cheap that they redefine the social contract. Sources: Tesla Q3 2025 Update Tesla Master Plan Part IV Amazon's Automation Challenge Meanwhile, Amazon is preparing for massive automation in its fulfillment operations. Reports suggest Amazon could avoid hiring 600,000 employees by automating large parts of its operations by around 2033. This isn't just about eliminating jobs - it's about automating role after role so that output rises, costs drop, but the human share of the value chain shrinks . Lower prices may benefit consumers, but what happens to the livelihoods of displaced workers? Source: Amazon's Robotics Plan Could Replace 600,000 Jobs Who Gets the Gains? If automation makes goods and services cheaper , great. But if only a small slice of society owns the automation infrastructure or reaps the capital gains, then the rest of us face cheaper stuff but fewer jobs, lower wages, and weaker bargaining power. Three possible futures: Growth + widely shared ownership → Abundance for many Growth + concentrated ownership → Wealth polarization, social strain No inclusive growth → Political backlash, populism, push for socialism (Mamdani) or protectionism (Trump) The left worries about job loss; the right celebrates efficiency. But the real issue is how the productivity dividend is distributed. The trick is getting everyone a stake via equity, ownership, or new social dividends. Automation and "efficiency" sound like good things - until your job disappears. Then "cheaper goods" don't feel like progress; they feel like a hollow promise. The backlash won't come from anti-tech activists. It'll come from emotional ex-employees and overlooked communities - people left behind by automation's quiet revolution. If productivity gains don't trickle down - or aren't perceived to - voters will reject capitalism as they are doing in NYC. Without broad-based stakes in productivity growth, voters will turn toward systems that promise fairness - even if it means sacrificing efficiency. A Final Thought We're not entering the era of automation ; we're entering the era of distribution . As Tesla pivots to "sustainable abundance" and Amazon rolls out fleets of warehouse robots, we're seeing less jobs and scarcity of opportunity. 1 Let's shift the debate. Not robots vs. jobs . Not efficiency vs. public goods. But: How do we all get a piece of the pie when the pie gets bigger? See employment trends showing nonfarm payroll growth slowing from +120k in March to just +22k in August 2025, per FRED data. ↩
